Throughout, $m \in \mathbb{N}$ with $m \ge 1$, and vector-valued functions, their
components and their limits are as in
[[def-vector-valued-functions-limits-and-continuity]].

### The derivative

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $f : A \to \mathbb{R}^{m}$ and let $c \in A$ be
a **limit point of $A$** ([[def-limit-point-r]]). The **difference quotient of
$f$ at $c$** is the vector-valued function

$$q_{f,c} : A \setminus \{c\} \to \mathbb{R}^{m}, \qquad q_{f,c}(x) \;:=\; \frac{1}{x - c}\,\bigl(f(x) - f(c)\bigr),$$

the scalar multiple being that of the vector space $\mathbb{R}^{m}$
([[def-function-space]]); the division is legitimate because $x \ne c$ gives
$x - c \ne 0$. As in [[def-derivative]], $c$ is a limit point of
$A \setminus \{c\}$ as well, since a punctured neighbourhood of $c$ omits $c$.

$f$ is **differentiable at $c$** when $\lim_{x \to c} q_{f,c}(x)$ exists in
$\mathbb{R}^{m}$, and then the **derivative** is

$$f'(c) \;:=\; \lim_{x\to c} q_{f,c}(x) \;\in\; \mathbb{R}^{m}.$$

**The notation denotes a single vector.** At most one $L \in \mathbb{R}^{m}$
satisfies the limit condition, as proved in
[[def-vector-valued-functions-limits-and-continuity]]; this is the vector-valued
form of the obligation [[lem-function-limit-unique]] discharges for real-valued
functions and [[lem-metric-limits-unique]] for sequences.

**The intrinsic form is the definition; the componentwise form is a theorem.**
For $i < m$ the $i$-th component of $q_{f,c}(x)$ is
$\bigl(f_i(x)-f_i(c)\bigr)/(x-c)$, which is the real difference quotient of
$f_i$ at $c$ ([[def-derivative]]). So by
[[thm-componentwise-limits-and-continuity]] clause 2:

> $f$ is differentiable at $c$ **if and only if** every $f_i$ is differentiable
> at $c$, and then $f'(c)_i = f_i'(c)$ for every $i<m$.

Nothing below reverses this order of presentation: the intrinsic limit is what is
defined, and the coordinates are read off it.

**Algebra of derivatives.** If $f, g : A \to \mathbb{R}^{m}$ are differentiable at
$c$ and $\lambda \in \mathbb{R}$, then $f + g$ and $\lambda f$ are differentiable
at $c$ with $(f+g)'(c) = f'(c)+g'(c)$ and $(\lambda f)'(c) = \lambda f'(c)$: read
componentwise through the displayed equivalence, these are clauses 1 and 2 of the
published [[thm-algebra-of-derivatives]].

### The integral

Let $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$ with $a < b$ and let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}^{m}$
([[def-interval]]). $f$ is **integrable on $[a,b]$** when every component
$f_i : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ is bounded ([[def-bounded-set]]) and Darboux
integrable in the sense of [[def-darboux-integral]], and then

$$\int_a^b f \;:=\; \text{the function } m \to \mathbb{R} \text{ sending } i \mapsto \int_a^b f_i .$$

**That really is an element of $\mathbb{R}^{m}$.** In this library
$\mathbb{R}^{m}$ is the set of functions $m \to \mathbb{R}$
([[def-function-space]]), not a set of tuples, so the displayed assignment is
literally an element of it; each value $\int_a^b f_i$ is a single real by
[[def-darboux-integral]]. In the standard basis
([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]]) the same object is
$\int_a^b f = \sum_{i<m}\bigl(\int_a^b f_i\bigr)e_i$.

**Oriented limits.** Following [[def-oriented-integral]] componentwise, set

$$\int_a^a f \;:=\; 0 \in \mathbb{R}^{m}, \qquad \int_b^a f \;:=\; -\int_a^b f \quad (a < b),$$

so that $\int_u^v f = -\int_v^u f$ for all $u,v$ in an interval on which $f$ is
integrable. The clauses do not overlap with the case $a<b$, so nothing has to be
checked for consistency, exactly as in [[def-oriented-integral]].

**Linearity.** If $f, g : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}^{m}$ are integrable and
$\lambda,\mu \in \mathbb{R}$ then $\lambda f + \mu g$ is integrable with

$$\int_a^b (\lambda f + \mu g) \;=\; \lambda\int_a^b f + \mu\int_a^b g ,$$

since each side has $i$-th coordinate $\int_a^b(\lambda f_i + \mu g_i)$ and
$\lambda\int_a^b f_i + \mu\int_a^b g_i$ respectively, and those agree by
[[thm-linearity-of-the-integral]].

**Restriction and splitting.** If $f$ is integrable on $[a,b]$ then it is
integrable on every nondegenerate closed subinterval $[c,d]$ with
$a\le c<d\le b$, and for $a<c<b$,
$\int_a^b f = \int_a^c f + \int_c^b f$; both are the componentwise readings of
[[lem-integrability-on-a-subinterval]] and
[[thm-additivity-over-subintervals]], applied to each $f_i$ and reassembled
coordinate by coordinate.

Let $x:I\to A$ be a $C^2$ future timelike worldline with four-velocity $U=dx/d\tau$ and four-acceleration $A=dU/d\tau$ ([[def-sr-four-velocity-and-four-acceleration]], [[def-sr-regular-causal-curve-and-worldline]]), so that $\eta(U,U)=-c^2$ and $\eta(U,A)=0$ ([[thm-sr-proper-time-and-observer-decomposition]]), write $s$ for its given parameter and $\tau$ for its proper-time function, with $\tau'(s)>0$, and let $X:I\to V$ be a $C^1$ field along $x$ ([[def-vector-field-and-section-along-a-smooth-curve]]).

**(a) Fermi–Walker derivative.** The **Fermi–Walker derivative of $X$** is

$$\frac{D_{\mathrm{FW}}X}{d\tau}:=\frac{X'}{\tau'}-\frac{1}{c^2}\bigl(\eta(A,X)U-\eta(U,X)A\bigr),$$

where $X'$ denotes differentiation with respect to $s$ and $dX/d\tau:=X'/\tau'$. Here $\tau'=c^{-1}\sqrt{-\eta(x',x')}>0$ by [[def-sr-four-velocity-and-four-acceleration]]. The derivative $X'$ is the ordinary $V$-valued derivative of $X$, which is the covariant derivative of $X$ along $x$ in the flat model ([[def-flat-covariant-derivative-on-affine-minkowski-space]], clause (d)). The field $X$ is **Fermi–Walker transported along $x$** when $D_{\mathrm{FW}}X/d\tau=0$, that is, when

$$X'=\frac{\tau'}{c^2}\bigl(\eta(A,X)U-\eta(U,X)A\bigr).$$

**(b) The four-velocity is Fermi–Walker transported.** Substituting $X=U$ and using $\eta(A,U)=0$ and $\eta(U,U)=-c^2$ gives $D_{\mathrm{FW}}U/d\tau=U'/\tau'-c^{-2}\bigl(\eta(A,U)U-\eta(U,U)A\bigr)=A-A=0$.

**(c) Comparison with parallel transport.** If $A=0$ on an interval $J\subseteq I$, then on $J$ the Fermi–Walker equation reduces to $X'=0$ and coincides with ordinary parallel transport; if $A$ is not zero, the definition includes exactly the correction that also transports the time leg $U/c$ along the worldline.

**(d) Fermi–Walker transported tetrad.** A **Fermi–Walker transported tetrad along $x$** is a tuple $(E_0,E_1,E_2,E_3)$ of $C^1$ fields along $x$ with $\eta(E_a(s),E_b(s))=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)_{ab}$ at every $s\in I$, $E_0=U/c$ future, and every $E_a$ Fermi–Walker transported along $x$. These pairings make the four vectors a basis: pairing a linear relation with each $E_b$ forces every coefficient to vanish. Existence and uniqueness from initial data are proved in the following lemma; metric preservation is proved in the subsequent theorem. The physical interpretation as a nonrotating spatial frame carried by an accelerated observer is not asserted here; only the transport rule is defined.

Let $(A,V,\eta,C^+)$ be the affine Minkowski space of
[[def-sr-affine-minkowski-model]], with its inertial smooth structure
([[lem-affine-minkowski-charts-form-a-smooth-atlas]], [[def-smooth-manifold]]).
Let $\Omega\subseteq A$ be open, let $r,s\in\mathbb N$, and let
$k\in\mathbb N\cup\{\infty\}$. Empty $\Omega$ is allowed; it has the unique
empty field of each type.

Write $T^{r,s}(V)$ for the real vector space, under pointwise operations, of
multilinear maps $(V^*)^r\times V^s\to\mathbb R$
([[def-type-r-s-tensor-on-a-finite-dimensional-vector-space]],
[[def-algebraic-dual-and-linear-functional]]). Identify $T_pA$ with $V$ by
[[lem-tangent-space-of-affine-minkowski-space-is-v]]. For an inertial frame
$(o;e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$ with chart $x$, let $(e^{*a})$ be its dual basis,
defined by $e^{*a}(e_b)=\delta^a_b$
([[def-dual-family-associated-to-a-basis]]). The components of a map
$T:\Omega\to T^{r,s}(V)$ are

$$T^{a_1\dots a_r}{}_{b_1\dots b_s}(p):=T(p)(e^{*a_1},\dots,e^{*a_r},e_{b_1},\dots,e_{b_s}).$$

A **$\mathcal C^k$ type-$(r,s)$ tensor field on $\Omega$** is such a map for
which each component, regarded as a function of $u=x(p)$ on the open set
$x(\Omega)\subseteq\mathbb R^4$, is of class $C^k$ in the sense of
[[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]; for $k=\infty$ all finite
orders are required.

**Finite-dimensional construction and intrinsic regularity.** Put
$N=4^{r+s}\ge1$, with the component array ordered lexicographically. Every
array of $N$ real numbers defines exactly one tensor: expand each input as
$\alpha_i=\sum_a\alpha_i(e_a)e^{*a}$ and
$v_j=\sum_b e^{*b}(v_j)e_b$, then sum the array entries multiplied by
$\prod_i\alpha_i(e_{a_i})\prod_j e^{*b_j}(v_j)$. This is multilinear and
recovers the array by evaluation on the indicated basis inputs; multilinearity
forces the same formula for any tensor. Thus the component map is a linear
isomorphism $T^{r,s}(V)\to\mathbb R^N$. Pulling back the Euclidean norm gives
a norm on this space ([[def-norm-and-normed-space]]), and every norm makes it
Banach by [[cor-finite-dimensional-normed-spaces-are-banach]]. Any two norms
are equivalent by transporting them to $\mathbb R^N$ and applying
[[thm-all-norms-on-rn-are-equivalent]].

A change of inertial frame expresses each new basis and dual-basis vector as
a constant finite linear combination of the old ones; multilinearity therefore
makes the new component array an invertible constant linear transformation of
the old array. The coordinate precomposition is an invertible affine map by
[[lem-affine-minkowski-charts-form-a-smooth-atlas]]. Finite linear combinations
and affine precomposition preserve $C^k$: each first derivative follows from
[[thm-chain-rule-for-total-derivatives]], and successive derivatives repeat
that rule with constant affine coefficients. Applying the inverse transformations
proves the converse. Hence the definition is independent of frame. Continuous
partials give total derivatives by
[[thm-continuous-partial-derivatives-imply-total-differentiability]], and
induction on order gives the equivalent finite-dimensional Banach-space
$C^k$ definition of [[def-c-k-map-between-banach-spaces]] for $T\circ x^{-1}$.
The norm equivalence inequalities preserve the derivative remainder limits and
continuity of each iterated derivative, so this formulation is also independent
of norm. No definition of a Banach-space map with manifold domain is presumed.

A type-$(0,0)$ field is a **scalar field**, a $C^k$ real-valued function.
A type-$(1,0)$ field is a **vector field**, with the vector $v$ identified with
$\alpha\mapsto\alpha(v)$: conversely a linear functional $Q$ on $V^*$ has
$v=\sum_aQ(e^{*a})e_a$ and $Q(\alpha)=\alpha(v)$. A type-$(0,1)$ field is a
**covector field**, taking values in $V^*$.

Let $(A,V,\eta,C^+)$ be an oriented time-oriented affine Minkowski space
([[def-sr-affine-minkowski-model]]), with orientation fixed as a positive ray of
the determinant line $\Lambda^4V$
([[def-determinant-line-orientation-of-a-finite-dimensional-real-vector-space]])
and with the corresponding class of positively oriented ordered bases of $V$
([[def-orientation-of-a-finite-dimensional-real-vector-space]]); by
[[prop-orientations-and-positive-basis-classes-agree-in-positive-dimension]] the
positive ray selects exactly one such class for $\dim V=4>0$.

An **inertial frame** of the model is a tuple $(o;e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$ consisting
of an event $o\in A$ and an ordered basis $(e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$ of $V$ that is

1. **$\eta$-orthonormal**: $\eta(e_a,e_b)=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)_{ab}$ for all $a,b$ ([[lem-lorentz-form-has-orthonormal-basis]]);
2. **future**: $e_0\in C^+$, i.e. $e_0$ is future timelike; and
3. **positively oriented**: the ordered basis lies in the positive-basis class
   selected by the fixed orientation.

The event $o$ is the **origin** of the frame and $e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3$ are its
**basis vectors**.

**Inertial charts.** For an inertial frame $(o;e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$, define

$$E:\mathbb R^4\longrightarrow V,\qquad E(u):=\sum_{a=0}^3u^ae_a .$$

Then $E$ is a linear isomorphism ([[def-linear-isomorphism-and-invertible-linear-map]]):
it is linear by construction, and it is bijective because
$(e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$ is an ordered basis, every $v\in V$ having exactly one
coordinate list $u$ with $v=\sum_au^ae_a$
([[thm-unique-coordinates-with-respect-to-an-ordered-basis]]). The **inertial
chart** of the frame is the map

$$x:A\longrightarrow\mathbb R^4,\qquad x(p):=E^{-1}(p-o),$$

and its values $x^a(p)$ are the **inertial coordinates of the event $p$** in the
frame. Since $E$ and $v\mapsto p+v$ are bijections, $x$ is a bijection
$A\to\mathbb R^4$; and $x(p)=0$ exactly when $p-o=0_V$, that is, exactly when
$p=o$.

**Transition law.** Let $(o';e'_0,e'_1,e'_2,e'_3)$ be another inertial frame
with chart $x'$, and let $M=(M^b_a)$ be the change-of-basis matrix defined by
$e'_a=\sum_bM^b_ae_b$, a $4\times4$ real matrix that is invertible because both
families are ordered bases. Then $E'(u)=\sum_au^ae'_a=E(Mu)$ for all
$u\in\mathbb R^4$, for the matrix-vector product $Mu$ in the coordinates of the
first frame, because $\sum_au^a\sum_bM^b_ae_b=\sum_b(\sum_aM^b_au^a)e_b$; hence
$E'=E\circ M$ and $E'^{-1}=M^{-1}\circ E^{-1}$, so for every event $p$,

$$x'(p)=M^{-1}\bigl(x(p)-x(o')\bigr)=M^{-1}x(p)-M^{-1}x(o') .$$

In particular the transition between two inertial charts is an affine map of
$\mathbb R^4$ with invertible linear part $M^{-1}$ and constant part
$-M^{-1}x(o')$, and it is a bijection of $\mathbb R^4$ with inverse
$u\mapsto Mu+x(o')$, which is the transition in the reverse direction.

**The inertial atlas.** The **inertial atlas** of the model is the family of
all inertial frames together with their inertial charts. Its charts are
available at every event by [[lem-future-oriented-inertial-frames-exist]], which
supplies for every $o\in A$ an inertial frame with origin $o$; and any two of
its charts are related by the affine transition displayed above.

Let $c > 0$ and let $x : I \to A$ be a $C^{1}$ future timelike worldline with
proper-time function $\tau$ and inverse $\rho$ of
[[def-sr-proper-time]] and [[lem-sr-proper-time-parametrization]].

**(a) Four-velocity.** The **four-velocity** of $x$ is the map $U : I \to V$
defined by

$$U(s) := \frac{x'(s)}{\tau'(s)} = \frac{c\,x'(s)}{\sqrt{-\eta(x'(s),x'(s))}} ;$$

equivalently, $U(s)$ is the tangent at parameter value $s$ of the proper-time
parametrized worldline $x \circ \rho$, read at the proper-time parameter
$\tau(s)$: by clause (iv) of [[lem-sr-proper-time-parametrization]],
$(x \circ \rho)'(\tau(s)) = x'(s)/\tau'(s) = U(s)$. The map $U$ is continuous,
$U(s)$ is future timelike for every $s \in I$, and $U$ does not depend on the
base point chosen for $\tau$ (changing the base point adds a constant to
$\tau$).

**(b) Four-acceleration.** If $x$ is $C^{2}$, that is, $x'$ is differentiable
with continuous derivative ([[def-sr-regular-causal-curve-and-worldline]]), the
**four-acceleration** of $x$ is the map $A : I \to V$ defined by

$$A(s) := \frac{U'(s)}{\tau'(s)} = \frac{c\,U'(s)}{\sqrt{-\eta(x'(s),x'(s))}} ;$$

equivalently, $A(s)$ is the derivative with respect to the proper-time parameter
of the four-velocity along the worldline: by the chain rule,
$A(s) = (U \circ \rho)'(\tau(s))$. The map $A$ is continuous.

**(c) Observer.** The **dimensionless four-velocity** of $x$ is $u := U/c$. A
**point observer** of the model at an event is a future unit timelike vector
$n \in V$, $\eta(n,n) = -1$ ([[def-causal-classification-of-lorentz-vectors]],
[[def-time-orientation-and-future-causal-sets]]); the four-velocity of the
observer's own worldline, the straight future timelike line through the event
with tangent $cn$, is $cn$ at each of its events.

**(d) Names and scope.** The names four-velocity and four-acceleration are the
model's names for $U$ and $A$; the physical interpretation, including the units
in which $U$ and $A$ are measured, is supplied with the coordinate conventions
of the framework and is not part of the affine geometry. The definition makes no
claim that $U$ has norm $-c^{2}$ or that $A$ is orthogonal to $U$; those are
proved in [[thm-sr-proper-time-and-observer-decomposition]].

Let $m\ge1$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ be open, and let $f:U\to\mathbb R$. A **multi-index** is $\alpha=(\alpha_0,\ldots,\alpha_{m-1})\in\mathbb N^m$. Put

$$|\alpha|:=\sum_{i<m}\alpha_i,\qquad \alpha!:=\prod_{i<m}\alpha_i!,\qquad h^\alpha:=\prod_{i<m}h_i^{\alpha_i}\quad(h\in\mathbb R^m).$$

Here $|\alpha|$ and $\alpha!$ use the natural-number sum and product of [[def-nat-finite-sum-and-product]], and $n!$ is the factorial of [[def-factorial-and-falling-factorial]]. By contrast, $h^\alpha$ is the finite product in $\mathbb R$ of [[def-finite-sum]], with the natural exponents interpreted by [[def-integer-power]]. For the zero multi-index $0$, set $D^0f:=f$. For nonzero $\alpha$, write

$$D^\alpha f:=\partial_0^{\alpha_0}\cdots\partial_{m-1}^{\alpha_{m-1}}f$$

for this displayed, canonical order whenever it exists. Coordinate partial derivatives have the meaning fixed in [[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]].

For $k\in\mathbb N$, $f$ is of class $C^k$ on $U$ when, for every word $(i_1,\ldots,i_r)$ of coordinate indices with $0\le r\le k$, the iterated derivative $\partial_{i_r}\cdots\partial_{i_1}f$ exists and is continuous on $U$; the word of length $0$ denotes $f$. Thus this definition does **not** presuppose that differently ordered derivatives are equal. Equality of their values is a later theorem under these regularity hypotheses.

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $c \in A$ be a limit point of $A$
([[def-limit-point-r]]), let $f, g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at $c$
([[def-derivative]]) and let $\alpha \in \mathbb{R}$. Then:

1. $f + g$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(f+g)'(c) = f'(c) + g'(c)$;
2. $\alpha f$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(\alpha f)'(c) = \alpha f'(c)$;
3. $fg$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(fg)'(c) = f'(c)g(c) + f(c)g'(c)$;
4. if $g(c) \ne 0$ then, writing $A_0 := \{\, x \in A : g(x) \ne 0 \,\}$, the
   point $c$ lies in $A_0$ and is a limit point of $A_0$, the quotient
   $(f/g)|_{A_0} : A_0 \to \mathbb{R}$, $x \mapsto f(x)/g(x)$, is differentiable
   at $c$ as a function on $A_0$, and
   $$\bigl((f/g)|_{A_0}\bigr)'(c) \;=\; \frac{f'(c)\,g(c) - f(c)\,g'(c)}{g(c)^{2}} .$$

Each claim asserts two things: that the derivative on the left exists, and that
it has the stated value. Both are proved.

**Why claim 4 is stated on $A_0$.** The function $f/g$ is not defined where $g$
vanishes, and $g$ may vanish at points of $A$ far from $c$; restricting to $A_0$
is forced. That the restriction still has $c$ as a limit point, so that a
derivative there means anything at all, is not free either, and it is the last
claim of [[lem-sign-preservation-near-a-limit]] applied to $g$. The hypothesis
is $g(c) \ne 0$, not "$g$ vanishes nowhere".

**Everything is proved through
[[thm-caratheodory-characterisation]].** No difference quotient is estimated and
no limit theorem beyond continuity is used, so no choice principle is spent.
The four identities are four algebraic rearrangements of an increment, each
followed by a reading of [[thm-algebra-of-continuous-functions]].

Let $I=[a,b]\subseteq\mathbb R$ be a compact interval, let
$C:I\to M_n(\mathbb R)$ be continuous, let $t_0\in I$, and let
$Y_0\in M_n(\mathbb R)$. Then the linear matrix initial value problem

$$Y'(t)=C(t)Y(t),\qquad Y(t_0)=Y_0,$$

has a unique solution on all of $I$.

Let $m\ge1$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ be open, and let $f:U\to\mathbb R$. A **multi-index** is $\alpha=(\alpha_0,\ldots,\alpha_{m-1})\in\mathbb N^m$. Put

$$|\alpha|:=\sum_{i<m}\alpha_i,\qquad \alpha!:=\prod_{i<m}\alpha_i!,\qquad h^\alpha:=\prod_{i<m}h_i^{\alpha_i}\quad(h\in\mathbb R^m).$$

Here $|\alpha|$ and $\alpha!$ use the natural-number sum and product of [[def-nat-finite-sum-and-product]], and $n!$ is the factorial of [[def-factorial-and-falling-factorial]]. By contrast, $h^\alpha$ is the finite product in $\mathbb R$ of [[def-finite-sum]], with the natural exponents interpreted by [[def-integer-power]]. For the zero multi-index $0$, set $D^0f:=f$. For nonzero $\alpha$, write

$$D^\alpha f:=\partial_0^{\alpha_0}\cdots\partial_{m-1}^{\alpha_{m-1}}f$$

for this displayed, canonical order whenever it exists. Coordinate partial derivatives have the meaning fixed in [[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]].

For $k\in\mathbb N$, $f$ is of class $C^k$ on $U$ when, for every word $(i_1,\ldots,i_r)$ of coordinate indices with $0\le r\le k$, the iterated derivative $\partial_{i_r}\cdots\partial_{i_1}f$ exists and is continuous on $U$; the word of length $0$ denotes $f$. Thus this definition does **not** presuppose that differently ordered derivatives are equal. Equality of their values is a later theorem under these regularity hypotheses.

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $c \in A$ be a limit point of $A$
([[def-limit-point-r]]), let $f, g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at $c$
([[def-derivative]]) and let $\alpha \in \mathbb{R}$. Then:

1. $f + g$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(f+g)'(c) = f'(c) + g'(c)$;
2. $\alpha f$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(\alpha f)'(c) = \alpha f'(c)$;
3. $fg$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(fg)'(c) = f'(c)g(c) + f(c)g'(c)$;
4. if $g(c) \ne 0$ then, writing $A_0 := \{\, x \in A : g(x) \ne 0 \,\}$, the
   point $c$ lies in $A_0$ and is a limit point of $A_0$, the quotient
   $(f/g)|_{A_0} : A_0 \to \mathbb{R}$, $x \mapsto f(x)/g(x)$, is differentiable
   at $c$ as a function on $A_0$, and
   $$\bigl((f/g)|_{A_0}\bigr)'(c) \;=\; \frac{f'(c)\,g(c) - f(c)\,g'(c)}{g(c)^{2}} .$$

Each claim asserts two things: that the derivative on the left exists, and that
it has the stated value. Both are proved.

**Why claim 4 is stated on $A_0$.** The function $f/g$ is not defined where $g$
vanishes, and $g$ may vanish at points of $A$ far from $c$; restricting to $A_0$
is forced. That the restriction still has $c$ as a limit point, so that a
derivative there means anything at all, is not free either, and it is the last
claim of [[lem-sign-preservation-near-a-limit]] applied to $g$. The hypothesis
is $g(c) \ne 0$, not "$g$ vanishes nowhere".

**Everything is proved through
[[thm-caratheodory-characterisation]].** No difference quotient is estimated and
no limit theorem beyond continuity is used, so no choice principle is spent.
The four identities are four algebraic rearrangements of an increment, each
followed by a reading of [[thm-algebra-of-continuous-functions]].

Let $A, B \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ with
$g[A] \subseteq B$ and let $f : B \to \mathbb{R}$, so that the composite
$f \circ g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ is defined. Let $c \in A$ be a limit point of
$A$ ([[def-limit-point-r]]) at which $g$ is differentiable
([[def-derivative]]), put $b := g(c)$, and suppose $b$ is a limit point of $B$
at which $f$ is differentiable. Then $f \circ g$ is differentiable at $c$ and

$$(f \circ g)'(c) \;=\; f'\bigl(g(c)\bigr)\,g'(c) .$$

**Both limit-point hypotheses are needed, and neither is automatic.** That $c$
is a limit point of $A$ is what makes $g'(c)$ and $(f \circ g)'(c)$ defined
symbols; that $b = g(c)$ is a limit point of $B$ is what makes $f'(b)$ one.
Nothing forces the second: $g$ may be differentiable at $c$ and send $c$ to an
isolated point of $B$, and there $f'(b)$ is not defined and the formula asserts
nothing.

**No case analysis appears anywhere.** The naive difference-quotient proof
writes $\frac{f(g(x)) - f(g(c))}{g(x) - g(c)} \cdot \frac{g(x) - g(c)}{x - c}$
and then has to say what happens where $g(x) = g(c)$, which may occur at points
arbitrarily close to $c$. Carathéodory's factorisation never divides by the
inner increment, so the difficulty does not arise.

Throughout, $\mathbb{R}$ is the complete ordered field
([[def-complete-ordered-field]]), neighbourhoods are those of
[[def-neighbourhood-r]] and limit points those of [[def-limit-point-r]].

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $f : A \to \mathbb{R}$ and let $c \in A$ be a
**limit point of $A$**. The **difference quotient of $f$ at $c$** is the function

$$q_{f,c} : A \setminus \{c\} \to \mathbb{R}, \qquad q_{f,c}(x) := \frac{f(x) - f(c)}{x - c} .$$

The division is legitimate at every point of the domain, since $x \ne c$ gives
$x - c \ne 0$.

**The point $c$ is a limit point of $A \setminus \{c\}$, not merely of $A$.**
For every real $\varepsilon > 0$ the punctured neighbourhood
$N^{*}_{\varepsilon}(c)$ omits $c$, so

$$N^{*}_{\varepsilon}(c) \cap A \;=\; N^{*}_{\varepsilon}(c) \cap (A \setminus \{c\}) ,$$

and the left-hand side is nonempty because $c$ is a limit point of $A$. So
$q_{f,c}$ is a function on a set having $c$ as a limit point, and
$\lim_{x \to c} q_{f,c}(x)$ is a notion that [[def-function-limit]] defines.

$f$ is **differentiable at $c$** when that limit exists, and then the
**derivative of $f$ at $c$** is

$$f'(c) \;:=\; \lim_{x \to c} q_{f,c}(x) \;=\; \lim_{x \to c} \frac{f(x) - f(c)}{x - c} .$$

**Two obligations are carried by that notation, and both are discharged here.**

1. **Uniqueness.** Writing $f'(c)$ treats the right-hand side as a name for a
   single real number. That is legitimate: $c$ is a limit point of the domain
   $A \setminus \{c\}$ of $q_{f,c}$, so at most one real can satisfy the
   $\varepsilon$-$\delta$ condition, by [[lem-function-limit-unique]] applied to
   $q_{f,c}$. Two reals both meeting the condition are therefore equal, and the
   symbol denotes.
2. **Meaningfulness.** The hypothesis that $c$ is a limit point of $A$ is not
   decoration. At an **isolated** point of $A$ the punctured condition
   $0 < |x - c| < \delta$ is met by no point of the domain at all, so the
   $\varepsilon$-$\delta$ formula is satisfied vacuously by *every* real at
   once; this is why [[def-function-limit]] leaves the limit undefined there,
   and it is why this library defines $f'(c)$ only at a limit point of $A$. At
   an isolated point of its domain a function is neither differentiable nor
   non-differentiable here: the question is not posed.

**The limit sees only $A \setminus \{c\}$, so how the difference quotient is
extended to $c$ is irrelevant.** Let $Q : A \to \mathbb{R}$ agree with
$q_{f,c}$ at every point of $A \setminus \{c\}$, and let $L \in \mathbb{R}$.
Then $\lim_{x \to c} Q(x) = L$ if and only if $\lim_{x \to c} q_{f,c}(x) = L$.
Both conditions read: for every real $\varepsilon > 0$ there is a real
$\delta > 0$ such that every point $x$ of the relevant domain with
$0 < |x - c| < \delta$ satisfies $|{\cdot} - L| < \varepsilon$
([[def-function-limit]]). The clause $0 < |x - c|$ removes $x = c$ from both
quantifiers, so in both cases the points quantified over are exactly the
$x \in A \setminus \{c\}$ with $0 < |x - c| < \delta$, at which $Q$ and
$q_{f,c}$ take the same value. The two conditions are the same condition.

**Differentiability on a set.** For $S \subseteq A$, $f$ is **differentiable on
$S$** when it is differentiable at every $c \in S$; implicit in that phrase is
that every point of $S$ is a limit point of $A$. $f$ is **differentiable** when
it is differentiable on the whole of $A$.

**Restriction of the domain.** Let $B \subseteq A$, let $c \in B$ and suppose
$c$ is a limit point of $B$. If $f$ is differentiable at $c$, then so is the
restriction $f|_B : B \to \mathbb{R}$, and

$$(f|_B)'(c) \;=\; f'(c) .$$

Indeed $B \setminus \{c\} \subseteq A \setminus \{c\}$; the displayed identity
of punctured neighbourhoods above, applied to $B$, shows that $c$ is a limit
point of $B \setminus \{c\}$; the difference quotient $q_{f|_B, c}$ is the
restriction of $q_{f,c}$ to $B \setminus \{c\}$, since $f|_B(c) = f(c)$; and
claim 2 of [[lem-limit-is-local]] carries the limit to that restriction.

**Every point of a nondegenerate interval is a limit point of it.** Let
$J \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ be order-convex ([[def-interval]]) with at least two
elements and let $p \in J$. Choose $q \in J$ with $q \ne p$, and let a real
$\varepsilon > 0$ be given. If $p < q$, put $y := p + \tfrac{1}{2}\min\{\varepsilon,\ q - p\}$;
then $p < y$, and $y - p \le \tfrac{1}{2}(q-p) < q - p$, so $p < y < q$ and
order-convexity gives $y \in J$, while $0 < |y - p| < \varepsilon$. If $q < p$,
the point $y := p - \tfrac{1}{2}\min\{\varepsilon,\ p - q\}$ serves in the same
way. So $N^{*}_{\varepsilon}(p) \cap J \ne \varnothing$ for every real
$\varepsilon > 0$, that is, $p$ is a limit point of $J$
([[def-limit-point-r]]).

Consequently, for $f$ defined on a nondegenerate interval $I$, the symbol
$f'(c)$ is meaningful at **every** $c \in I$, endpoints included. At an endpoint
the difference quotient is taken over the points of $I$ lying on the one side
that is available, so what other texts call a one-sided derivative is, here,
simply the derivative of $f$ on $I$.

Throughout, $\mathbb{R}$ is the complete ordered field
([[def-complete-ordered-field]], [[def-ordered-field]]) with its order
([[def-real-order]]).

A subset $I \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ is **order-convex** when

$$x, y \in I \text{ and } x \le z \le y \;\Longrightarrow\; z \in I .$$

The **intervals** of $\mathbb{R}$ are the sets of the following nine forms, where
$a, b \in \mathbb{R}$:

| | bounded forms | | one-sided and full forms |
|---|---|---|---|
| $(a,b)$ | $\{x : a < x < b\}$ | $(a,\infty)$ | $\{x : a < x\}$ |
| $[a,b]$ | $\{x : a \le x \le b\}$ | $[a,\infty)$ | $\{x : a \le x\}$ |
| $[a,b)$ | $\{x : a \le x < b\}$ | $(-\infty,b)$ | $\{x : x < b\}$ |
| $(a,b]$ | $\{x : a < x \le b\}$ | $(-\infty,b]$ | $\{x : x \le b\}$ |
| | | $(-\infty,\infty)$ | $\mathbb{R}$ |

An interval is **open** when both of its written endpoints are excluded, that is
for the forms $(a,b)$, $(a,\infty)$, $(-\infty,b)$ and $(-\infty,\infty)$; it is
**closed** when both written endpoints are included, that is for $[a,b]$,
$[a,\infty)$, $(-\infty,b]$ and $(-\infty,\infty)$. The forms $[a,b)$ and
$(a,b]$ are **half-open**.

**The symbols $\pm\infty$ are notation and not elements of $\mathbb{R}$.** They
mark which side carries no endpoint condition at all; the five forms in the right
column are defined by the displayed conditions on $x$ alone, and no arithmetic is
ever performed with $\infty$. This is the same refusal to extend $\mathbb{R}$
silently that [[rem-sup-conventions]] records for suprema.

**Every one of the nine forms is order-convex.** Each is defined by a conjunction
of at most two conditions, each of the shape $a < x$, $a \le x$, $x < b$ or
$x \le b$, and each such condition is inherited by an intermediate point: if
$a < x$ and $x \le z$ then $a < z$, and if $z \le y$ and $y < b$ then $z < b$,
by transitivity of the order ([[def-ordered-field]]). Applying this to whichever
one or two conditions define the form in question gives $z \in I$ whenever
$x, y \in I$ and $x \le z \le y$.

**Bounded intervals.** An interval is **bounded** ([[def-bounded-set]]) exactly
when it is of one of the four forms in the left column: for those, $a$ is a lower
bound and $b$ an upper bound. The other five forms are unbounded, on the side or
sides written with $\infty$; the verification is in the remarks below.

**Nondegeneracy.** An interval is **degenerate** when it has at most one element,
and **nondegenerate** when it has at least two. For the four bounded forms with
endpoints $a$ and $b$:

- $[a,b]$ is nonempty exactly when $a \le b$, and it is nondegenerate exactly
  when $a < b$. It is the singleton $\{a\}$ when $a = b$.
- $(a,b)$, $[a,b)$ and $(a,b]$ are nonempty exactly when $a < b$, and then each
  is nondegenerate.

The only assertion here that is not immediate from the defining conditions is
that $a < b$ makes $(a,b)$ nonempty with at least two points. It holds because
$a < (a+b)/2 < b$, which follows from $a < b$ by adding $a$, respectively $b$, to
both sides and halving ([[def-ordered-field]]); repeating the halving inside
$(a, (a+b)/2)$ produces a second point.

**Closed bounded intervals.** These are the sets $[a,b]$ with $a \le b$, which is
exactly the condition making them nonempty. They are the intervals the nested
interval property is stated for, and the phrase *closed bounded interval* always
carries the hypothesis $a \le b$ in this library.

**Length.** The **length** of a bounded interval presented by its endpoints
$a \le b$ is

$$\ell = b - a \;\ge\; 0 .$$

Length is attached to the presentation by endpoints and is not recovered from the
set: $(a,b)$, $[a,b)$ and $(a,b]$ are all empty when $a = b$, and so is
$(c,c)$ for any other $c$, while each of these presentations has length $0$, so
nothing inconsistent arises; but the endpoints are named explicitly at every
point where a length is used in this library, and never inferred from the set.
Unbounded intervals are assigned no length.

derivations.claim: Work in the inertial chart of one inertial frame and identify $V$ with $\mathbb R^4$ by its ordered basis, so that fields along $x$ are $\mathbb R^4$-valued functions; by [F1] and [F2] the transport equation is the linear system $X'=C(s)X$ with coefficient matrix $C^a{}_b(s)=\tau'(s)c^{-2}(U^a(s)A_b(s)-A^a(s)U_b(s))$. By [F3] the entries of $C$ are continuous when $x$ is $C^2$, so $C:I\to M_4(\mathbb R)$ is a continuous matrix-valued function on the interval $I$; and if $x$ is $C^k$ with $k\ge2$ then $U$ is $C^{k-1}$ and $A$ is $C^{k-2}$, so $C$ is $C^{k-2}$.

Fundamental solution on $I$: by [F7], every point $s\in I$ lies in a nondegenerate compact interval $K\subseteq I$ containing $\tau_0$; if $s$ is interior to $I$, choose $K$ with $s$ interior to $K$, and use the corresponding one-sided endpoint reading otherwise. Such intervals exist because $I$ is order-convex and has at least two points; enlarge the segment between $s$ and $\tau_0$ using another point when necessary. By [F4], $\Phi'=C\Phi$, $\Phi(\tau_0)=I_4$ has a unique solution on every such $K$. On the intersection of two intervals the solutions agree by [F4] if the intersection is nondegenerate, and by their common initial value if it is the singleton $\{\tau_0\}$. Thus $\Phi(s)$ is their unique common value. Using a compact interval containing a neighbourhood of each interior $s$, or a relative one-sided neighbourhood at an included endpoint, shows that $\Phi$ is $C^1$, $\Phi'=C\Phi$ and $\Phi(\tau_0)=I_4$ on $I$. Unique values define the map without a choice principle.

Uniqueness of the vector initial value problem: let $\tilde X:I\to V$ solve $X'=CX$ with $\tilde X(\tau_0)=X_0$. Form the matrix $\Psi$ whose first column is $\tilde X$ and whose other columns are zero, and let $\Psi_0$ be the corresponding constant initial matrix with first column $X_0$. Then $\Psi'=C\Psi$ and $\Psi(\tau_0)=\Psi_0$. The matrix $\Phi\Psi_0$ satisfies the same problem by step 2.1 and the product rule with constant right factor. Uniqueness in [F4] on every nondegenerate compact subinterval containing the initial point gives $\Psi=\Phi\Psi_0$ on $I$. Their first columns therefore give $\tilde X=\Phi X_0$, proving uniqueness.

Existence and linearity: with $\Phi$ as in step 2.1 and $X:=\Phi X_0$, the field $X$ is $C^1$, satisfies $X'=\Phi'X_0=C\Phi X_0=CX$ and $X(\tau_0)=\Phi(\tau_0)X_0=X_0$; hence $X$ is a $C^1$ solution on $I$ of the transport equation with initial value $X_0$, and step 3.1 shows that it is the only one. Since matrix multiplication is linear in its second factor, the map $X_0\mapsto X=\Phi X_0$ is linear from $V$ to the space of $C^1$ fields along $x$ satisfying the transport equation.

Regularity: assume $x$ is $C^k$ with $k\ge2$, so that $C$ is $C^{k-2}$ by step 1.1, and let $X$ be the solution of step 4.1, which satisfies $X'=CX$. For $k=2$ the $C^1$ conclusion is already step 4.1. For $k\ge3$, one proves by induction on $j=1,\dots,k-2$ that $X$ is $C^j$: for $j=1$ this is step 4.1; if $X$ is $C^j$ with $j\le k-2$, then the product $CX$ is $C^j$ by [F6], because $C$ is $C^{k-2}$ and $j\le k-2$; hence $X'=CX$ is $C^j$, so $X$ is $C^{j+1}$. The induction ends at $j=k-2$, giving that $X$ is $C^{k-1}$.

The initial-tetrad clause: let $E_0(\tau_0),\dots,E_3(\tau_0)$ be a tetrad at $x(\tau_0)$ with $E_0(\tau_0)=U(\tau_0)/c$ ([[def-sr-chart-tetrad-and-congruence-distinction]]). By steps 4.1 and 3.1, for each $a$ there is exactly one $C^1$ Fermi–Walker transported field $E_a:I\to V$ along $x$ with $E_a(\tau_0)$ equal to the prescribed value. For $a=0$ the field $U/c$ is $C^1$, satisfies $D_{\mathrm{FW}}(U/c)/d\tau=0$ by clause (b) of [[def-sr-fermi-walker-transport]], and has the same initial value $U(\tau_0)/c$; by the uniqueness of step 3.1, $E_0=U/c$. Hence there is a unique tuple of Fermi–Walker transported fields with the prescribed initial values, and its time component is the four-velocity up to the factor $1/c$.

Conclusion: step 4.1 and step 3.1 establish existence, uniqueness and linearity in the initial value for the $C^1$ solution of the Fermi–Walker transport equation on $I$; step 5.1 establishes the $C^{k-1}$ regularity when the worldline is $C^k$ with $k\ge2$ (in particular $C^1$ when $k=2$); and step 5.2 establishes the uniquely determined tuple with prescribed tetrad initial values and identifies its time component as $U/c$. Whether such a tuple remains a tetrad at every time is not claimed here and is proved in the following item.

boundaries.evidence: The initial value $X_0\in V$ and the initial time $\tau_0\in I$ are given data; the solution exists on the whole parameter interval, so no empty domain arises. This disposition is part of the statement.

The zero initial value is covered: linearity of the solution map sends $X_0=0$ to the zero field, which satisfies the transport equation; the uniqueness clause identifies it. This disposition is part of the statement.
The solution map is linear and the uniqueness statement is for one prescribed initial vector at one initial time; the tetrad corollary applies it once per leg.
The statement sets up a linear transport equation with displayed coefficient fields; no division by a possibly vanishing quantity and no degeneracy of the coefficient data occurs.
The initial time $\tau_0$ is a given point of the parameter interval $I$, and the solution is asserted as a $C^1$ field on all of $I$; the endpoint values are therefore covered by the statement.
The solution is produced from the prescribed initial vector and the linear equation; no selection of initial data from a family is made. This disposition is part of the statement.

The forward direction is the existence clause: the displayed transport equation with the prescribed initial value has a solution, constructed so that the initial condition holds. This disposition is part of the statement.
The reverse direction is the uniqueness clause of the statement: any two $C^1$ fields satisfying the transport equation with the same initial value coincide.

risk_review.notes: Read Statement, F1–F7, all seven steps and the full published compact-interval matrix-ODE proof as prerequisite context. The generic coefficient C=tau′ c^(−2)(U tensor A-flat−A tensor U-flat) is continuous for C2 worldlines, and C^(k−2) for Ck. The worldline domain has at least two points. Every point and initial parameter lies in a nondegenerate compact interval; overlapping solutions agree by the ODE uniqueness theorem, or at the common singleton initial point by the initial value. Let $c > 0$ and let $(A,V,\eta,C^{+})$ be an oriented time-oriented affine
Minkowski space ([[def-sr-affine-minkowski-model]]).

**(a) Norm of the four-velocity.** Let $x : I \to A$ be a $C^{1}$ future
timelike worldline with four-velocity $U$
([[def-sr-four-velocity-and-four-acceleration]]). Then
$\eta(U(s),U(s)) = -c^{2}$ for every $s \in I$; equivalently the dimensionless
four-velocity $u = U/c$ satisfies $\eta(u,u) = -1$, and $U(s)$ is future
timelike. Thus the dimensionless four-velocity lies on the future unit
hyperboloid $\{v \in C^{+}:\eta(v,v)=-1\}$.

**(b) Orthogonality of the four-acceleration.** If $x$ is $C^{2}$ at $s$, then
$\eta(U(s),A(s)) = 0$: the four-acceleration has no component along the
four-velocity; if in addition $A(s) \ne 0$, then $A(s)$ is spacelike.

**(c) Rest space and projection.** Let $n \in V$ be future unit timelike,
$\eta(n,n) = -1$, and put $n^{\perp} := \{\,v \in V : \eta(n,v) = 0\,\}$
([[def-lorentz-orthogonality-and-orthogonal-complement]]). Then $n^{\perp}$ is a
3-dimensional linear subspace of $V$, the restriction of $\eta$ to $n^{\perp}$
is positive definite, and the map $h : V \to V$, $h(v) := v + \eta(n,v)\,n$, is
linear, idempotent with $h \circ h = h$, has image $n^{\perp}$ and kernel
$\operatorname{span}(n)$, satisfies $h(n) = 0$ and $\eta(n,h(v)) = 0$ for all
$v \in V$, and every $v \in V$ has the unique decomposition
$v = -\eta(n,v)\,n + h(v)$. Moreover $|w| := \sqrt{\eta(w,w)}$ defines a norm
on $n^{\perp}$.

**(d) Relative velocity and Lorentz factor.** Let $n$ and $u$ be future unit
timelike vectors, put $\gamma := -\eta(n,u)$ and $w := c\,h(u)/\gamma$. Then
$\gamma \ge 1$, $w$ lies in $n^{\perp}$,
$u = \gamma\,(n + w/c)$, $|w|^{2} = c^{2}(1-\gamma^{-2}) < c^{2}$,
$\gamma = (1-|w|^{2}/c^{2})^{-1/2}$, and $\gamma = 1$ if and only if $u = n$.
The vector $w$ is the velocity of a worldline with four-velocity $cu$ relative
to the observer $n$, and $\gamma$ is its Lorentz factor.

**(e) Coordinate form.** Let $(o;e_0,\dots,e_3)$ be an inertial frame and let
$y$ be a $C^{1}$ future timelike worldline whose inertial coordinates are
$t \mapsto (ct,r(t))$, with coordinate velocity $w(t) := r'(t)$ in
$\mathbb{R}^{3}$ and, when $y$ is $C^{2}$, coordinate acceleration
$a(t) := w'(t)$. Then $|w(t)| < c$, the four-velocity is
$U = \gamma_w\,(c,w)$ with $\gamma_w := (1-|w|^{2}/c^{2})^{-1/2}$, and the
four-acceleration is $A = \gamma_w\,\frac{d}{dt}\bigl(\gamma_w(c,w)\bigr)$, so
that

$$A^{0} = \gamma_w^{4}\,\frac{w \cdot a}{c}, \qquad A_{\mathrm{vec}} = \gamma_w^{2}\,a + \gamma_w^{4}\,\frac{(w \cdot a)\,w}{c^{2}} ;$$

consequently
$\eta(A,A) = \gamma_w^{4}|a|^{2} + \gamma_w^{6}(w \cdot a)^{2}/c^{2} \ge 0$,
with $\eta(A,A) = 0$ if and only if $a = 0$, and $\eta(U,A) = 0$. For the
observer $n = e_0$ of the chart, clauses (c) and (d) specialize to
$\gamma = \gamma_w$ and $w_{\mathrm{rel}} = (0,w)$ in the frame coordinates, identified with $w$ via the spatial basis.

**(f) Scope.** The statement is a theorem about the affine Minkowski model with
a fixed positive constant $c$; it asserts no clock reading and identifies no
physical four-velocity. No choice principle is used.

Let $(V,\eta)$ be a Lorentz vector space of signature $(-,+,+,+)$
([[def-lorentz-form-and-inertia]]). Two vectors $u,v\in V$ are
**$\eta$-orthogonal**, written $u\perp v$, when $\eta(u,v)=0$. For a subset
$S\subseteq V$ the **orthogonal complement** of $S$ is

$$S^{\perp}:=\{v\in V:\eta(v,s)=0\text{ for every }s\in S\},$$

and for a vector $u$ one writes $u^{\perp}:=\{u\}^{\perp}$.

**Elementary properties.** For every subset $S\subseteq V$:

- $S^{\perp}$ is a linear subspace of $V$: if $v,w\in S^{\perp}$ and
  $\lambda\in\mathbb R$, then for every $s\in S$ bilinearity gives
  $\eta(v+\lambda w,s)=\eta(v,s)+\lambda\eta(w,s)=0$, so $v+\lambda w\in S^{\perp}$.
  In particular the zero vector lies in $S^{\perp}$ and $S^{\perp}$ is never
  empty.
- $S\subseteq (S^{\perp})^{\perp}$: if $s\in S$, then $\eta(v,s)=0$ for every
  $v\in S^{\perp}$ by the definition of $S^{\perp}$, and symmetry of $\eta$
  gives $\eta(s,v)=0$ for every $v\in S^{\perp}$, that is,
  $s\in(S^{\perp})^{\perp}$.
- $S^{\perp}=(\operatorname{span}S)^{\perp}$: the inclusion
  $S\subseteq\operatorname{span}S$ gives
  $(\operatorname{span}S)^{\perp}\subseteq S^{\perp}$; conversely, if
  $v\in S^{\perp}$ and $u=\sum_i\lambda_i s_i$ is a finite linear combination
  with $s_i\in S$, then linearity in the second argument gives
  $\eta(v,u)=\sum_i\lambda_i\eta(v,s_i)=0$, so $v\in(\operatorname{span}S)^{\perp}$.

In particular, for every $u\in V$ one has $u\in u^{\perp}$ exactly when
$\eta(u,u)=0$, that is, exactly when $u$ is null or $u=0$
([[def-causal-classification-of-lorentz-vectors]]).

**A nonzero vector can be orthogonal to itself.** Take a basis
$e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3$ of $V$ in which the matrix of $\eta$ is diagonal with
diagonal entries $-1,1,1,1$; such a basis exists by clause 2 of the definition
of a Lorentz form. Then $v:=e_0+e_1$ is nonzero while
$\eta(v,v)=\eta(e_0,e_0)+2\eta(e_0,e_1)+\eta(e_1,e_1)=-1+0+1=0$, so
$v\in v^{\perp}$ with $v\neq 0$. This is exactly what fails for a
positive-definite inner product and is why orthogonal complements in a Lorentz
vector space need not be positive definite.

Let $(V,\eta)$ be a Lorentz vector space of signature $(-,+,+,+)$
([[def-lorentz-form-and-inertia]]), with causal terminology as in
[[def-causal-classification-of-lorentz-vectors]], and let

$$T:=\{v\in V:\eta(v,v)<0\}$$

be its **timelike set**. Components and closures refer to the topology obtained
by using any ordered basis to identify $V$ with Euclidean $\mathbb R^4$;
[[lem-timelike-cone-has-two-convex-components]], step 5.1, proves that the
resulting open sets are independent of the basis. By that lemma the
set $T$ has exactly two connected components, and each of them is nonempty,
open, convex and path-connected. A **time orientation** of $(V,\eta)$ is a
choice of one of these two components. Fixing such a choice, write $C^+$ for the
chosen component and

$$C^-:=T\setminus C^+$$

for the other component; thus $T=C^+\sqcup C^-$ is a disjoint union and
$C^+$, $C^-$ are exactly the two components supplied by the lemma. Relative to
this choice a vector $v\in V$ is

- **future timelike** when $v\in C^+$;
- **past timelike** when $v\in C^-$;
- **future null** when $v\neq 0$, $\eta(v,v)=0$ and $v\in\operatorname{cl}(C^+)$;
- **past null** when $v\neq 0$, $\eta(v,v)=0$ and $v\in\operatorname{cl}(C^-)$;
- **future causal** when it is future timelike or future null;
- **past causal** when it is past timelike or past null.

The sets $\operatorname{cl}(C^+)$ and $\operatorname{cl}(C^-)$ are the
**future closed cone** and the **past closed cone** of the time-oriented space
$(V,\eta,C^+)$. By [[lem-timelike-cone-has-two-convex-components]] each of them
is a convex cone, their intersection is $\{0\}$, and a vector is causal exactly
when it is future causal or past causal, in which case exactly one of these two
alternatives holds: no nonzero vector is both future causal and past causal.
The timelike vectors are exactly the points of $T=C^+\cup C^-$, and
$0\notin T$ because $\eta(0,0)=0$; since a null vector is nonzero with
$\eta(v,v)=0$, no vector is both timelike and null, so the classes above are
mutually exclusive where the definitions say they are: no vector is both future
and past causal, and no timelike vector is null.

Let $(V,\eta)$ be a Lorentz vector space of signature $(-,+,+,+)$
([[def-lorentz-form-and-inertia]]), with associated quadratic form
$q(v)=\eta(v,v)$. A vector $v\in V$ is

- **timelike** when $q(v)<0$;
- **null**, or **lightlike**, when $v\neq 0$ and $q(v)=0$;
- **spacelike** when $q(v)>0$;
- **causal** when it is timelike or null.

The zero vector $0\in V$ satisfies $q(0)=0$ and is consequently **none** of
timelike, null or spacelike: the null case explicitly excludes it, and the
timelike and spacelike cases exclude it by $q(0)=0$ together with the strict
inequalities. The **causal character** of a nonzero vector $v$ is the sign of
the real number $q(v)$, and the three names are attached to the three signs as
above. When no confusion arises, the pairing $\eta$ itself is written
$\langle v,w\rangle:=\eta(v,w)$.

**Each nonzero vector has exactly one causal character.** For a nonzero
$v\in V$ the real number $q(v)$ satisfies exactly one of $q(v)<0$, $q(v)=0$,
$q(v)>0$ by trichotomy of the order on $\mathbb R$, so $v$ is timelike, null or
spacelike, and no two of the three alternatives can hold at once. The causal
vectors are therefore exactly the nonzero vectors that are timelike or null,
and the zero vector is causal in no sense introduced here.

An **oriented time-oriented affine Minkowski space** is a quadruple
$(A,V,\eta,C^+)$ with the following data. In this notation $V$ includes its
specified orientation; forgetting that orientation gives only the underlying
real vector space, not the full datum $V$ of the model.

1. A nonempty affine space $A$ over a $4$-dimensional real vector space $V$,
   with action $(p,v)\mapsto p+v$ and displacement $q-p\in V$
   ([[def-affine-space-and-displacement]]). In particular $V$ is a real vector
   space of dimension $4$.
2. A Lorentz form $\eta$ on $V$, i.e. a nondegenerate symmetric bilinear form of
   inertia $(3,1,0)$ ([[def-lorentz-form-and-inertia]]). Its associated quadratic
   form is $q(v)=\eta(v,v)$.
3. An **orientation** of $V$: a positive ray of the determinant line
   $\Lambda^4V$, fixed once and for all
   ([[def-determinant-line-orientation-of-a-finite-dimensional-real-vector-space]]).
4. A **time orientation** $C^+$ of $(V,\eta)$: one of the two connected
   components of the timelike set $T=\{v\in V:\eta(v,v)<0\}$, the other being
   $C^-:=T\setminus C^+$ ([[def-time-orientation-and-future-causal-sets]]).

The following terminology is attached to such a quadruple.

- The elements $p$ of $A$ are the **events**; for events $p,q$ the vector
  $q-p\in V$ is the **displacement from $p$ to $q$**.
- The **interval** of $p,q\in A$ is the real number
  $I(p,q):=\eta(q-p,q-p)=q(q-p)$.
- Events $p,q$ are **timelike**, **null**, **spacelike** or **causally
  related** when the displacement $q-p$ is timelike, null, spacelike or causal
  in the sense of [[def-causal-classification-of-lorentz-vectors]]; they are
  **future-related** when $q-p$ is future causal and **past-related** when
  $q-p$ is past causal in the sense of
  [[def-time-orientation-and-future-causal-sets]].

**No point of $A$ is distinguished.** For every $v\in V$ the translation
$\tau_v:A\to A$, $\tau_v(p):=p+v$, is a bijection, since it is inverse to
$\tau_{-v}$: $\tau_{-v}(\tau_v(p))=(p+v)+(-v)=p+(v-v)=p$ and symmetrically, by
the affine action axioms ([[def-affine-space-and-displacement]]). Displacements
are translation invariant, $\tau_v(q)-\tau_v(p)=q-p$, so every $\tau_v$ preserves
the interval, the causal classification of every ordered pair, and the sets
$C^+$, $C^-$ (which are subsets of $V$, independent of the point of $A$); it
changes only the labelling of points. The mathematical structure of the model is
exactly the quadruple $(A,V,\eta,C^+)$; no derived physical quantity (proper
time, four-velocity, momentum, energy, charge or any field) is part of this
definition, and all later structure of the framework (frames, charts, tensor
fields, worldlines) is built on this model.

**Well-definedness.** The affine-space definition supplies the action and the
unique displacements; the Lorentz-form definition supplies $\eta$ and its
inertia; the determinant-line definition supplies orientations; and the two
components of $T$ between which the time-orientation definition chooses exist by
the components lemma recorded in the well-definedness clause of
[[def-time-orientation-and-future-causal-sets]], which is also what makes the
names future and past causal in item 4 well defined.

Let $(A,V,\eta,C^+)$ be the affine Minkowski space ([[def-sr-affine-minkowski-model]]) and let $n\in V$ be future unit timelike, $\eta(n,n)=-1$ ([[def-causal-classification-of-lorentz-vectors]], [[def-time-orientation-and-future-causal-sets]]).

**(a) Rest space.** The **rest space** of $n$ is the hyperplane $n^\perp=\{v\in V:\eta(n,v)=0\}$; by [[thm-sr-proper-time-and-observer-decomposition]] clause (c) it is a three-dimensional linear subspace on which $\eta$ restricts to a positive-definite symmetric form, and the orthogonal projection onto it is $h(v)=v+\eta(n,v)n$ ([[def-lorentz-orthogonality-and-orthogonal-complement]]).

**(b) Simultaneity slice.** For $p\in A$ the **simultaneity slice of $p$ relative to $n$** is the affine hyperplane $H(p,n):=p+n^\perp=\{q\in A:\eta(n,q-p)=0\}$; it contains $p$ and is three-dimensional, not a single point.

**(c) Simultaneity relation.** Define $q\sim_nq'$ if and only if $\eta(n,q'-q)=0$, that is, if and only if $q'-q\in n^\perp$. Then $\sim_n$ is an equivalence relation on $A$ whose equivalence classes are exactly the slices $H(p,n)$; reflexivity, symmetry and transitivity are consequences of $n^\perp$ being a linear subspace and are not physical assumptions.

**(d) Rest distance.** For $p,q$ with $q\in H(p,n)$ define $d_n(p,q):=\sqrt{\eta(q-p,q-p)}$. This is a real number $\ge0$, symmetric in $p,q$, vanishes exactly when $p=q$, and satisfies the triangle inequality on each slice, because the restriction of $\eta$ to $n^\perp$ is a positive-definite inner product.

**(e) Dependence on $n$ and scope.** The relation $\sim_n$ and the slices $H(p,n)$ depend on the chosen future unit timelike vector $n$: an event $q$ with $\eta(n,q-p)=0$ generally has $\eta(n',q-p)\ne0$ for another future unit $n'$ (an explicit witness is given on this page). Simultaneity here is defined relative to a prescribed observer vector and is not an absolute relation. For a congruence $n(\cdot)$ one may form the pointwise slices $H\bigl(p,n(p)\bigr)$; the separate integrability question concerns the tangent distribution $p\mapsto n(p)^\perp$, not the assertion that these affine hyperplanes themselves are its integral hypersurfaces. Integral hypersurfaces can be curved; no global foliation is asserted.

derivations.claim: Set $d:=q-e_-$ and $r:=e_+-q$, so that $d+r=e_+-e_-=(\lambda_+-\lambda_-)n$. By [F1] write $d=-\eta(n,d)n+h(d)$ with $h(d)\in n^\perp$; by [F2] and [F3] a nonzero vector $v$ is future null exactly when $\eta(v,v)=0$ and $\eta(n,v)<0$, and for such a $v$ the decomposition satisfies $\eta(n,v)^2=|h(v)|^2$ by [F3] applied to $\eta(v,v)=0$. Also $r=(\lambda_+-\lambda_-)n-d=\bigl(\lambda_+-\lambda_-+\eta(n,d)\bigr)n-h(d)$ by [F1], because $-d=\eta(n,d)n-h(d)$.

(ii) implies (i): assume $q=o+\tfrac{\lambda_-+\lambda_+}{2}n+u$ with $u\in n^\perp$ and $|u|=(\lambda_+-\lambda_-)/2=:\rho$. Then $q-e_-=\rho n+u$ by the affine action, and by [F3] $\eta(q-e_-,q-e_-)=-\rho^2+|u|^2=0$ while $\eta(n,q-e_-)=-\rho<0$, so $q-e_-$ is future null by [F2]; likewise $e_+-q=\rho n-u$ satisfies $\eta(e_+-q,e_+-q)=-\rho^2+|u|^2=0$ and $\eta(n,e_+-q)=-\rho<0$, so $e_+-q$ is future null.

(i) implies (ii): assume $d$ and $r$ are future null. By step 1.1 applied to $d$ one has $\eta(n,d)<0$; put $\mu:=-\eta(n,d)>0$, so $d=\mu n+h(d)$ and $|h(d)|^2=\eta(n,d)^2=\mu^2$, hence $|h(d)|=\mu$ by [F1]. Applying step 1.1 to $r$, whose expression is $\bigl(\lambda_+-\lambda_--\mu\bigr)n-h(d)$: its future nullness gives $\eta(n,r)=-\bigl(\lambda_+-\lambda_--\mu\bigr)<0$, and $\eta(r,r)=-\bigl(\lambda_+-\lambda_--\mu\bigr)^2+|h(d)|^2=0$ by [F3]. Hence $\bigl(\lambda_+-\lambda_--\mu\bigr)^2=\mu^2$, and since $\eta(n,r)=-\bigl(\lambda_+-\lambda_--\mu\bigr)<0$ we have $\lambda_+-\lambda_--\mu>0$, so the positive root applies: $\lambda_+-\lambda_--\mu=\mu$, that is $\mu=(\lambda_+-\lambda_-)/2$. Therefore $q=e_-+d=o+(\lambda_-+\mu)n+h(d)=o+\tfrac{\lambda_-+\lambda_+}{2}n+u$ with $u:=h(d)\in n^\perp$, $|u|=\mu=(\lambda_+-\lambda_-)/2$; this is (ii).

Midpoint and distance: assume (i), hence (ii) with $q=o+\tfrac{\lambda_-+\lambda_+}{2}n+u$ as produced in step 2.1. Put $m:=o+\tfrac{\lambda_-+\lambda_+}{2}n$; since $e_\pm=o+\lambda_\pm n$, the displacement identity $m-e_-=\tfrac{\lambda_+-\lambda_-}{2}n=e_+-m$ shows that $m$ is the affine midpoint $\tfrac{e_-+e_+}{2}$. Then $q-m=u\in n^\perp$, so $\eta(n,q-m)=0$, that is $q\in H(m,n)$; and $d_n(m,q)=\sqrt{\eta(u,u)}=|u|=(\lambda_+-\lambda_-)/2$ by [F4] and step 2.1.

Conclusion: step 2.1 proves (i)$\Rightarrow$(ii) and step 1.2 proves (ii)$\Rightarrow$(i), so the two conditions are equivalent; step 3.1 shows that whenever they hold the reflection event satisfies $q-e_-=\tfrac{\lambda_+-\lambda_-}{2}n+u$ and $e_+-q=\tfrac{\lambda_+-\lambda_-}{2}n-u$ with the same horizontal vector $u$, lies in the slice $H(m,n)$ of the fixed midpoint $m=\tfrac{e_-+e_+}{2}$, and has the fixed rest distance $(\lambda_+-\lambda_-)/2$. Since the data $e_-$, $e_+$ determine $m$ and the norm $\rho=(\lambda_+-\lambda_-)/2$, two admissible reflection events differ only by the choice of $u\in n^\perp$ with $|u|=\rho$; such $u$ exist because $n^\perp$ is three-dimensional and $\rho>0$. This is the full assertion.

boundaries.evidence: The lemma is about a given event $q$ and given events $e_-=o+\lambda_-n$, $e_+=o+\lambda_+n$; no empty set of events is quantified over. This disposition is part of the statement.
The case $q=m$ (rest vector $u=0$) is included: then $\lambda_+=\lambda_-$, and step 3.1 gives rest distance $0$; the equivalence remains valid.

All admissible reflection events for a fixed pair differ only in the direction of the single rest vector $u\in n^\perp$ of prescribed norm; the midpoint is unique. This disposition is part of the statement.
The hypothesis $\lambda_-<\lambda_+$ excludes the degenerate round trip, and the proof of step 2.1 uses positivity of $\lambda_+-\lambda_-$ when taking the positive root.

The strict inequality $\lambda_-<\lambda_+$ is an open, nondegenerate reception interval; the endpoints $e_-,e_+$ are part of the data and are not limits of the construction. This disposition is part of the statement.

For each admissible data set the rest vector is produced from a displayed decomposition; the remark notes that the admissible set is nonempty by scaling any nonzero rest vector, with no choice principle used. This disposition is part of the statement.
Step 2.1 proves (i)$\Rightarrow$(ii): future nullity of the two segments forces $\mu=(\lambda_+-\lambda_-)/2$ and the displayed midpoint decomposition.
Step 1.2 proves (ii)$\Rightarrow$(i): the displayed midpoint decomposition makes both segments future null by direct evaluation of $\eta$.
