$p=o$.

**Transition law.** Let $(o';e'_0,e'_1,e'_2,e'_3)$ be another inertial frame
with chart $x'$, and let $M=(M^b_a)$ be the change-of-basis matrix defined by
$e'_a=\sum_bM^b_ae_b$, a $4\times4$ real matrix that is invertible because both
families are ordered bases. Then $E'(u)=\sum_au^ae'_a=E(Mu)$ for all
$u\in\mathbb R^4$, for the matrix-vector product $Mu$ in the coordinates of the
first frame, because $\sum_au^a\sum_bM^b_ae_b=\sum_b(\sum_aM^b_au^a)e_b$; hence
$E'=E\circ M$ and $E'^{-1}=M^{-1}\circ E^{-1}$, so for every event $p$,

$$x'(p)=M^{-1}\bigl(x(p)-x(o')\bigr)=M^{-1}x(p)-M^{-1}x(o') .$$

In particular the transition between two inertial charts is an affine map of
$\mathbb R^4$ with invertible linear part $M^{-1}$ and constant part
$-M^{-1}x(o')$, and it is a bijection of $\mathbb R^4$ with inverse
$u\mapsto Mu+x(o')$, which is the transition in the reverse direction.

**The inertial atlas.** The **inertial atlas** of the model is the family of
all inertial frames together with their inertial charts. Its charts are
available at every event by [[lem-future-oriented-inertial-frames-exist]], which
supplies for every $o\in A$ an inertial frame with origin $o$; and any two of
its charts are related by the affine transition displayed above.

Let $c > 0$ and let $x : I \to A$ be a $C^{1}$ future timelike worldline with
proper-time function $\tau$ and inverse $\rho$ of
[[def-sr-proper-time]] and [[lem-sr-proper-time-parametrization]].

**(a) Four-velocity.** The **four-velocity** of $x$ is the map $U : I \to V$
defined by

$$U(s) := \frac{x'(s)}{\tau'(s)} = \frac{c\,x'(s)}{\sqrt{-\eta(x'(s),x'(s))}} ;$$

equivalently, $U(s)$ is the tangent at parameter value $s$ of the proper-time
parametrized worldline $x \circ \rho$, read at the proper-time parameter
$\tau(s)$: by clause (iv) of [[lem-sr-proper-time-parametrization]],
$(x \circ \rho)'(\tau(s)) = x'(s)/\tau'(s) = U(s)$. The map $U$ is continuous,
$U(s)$ is future timelike for every $s \in I$, and $U$ does not depend on the
base point chosen for $\tau$ (changing the base point adds a constant to
$\tau$).

**(b) Four-acceleration.** If $x$ is $C^{2}$, that is, $x'$ is differentiable
with continuous derivative ([[def-sr-regular-causal-curve-and-worldline]]), the
**four-acceleration** of $x$ is the map $A : I \to V$ defined by

$$A(s) := \frac{U'(s)}{\tau'(s)} = \frac{c\,U'(s)}{\sqrt{-\eta(x'(s),x'(s))}} ;$$

equivalently, $A(s)$ is the derivative with respect to the proper-time parameter
of the four-velocity along the worldline: by the chain rule,
$A(s) = (U \circ \rho)'(\tau(s))$. The map $A$ is continuous.

**(c) Observer.** The **dimensionless four-velocity** of $x$ is $u := U/c$. A
**point observer** of the model at an event is a future unit timelike vector
$n \in V$, $\eta(n,n) = -1$ ([[def-causal-classification-of-lorentz-vectors]],
[[def-time-orientation-and-future-causal-sets]]); the four-velocity of the
observer's own worldline, the straight future timelike line through the event
with tangent $cn$, is $cn$ at each of its events.

**(d) Names and scope.** The names four-velocity and four-acceleration are the
model's names for $U$ and $A$; the physical interpretation, including the units
in which $U$ and $A$ are measured, is supplied with the coordinate conventions
of the framework and is not part of the affine geometry. The definition makes no
claim that $U$ has norm $-c^{2}$ or that $A$ is orthogonal to $U$; those are
proved in [[thm-sr-proper-time-and-observer-decomposition]].

Let $c > 0$ and let $(A,V,\eta,C^{+})$ be an oriented time-oriented affine
Minkowski space ([[def-sr-affine-minkowski-model]]).

**(a) Norm of the four-velocity.** Let $x : I \to A$ be a $C^{1}$ future
timelike worldline with four-velocity $U$
([[def-sr-four-velocity-and-four-acceleration]]). Then
$\eta(U(s),U(s)) = -c^{2}$ for every $s \in I$; equivalently the dimensionless
four-velocity $u = U/c$ satisfies $\eta(u,u) = -1$, and $U(s)$ is future
timelike. Thus the dimensionless four-velocity lies on the future unit
hyperboloid $\{v \in C^{+}:\eta(v,v)=-1\}$.

**(b) Orthogonality of the four-acceleration.** If $x$ is $C^{2}$ at $s$, then
$\eta(U(s),A(s)) = 0$: the four-acceleration has no component along the
four-velocity; if in addition $A(s) \ne 0$, then $A(s)$ is spacelike.

**(c) Rest space and projection.** Let $n \in V$ be future unit timelike,
$\eta(n,n) = -1$, and put $n^{\perp} := \{\,v \in V : \eta(n,v) = 0\,\}$
([[def-lorentz-orthogonality-and-orthogonal-complement]]). Then $n^{\perp}$ is a
3-dimensional linear subspace of $V$, the restriction of $\eta$ to $n^{\perp}$
is positive definite, and the map $h : V \to V$, $h(v) := v + \eta(n,v)\,n$, is
linear, idempotent with $h \circ h = h$, has image $n^{\perp}$ and kernel
$\operatorname{span}(n)$, satisfies $h(n) = 0$ and $\eta(n,h(v)) = 0$ for all
$v \in V$, and every $v \in V$ has the unique decomposition
$v = -\eta(n,v)\,n + h(v)$. Moreover $|w| := \sqrt{\eta(w,w)}$ defines a norm
on $n^{\perp}$.

**(d) Relative velocity and Lorentz factor.** Let $n$ and $u$ be future unit
timelike vectors, put $\gamma := -\eta(n,u)$ and $w := c\,h(u)/\gamma$. Then
$\gamma \ge 1$, $w$ lies in $n^{\perp}$,
$u = \gamma\,(n + w/c)$, $|w|^{2} = c^{2}(1-\gamma^{-2}) < c^{2}$,
$\gamma = (1-|w|^{2}/c^{2})^{-1/2}$, and $\gamma = 1$ if and only if $u = n$.
The vector $w$ is the velocity of a worldline with four-velocity $cu$ relative
to the observer $n$, and $\gamma$ is its Lorentz factor.

**(e) Coordinate form.** Let $(o;e_0,\dots,e_3)$ be an inertial frame and let
$y$ be a $C^{1}$ future timelike worldline whose inertial coordinates are
$t \mapsto (ct,r(t))$, with coordinate velocity $w(t) := r'(t)$ in
$\mathbb{R}^{3}$ and, when $y$ is $C^{2}$, coordinate acceleration
$a(t) := w'(t)$. Then $|w(t)| < c$, the four-velocity is
$U = \gamma_w\,(c,w)$ with $\gamma_w := (1-|w|^{2}/c^{2})^{-1/2}$, and the
four-acceleration is $A = \gamma_w\,\frac{d}{dt}\bigl(\gamma_w(c,w)\bigr)$, so
that

$$A^{0} = \gamma_w^{4}\,\frac{w \cdot a}{c}, \qquad A_{\mathrm{vec}} = \gamma_w^{2}\,a + \gamma_w^{4}\,\frac{(w \cdot a)\,w}{c^{2}} ;$$

consequently
$\eta(A,A) = \gamma_w^{4}|a|^{2} + \gamma_w^{6}(w \cdot a)^{2}/c^{2} \ge 0$,
with $\eta(A,A) = 0$ if and only if $a = 0$, and $\eta(U,A) = 0$. For the
observer $n = e_0$ of the chart, clauses (c) and (d) specialize to
$\gamma = \gamma_w$ and $w_{\mathrm{rel}} = (0,w)$ in the frame coordinates, identified with $w$ via the spatial basis.

**(f) Scope.** The statement is a theorem about the affine Minkowski model with
a fixed positive constant $c$; it asserts no clock reading and identifies no
physical four-velocity. No choice principle is used.

Let $(o;e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$ and $(o';e'_0,e'_1,e'_2,e'_3)$ be inertial frames whose bases are related by a boost along the common first spatial direction with parameter $v$, $|v|<c$:

$$e'_0=\gamma\Bigl(e_0+\frac{v}{c}e_1\Bigr),\qquad e'_1=\gamma\Bigl(e_1+\frac{v}{c}e_0\Bigr),\qquad e'_2=e_2,\qquad e'_3=e_3,$$

where $\gamma=(1-v^2/c^2)^{-1/2}$, with charts $x$, $x'$ ([[def-lorentz-boost]], [[lem-inertial-chart-transitions-are-affine-lorentz]]). For arbitrary origins put $b:=-B(v/c)x(o')$, the constant translation vector, and write the affine transition as

$$x'^0=\gamma\Bigl(x^0-\frac{v}{c}x^1\Bigr)+b^0,\qquad x'^1=\gamma\Bigl(x^1-\frac{v}{c}x^0\Bigr)+b^1,\qquad x'^2=x^2+b^2,\qquad x'^3=x^3+b^3.$$

Then:

**(i) Clock rate.** The straight worldline $y(\lambda):=x^{-1}\bigl(\lambda,\tfrac{v}{c}\lambda+a_1,a_2,a_3\bigr)$ (coordinate velocity $(v,0,0)$, the worldline of a clock at rest in the frame $x'$) is future timelike, and the elapsed proper time between $\lambda_0<\lambda_1$ is $(\lambda_1-\lambda_0)/(c\gamma)$; equivalently $d\tau/dt=1/\gamma$ along $y$, where $t$ is the coordinate time of $x$.

**(ii) Length comparison.** For $L_0>0$ let $y_a,y_b$ be the two straight worldlines at rest in the frame $x'$ through the events with $x'$-coordinates $(\lambda,0,0,0)$ and $(\lambda,L_0,0,0)$. Then (a) at equal $x'$-times their $x'$-coordinate separation is $L_0$, while (b) at equal $x$-times their $x$-coordinate separation is $L_0/\gamma$, so the measuring frame $x$ assigns the length $L_0/\gamma$ to a rod of rest length $L_0$ at rest in $x'$; (c) symmetrically, for two worldlines at rest in $x$ with constant $x$-spatial separation $(L_0,0,0)$ along the boost direction, the separation at equal $x'$-times is $L_0/\gamma$. In each case the comparison uses events at equal time in the measuring frame; comparing equal times of the other frame is a different pair of events.

**(iii) Simultaneity.** If $x^0(q)-x^0(p)=0$ and $x^1(q)-x^1(p)=L$, then $x'^0(q)-x'^0(p)=-\gamma\frac{v}{c}L$; in particular simultaneity in the chart $x$ is not simultaneity in the chart $x'$ whenever $vL\ne0$.

**(iv) Velocity transformation.** Let $y:J\to A$ be a $C^1$ future causal curve which in the chart $x$ is $t\mapsto(ct,r(t))$ with coordinate velocity $w(t):=r'(t)\in\mathbb R^3$, $|w(t)|\le c$ (the strict inequality is the timelike branch). Then the coordinate velocity $w'$ of $y$ in the chart $x'$ is given by $w'_1=(w_1-v)/(1-vw_1/c^2)$ and $w'_\perp=w_\perp/\bigl(\gamma(1-vw_1/c^2)\bigr)$, the denominators being positive; moreover $|w'|<c$ when $|w|<c$, and $|w'|=c$ exactly when $|w|=c$.

derivations.claim: The coordinate derivative of $y$ is $y'(t)=(c,\tfrac{3c}{5},0,0)$, and by [L1] $\eta(y',y')=-c^2+\tfrac{9}{25}c^2=-\tfrac{16}{25}c^2<0$ with $y'^0=c>0$, so $y$ is future timelike; the proper-time rate is $\tau'(t)=\tfrac1c\sqrt{\tfrac{16}{25}c^2}=\tfrac45$. Hence for $t_0<t_1$ the proper time elapsed is $\tfrac45(t_1-t_0)=\tfrac{t_1-t_0}{5/4}$, i.e. the model proper-time rate is $4/5=1/\gamma$; equivalently $\Delta t=\gamma\,\Delta\tau=\tfrac54\Delta\tau$.

The four-velocity is $U=y'/\tau'=\tfrac54(c,\tfrac{3c}{5},0,0)=(\tfrac{5c}{4},\tfrac{3c}{4},0,0)$, whose norm is $\eta(U,U)=-\tfrac{25}{16}c^2+\tfrac{9}{16}c^2=-c^2$ by [L1], in agreement with [L2]; the dimensionless velocity is $u=U/c=\tfrac54(1,\tfrac35,0,0)=\gamma(e_0+\tfrac35e_1)$, which is the unit tangent vector of clause (i) of [L3] with $v/c=3/5$ and $\gamma=5/4$.

In the chart $x'$ of the boost with parameter $v=3c/5$ the spatial coordinates of $y$ are constant, so the clock is at rest in $x'$; a clock at rest in its own chart has $\tau'=1$ with respect to that chart's coordinate time, so its $x'$-time rate equals its proper-time rate, and the relation $\Delta t=\gamma\Delta\tau$ of step 1.1 is the inverse statement with $\gamma=5/4$.

Conclusion: steps 1.1-2.1 verify the three clauses (a), (b), (c) of the Example: the worldline is future timelike with proper-time rate $4/5=(1/\gamma)$, its four-velocity is $(\tfrac{5c}{4},\tfrac{3c}{4},0,0)$ of norm $-c^2$, the dimensionless velocity is the inverse passive-boost image $\gamma(e_0+\tfrac35e_1)$, and in the rest chart of the clock the time rate is the proper-time rate, so the inverse dilation $\Delta t=\gamma\Delta\tau$ holds with $\gamma=5/4$.

Let $(o;e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$ and $(o';e'_0,e'_1,e'_2,e'_3)$ be inertial frames whose bases are related by a boost along the common first spatial direction with parameter $v$, $|v|<c$:

$$e'_0=\gamma\Bigl(e_0+\frac{v}{c}e_1\Bigr),\qquad e'_1=\gamma\Bigl(e_1+\frac{v}{c}e_0\Bigr),\qquad e'_2=e_2,\qquad e'_3=e_3,$$

where $\gamma=(1-v^2/c^2)^{-1/2}$, with charts $x$, $x'$ ([[def-lorentz-boost]], [[lem-inertial-chart-transitions-are-affine-lorentz]]). For arbitrary origins put $b:=-B(v/c)x(o')$, the constant translation vector, and write the affine transition as

$$x'^0=\gamma\Bigl(x^0-\frac{v}{c}x^1\Bigr)+b^0,\qquad x'^1=\gamma\Bigl(x^1-\frac{v}{c}x^0\Bigr)+b^1,\qquad x'^2=x^2+b^2,\qquad x'^3=x^3+b^3.$$

Then:

**(i) Clock rate.** The straight worldline $y(\lambda):=x^{-1}\bigl(\lambda,\tfrac{v}{c}\lambda+a_1,a_2,a_3\bigr)$ (coordinate velocity $(v,0,0)$, the worldline of a clock at rest in the frame $x'$) is future timelike, and the elapsed proper time between $\lambda_0<\lambda_1$ is $(\lambda_1-\lambda_0)/(c\gamma)$; equivalently $d\tau/dt=1/\gamma$ along $y$, where $t$ is the coordinate time of $x$.

**(ii) Length comparison.** For $L_0>0$ let $y_a,y_b$ be the two straight worldlines at rest in the frame $x'$ through the events with $x'$-coordinates $(\lambda,0,0,0)$ and $(\lambda,L_0,0,0)$. Then (a) at equal $x'$-times their $x'$-coordinate separation is $L_0$, while (b) at equal $x$-times their $x$-coordinate separation is $L_0/\gamma$, so the measuring frame $x$ assigns the length $L_0/\gamma$ to a rod of rest length $L_0$ at rest in $x'$; (c) symmetrically, for two worldlines at rest in $x$ with constant $x$-spatial separation $(L_0,0,0)$ along the boost direction, the separation at equal $x'$-times is $L_0/\gamma$. In each case the comparison uses events at equal time in the measuring frame; comparing equal times of the other frame is a different pair of events.

**(iii) Simultaneity.** If $x^0(q)-x^0(p)=0$ and $x^1(q)-x^1(p)=L$, then $x'^0(q)-x'^0(p)=-\gamma\frac{v}{c}L$; in particular simultaneity in the chart $x$ is not simultaneity in the chart $x'$ whenever $vL\ne0$.

**(iv) Velocity transformation.** Let $y:J\to A$ be a $C^1$ future causal curve which in the chart $x$ is $t\mapsto(ct,r(t))$ with coordinate velocity $w(t):=r'(t)\in\mathbb R^3$, $|w(t)|\le c$ (the strict inequality is the timelike branch). Then the coordinate velocity $w'$ of $y$ in the chart $x'$ is given by $w'_1=(w_1-v)/(1-vw_1/c^2)$ and $w'_\perp=w_\perp/\bigl(\gamma(1-vw_1/c^2)\bigr)$, the denominators being positive; moreover $|w'|<c$ when $|w|<c$, and $|w'|=c$ exactly when $|w|=c$.

Let $(o;e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$ be an inertial frame of the model
([[def-inertial-frame-and-inertial-chart]]), and let
$x=(x^0,x^1,x^2,x^3)$ be its coordinates, so that a vector is written
$x=x^0e_0+x^1e_1+x^2e_2+x^3e_3$ and the spatial part is the coordinate
column $x_{\mathrm{vec}}=(x^1,x^2,x^3)$ of $\mathbb R^3$ with its standard
Euclidean structure ([[def-euclidean-inner-product]]).

For $\boldsymbol\beta\in\mathbb R^3$ with $|\boldsymbol\beta|<1$, where
$|\boldsymbol\beta|$ is the Euclidean norm, set

$$\gamma(\boldsymbol\beta):=(1-|\boldsymbol\beta|^2)^{-1/2}\ \ge 1,$$

with equality exactly for $\boldsymbol\beta=\mathbf 0$ and strict inequality
for $\boldsymbol\beta\neq\mathbf 0$; here the power is the rational power
([[def-rational-power]], [[lem-rational-power-laws]]). The **passive Lorentz
boost with parameter $\boldsymbol\beta$** is the linear map
$B(\boldsymbol\beta):V\to V$ ([[def-linear-map]]) defined by its action on
coordinates: for $\boldsymbol\beta\neq\mathbf 0$,

$$x'^0=\gamma\,(x^0-\boldsymbol\beta\cdot x_{\mathrm{vec}}),\qquad x'_{\mathrm{vec}}=x_{\mathrm{vec}}+\frac{\gamma-1}{|\boldsymbol\beta|^2}\,(\boldsymbol\beta\cdot x_{\mathrm{vec}})\,\boldsymbol\beta-\gamma\,\boldsymbol\beta\,x^0,$$

and for $\boldsymbol\beta=\mathbf 0$, $B(\mathbf 0):=\operatorname{id}_V$.
Here $x'$ denotes the coordinates of $B(\boldsymbol\beta)$ applied to the
vector with coordinates $x$, and $\boldsymbol\beta\cdot x_{\mathrm{vec}}$ is
the Euclidean scalar product. Equivalently, in the ordered basis
$(e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$ the matrix of $B(\boldsymbol\beta)$ is

$$\begin{pmatrix}\gamma & -\gamma\boldsymbol\beta^{T}\\ -\gamma\boldsymbol\beta & I_3+\dfrac{\gamma-1}{|\boldsymbol\beta|^{2}}\,\boldsymbol\beta\boldsymbol\beta^{T}\end{pmatrix},$$

that is, $B^0{}_0=\gamma$, $B^0{}_i=B^i{}_0=-\gamma\beta_i$ for
$i=1,2,3$, and
$B^i{}_j=\delta^i{}_j+\frac{\gamma-1}{|\boldsymbol\beta|^2}\beta_i\beta_j$
for $i,j=1,2,3$, with the spatial block replaced by
$I_3$ when $\boldsymbol\beta=\mathbf 0$. In the $1+1$ case
$\boldsymbol\beta=\beta e_1$ this reads
$x'^0=\gamma(x^0-\beta x^1)$ and $x'^1=\gamma(x^1-\beta x^0)$. The vector
$\boldsymbol\beta$ is called the **boost parameter**; it is dimensionless and
mathematically independent of any unit convention.

**Consistency of the definition.** The displayed formulas assign to every
coordinate pair $(x^0,x_{\mathrm{vec}})$ a pair
$(x'^0,x'_{\mathrm{vec}})$; writing the result as the matrix product above and
using that $\mathbb R^4$ is identified with coordinates through
[[thm-unique-coordinates-with-respect-to-an-ordered-basis]] (see
[[def-coordinate-column-and-matrix-of-a-linear-map]]), the map
$v\mapsto E(M(E^{-1}(v)))$ is the unique linear map with that matrix. The case
$\boldsymbol\beta=\mathbf 0$ is declared separately because the expression
$(\gamma-1)/|\boldsymbol\beta|^2$ is undefined there. That the two cases fit
together is the limit computation recorded next.

**The limit as $\boldsymbol\beta\to\mathbf 0$.** For
$\boldsymbol\beta\neq\mathbf 0$ the identity
$\gamma^2-1=|\boldsymbol\beta|^2\gamma^2$ gives

$$\frac{\gamma-1}{|\boldsymbol\beta|^{2}}=\frac{\gamma^{2}}{\gamma+1}.$$

Since $|\boldsymbol\beta|^2\le3/4$ forces $1\le\gamma\le2$, the bounds
$|\beta_i|\le|\boldsymbol\beta|$ and $|\beta_i\beta_j|\le|\boldsymbol\beta|^2$
(from the Euclidean norm convention, [[def-abs-value]], [[lem-of-abs-value]])
show that $\gamma\to1$ as $\boldsymbol\beta\to\mathbf 0$; here continuity of
the positive-base power at fixed exponent $-1/2$ is
[[thm-real-power-continuity-and-derivatives]], with real and rational powers
identified by [[thm-real-power-agrees-with-rational-exponent]]. Hence
$(\gamma-1)/|\boldsymbol\beta|^2\to1/2$, so
$B^i{}_j=\delta^i{}_j+\frac12\beta_i\beta_j+o(|\boldsymbol\beta|^2)$ and
$B(\boldsymbol\beta)\to I$ entrywise, without a hidden division by zero.
Here $o(|\boldsymbol\beta|^2)$ denotes a remainder whose ratio to
$|\boldsymbol\beta|^2$ tends to $0$ through nonzero parameters: the ratio
of each spatial remainder is bounded by
$|\gamma^2/(\gamma+1)-1/2|\to0$. The time-space entries obey
$|\gamma\beta_i|\le2|\boldsymbol\beta|\to0$, and the time-time entry tends to
$1$ by $\gamma\to1$. The
definition asserts no Lorentz property: that $B(\boldsymbol\beta)$ is a proper
orthochronous Lorentz map with inverse $B(-\boldsymbol\beta)$ is proved in
[[lem-boost-is-proper-orthochronous-with-inverse]], and its collinear
composition law in
[[lem-collinear-boost-composition-and-velocity-addition]]. The physical
reading of $c\boldsymbol\beta$ as a relative velocity is not part of this
definition ([[def-lorentz-map-and-lorentz-group]]).

derivations.claim: Collinear case: with $w_1=4c/5$, $w_\perp=0$, $v=3c/5$, the denominator of [L1] is $1-\tfrac35\cdot\tfrac45=1-\tfrac{12}{25}=\tfrac{13}{25}>0$ and $w'_1=\tfrac{c/5}{13/25}=\tfrac{5c}{13}$; hence $w'=(5c/13,0,0)$ and $|w'|=5c/13<c$ because $5/13<1$. The Galilean difference for this passive change of frame is $4c/5-3c/5=c/5$, which is not the transformed velocity.

Transverse case: with $w_1=0$, $w_\perp=(c/2,0)$, the denominator is $1$ and [L1] gives $w'_1=(0-3c/5)/1=-3c/5$ and $w'_2=(c/2)/(\gamma\cdot1)=2c/5$, so $|w'|^2=(9/25+4/25)c^2=13c^2/25$ and $|w'|=(\sqrt{13}/5)c<c$ because $\sqrt{13}<5$.

Null limit: with $w_1=c$ the denominator of [L1] is $1-3/5=2/5>0$ and $w'_1=(c-3c/5)/(2/5)=(2c/5)/(2/5)=c$, so $w'=(c,0,0)$ and $|w'|=c$; this is the equality case of the subluminality statement, consistent with $|w|=c$.

Conclusion: steps 1.1-1.3 evaluate the transformation formula of [L1] in the three configurations and confirm $|w'|<c$ for subluminal $w$ and $|w'|=c$ in the null case; in particular the collinear case deviates from the Galilean difference by the relativistic denominator $1-vw_1/c^2$, and the transverse case exhibits the factor $1/\gamma$ in the perpendicular component.

Adopt as physical assumptions of the special-relativity framework the following
two statements, with the SI coordinate and unit conventions of
[[def-sr-si-units-and-coordinate-conventions]].

**(i) Ideal clocks.** Let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be a nondegenerate interval and
$\gamma:I\to A$ a curve. Choose an inertial chart $\chi$ with
$E(u)=\sum_au^ae_a$ as in [[def-inertial-frame-and-inertial-chart]]. Require
$y:=\chi\circ\gamma:I\to\mathbb R^4$ to be $C^1$ on the interior of $I$,
with its derivative extending continuously to any included endpoints, where
it is the one-sided derivative. Define the displacement-valued derivative by
$\dot\gamma(s):=E(y'(s))\in V$ and require $\dot\gamma(s)\in C^+$ everywhere,
including such endpoints. This derivative is chart-independent: a second
chart has coordinates $\widetilde y=M^{-1}(y-\chi(o'))$, so its
parameter derivative is $M^{-1}\mathrm dy/\mathrm ds$, while its basis map
is $E'=EM$; their product is $E\,\mathrm dy/\mathrm ds$.

An **ideal clock on this curve** has a reading map $\sigma:I\to\mathbb R$
in seconds, specified up to an additive constant, with, for all $a<b$ in $I$,

$$\sigma(b)-\sigma(a)=c^{-1}\int_a^b\sqrt{-\eta\bigl(\dot\gamma(s),\dot\gamma(s)\bigr)}\,\mathrm ds .$$

The integrand is positive and continuous on $[a,b]$: the coordinate derivatives
are continuous, $\eta$ is a finite bilinear expression, and the square root
is continuous at every positive argument, as follows from
$|\sqrt r-\sqrt q|=|r-q|/(\sqrt r+\sqrt q)$ for $r,q>0$.
Thus [[thm-continuous-implies-integrable]] applies to this compact interval
and gives a well-defined Riemann integral. The reading rule contains no
additional acceleration-dependent correction (**clock hypothesis**); it does
not require $C^2$ regularity or an acceleration to exist. This is an adopted
physical interpretation of the length integral, not a proof about real clocks.

**(ii) Ideal light.** In vacuum, the **ideal light rays** are the oriented
straight lines parametrized by $\ell:\mathbb R\to A$,
$\ell(\lambda)=p+\lambda v$, where $p\in A$ and $v\in V$ is future null;
increasing $\lambda$ specifies their future direction. In an inertial chart
$\chi$ their coordinate map is

$$\chi(\ell(\lambda))=\chi(p)+\lambda\,(v^0,v^1,v^2,v^3).$$

Since the chart's time-axis vector is future, the cone description of
[[lem-timelike-cone-has-two-convex-components]] gives
$v^0=\lvert v_{\mathrm{vec}}\rvert>0$. With $t=\chi^0/c$ the spatial
coordinate velocity is $c(v^1,v^2,v^3)/v^0$ and has Euclidean magnitude $c$
in every inertial chart. The conversion constant is the same across charts;
its exact SI numerical value is a unit convention as specified in
[[def-sr-si-units-and-coordinate-conventions]], while the ideal-vacuum-light
interpretation is an adopted, empirically testable model assumption.

Let $c > 0$ be a fixed real number, the conversion constant of the model, and
let $x : I \to A$ be a $C^{1}$ future timelike worldline
([[def-sr-regular-causal-curve-and-worldline]]).

**The integrand.** The function

$$g_x : I \to \mathbb{R}, \qquad g_x(s) := -\eta\bigl(x'(s),x'(s)\bigr),$$

is continuous and strictly positive. For continuity, fix an inertial frame and
write $y := x_A \circ x$ for the coordinate path; by the derivative and regularity definition in
[[def-sr-regular-causal-curve-and-worldline]] the $\mathbb{R}^{4}$-valued map
$y'$ is continuous, so each component $y'^{a}$, $a \in \{0,1,2,3\}$, is a
continuous real function ([[thm-componentwise-limits-and-continuity]]). In the
$\eta$-orthonormal basis underlying the frame one has
$\eta(e_a,e_b) = \operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)_{ab}$
([[def-inertial-frame-and-inertial-chart]]), whence

$$g_x(s) = -\eta\bigl(x'(s),x'(s)\bigr) = \bigl(y'^{0}(s)\bigr)^{2} - \bigl(y'^{1}(s)\bigr)^{2} - \bigl(y'^{2}(s)\bigr)^{2} - \bigl(y'^{3}(s)\bigr)^{2},$$

a finite sum of products of continuous real functions, hence continuous
([[thm-algebra-of-continuous-functions]], [[def-continuity-real]],
[[lem-lorentz-form-has-orthonormal-basis]]). Strict positivity
$g_x(s) = -\eta(x'(s),x'(s)) > 0$ is exactly the future timelike hypothesis on
$x'(s)$ ([[def-causal-classification-of-lorentz-vectors]]).

**The proper-time function.** Hence $u \mapsto \sqrt{g_x(u)}$ is continuous on
$I$: the square root is the power $t^{1/2}$ of [[def-rational-power]], which is
continuous and differentiable on $(0,\infty)$
([[thm-real-power-continuity-and-derivatives]]), and it is composed with the
continuous positive function $g_x$
([[thm-composition-of-continuous-functions]]); consequently it is Riemann
integrable on every compact subinterval of $I$
([[thm-continuous-implies-integrable]], [[def-interval]]). For $s_0, s \in I$
the **proper time from $s_0$ to $s$** is

$$\tau(s) := c^{-1} \int_{s_0}^{s} \sqrt{-\eta\bigl(x'(u),x'(u)\bigr)}\; du,$$

the integral being taken with oriented limits as in [[def-oriented-integral]];
for $a < b$ in $I$ this reads

$$\tau(b) - \tau(a) = c^{-1} \int_a^b \sqrt{-\eta\bigl(x'(u),x'(u)\bigr)}\; du,$$

by oriented additivity ([[thm-additivity-over-subintervals]]); equivalently,
the increment is the integral function with base point $a$ of the density
$c^{-1}\sqrt{g_x}$, evaluated at $b$ on $[a,b]$
([[def-the-integral-function]]). Changing the base point $s_0$ changes $\tau$
by an additive constant, so the elapsed times between parameter values are
intrinsic. $\tau$ depends on the parametrized history $x$ and on the parameter
values; its invariance under increasing $C^{1}$ reparametrizations with everywhere
positive derivative is proved in
[[lem-sr-proper-time-reparametrization-invariance]].

**Straight segments.** For the straight future timelike segment
$x(s) = p + (s-s_0)(q-p)$ of [[def-sr-affine-minkowski-model]] the difference
quotients are identically the future timelike displacement $q-p$, so
$x'(s) = q-p$ and

$$\tau(b) - \tau(a) = c^{-1} \sqrt{-\eta(q-p,q-p)}\,(b-a),$$

the straight-segment proper time of the model's coordinate conventions.

**Scope.** The construction is restricted to future timelike worldlines: on a
future null curve the length density vanishes identically, so its integral
is constant; a zero density at one isolated point does not imply constancy; for a spacelike
curve $-\eta(x',x')$ is negative and the square root is not a real number; and
for a past-directed timelike curve the same integral is defined but is not
attached to a worldline of this model. The construction asserts nothing about
physical clock readings.

Adopt the ideal-clock and ideal-light assumptions of [[post-sr-ideal-clocks-and-light]] and the SI conventions of [[def-sr-si-units-and-coordinate-conventions]]. Let $x:I\to A$ be a future timelike worldline ([[def-sr-regular-causal-curve-and-worldline]]) with proper-time function $\tau$ ([[def-sr-proper-time]]), and let $s_-<s_+$ be parameter values in $I$. Suppose an event $q$ and the events $e_-:=x(s_-)$, $e_+:=x(s_+)$ satisfy: $q-e_-$ is future null and $e_+-q$ is future null ([[def-causal-classification-of-lorentz-vectors]], [[def-time-orientation-and-future-causal-sets]], [[def-sr-affine-minkowski-model]]). Under the adopted ideal-light assumption an ideal ray is emitted at $e_-$, reaches $q$, and an ideal ray emitted at $q$ reaches $e_+$; the event $q$ is idealized as an instantaneous reflection that changes nothing else. The **radar protocol** of the observer assigns to $q$

(i) the **radar time** $\tau_{\mathrm{rad}}(q):=\tfrac12\bigl(\tau(s_-)+\tau(s_+)\bigr)$, the ideal clock's reading midway between emission and reception, and

(ii) the **radar distance** $\rho_{\mathrm{rad}}(q):=\tfrac{c}{2}\bigl(\tau(s_+)-\tau(s_-)\bigr)$, half the round-trip light time multiplied by $c$.

Two events measured by the same observer are **radar-simultaneous** when their radar times agree. The assignment does not change under increasing $C^1$ reparametrizations with everywhere positive derivative and the same clock origin of the observer's worldline, because the proper-time function does not ([[lem-sr-proper-time-reparametrization-invariance]]).

**Conventions and scope.** (a) The protocol is a definition of an operational assignment conditional on the existence of the emission, reflection and reception events, and it assumes an available ideal reflector and ideal apparatus. (b) The split of the round trip into a "time" and a "distance" uses the symmetric convention in which half of the round-trip time is assigned to the outgoing and half to the returning segment; the protocol determines the round-trip quantity $\tau(s_+)-\tau(s_-)$ operationally, while the derived one-way assignment is a convention and does not measure a one-way light speed independently of a synchronization convention. (c) The conditional assignment is defined for the stated future timelike worldline, including an accelerated one, but no general existence, uniqueness or synchronization theorem for accelerated observers is asserted. Nothing is claimed about dispersive or absorbing media, finite-resolution apparatus, global single-valuedness or detector models, and no measurement outcome, statistical inference or empirical comparison is asserted.

Let $n$ be a future unit timelike vector, $\eta(n,n)=-1$ ([[def-causal-classification-of-lorentz-vectors]], [[def-time-orientation-and-future-causal-sets]]), let $o$ be an event, and let $\lambda_-<\lambda_+$ be real numbers; put $e_-:=o+\lambda_-n$ and $e_+:=o+\lambda_+n$ ([[def-sr-affine-minkowski-model]]). For an event $q$ the following are equivalent:

(i) $q-e_-$ is future null and $e_+-q$ is future null;

(ii) there is $u\in n^\perp$ with $|u|:=\sqrt{\eta(u,u)}=(\lambda_+-\lambda_-)/2$ such that $q=o+\tfrac{\lambda_-+\lambda_+}{2}n+u$.

In that case $q-e_-=\tfrac{\lambda_+-\lambda_-}{2}n+u$ and $e_+-q=\tfrac{\lambda_+-\lambda_-}{2}n-u$, the affine midpoint $m:=o+\tfrac{\lambda_-+\lambda_+}{2}n=\tfrac{e_-+e_+}{2}$ satisfies $\eta(n,q-m)=0$ (so $q$ lies in the slice $H(m,n)$) and $|q-m|=(\lambda_+-\lambda_-)/2$ ([[def-sr-simultaneity-slice-and-rest-distance]]). In particular for fixed $e_-,e_+$ all admissible reflection events $q$ have the same midpoint $m$ and the same rest distance $(\lambda_+-\lambda_-)/2$, and differ only in the direction $u$ of $n^\perp$.

Let $(A,V,\eta,C^+)$ be the affine Minkowski space ([[def-sr-affine-minkowski-model]]) and let $n\in V$ be future unit timelike, $\eta(n,n)=-1$ ([[def-causal-classification-of-lorentz-vectors]], [[def-time-orientation-and-future-causal-sets]]).

**(a) Rest space.** The **rest space** of $n$ is the hyperplane $n^\perp=\{v\in V:\eta(n,v)=0\}$; by [[thm-sr-proper-time-and-observer-decomposition]] clause (c) it is a three-dimensional linear subspace on which $\eta$ restricts to a positive-definite symmetric form, and the orthogonal projection onto it is $h(v)=v+\eta(n,v)n$ ([[def-lorentz-orthogonality-and-orthogonal-complement]]).

**(b) Simultaneity slice.** For $p\in A$ the **simultaneity slice of $p$ relative to $n$** is the affine hyperplane $H(p,n):=p+n^\perp=\{q\in A:\eta(n,q-p)=0\}$; it contains $p$ and is three-dimensional, not a single point.

**(c) Simultaneity relation.** Define $q\sim_nq'$ if and only if $\eta(n,q'-q)=0$, that is, if and only if $q'-q\in n^\perp$. Then $\sim_n$ is an equivalence relation on $A$ whose equivalence classes are exactly the slices $H(p,n)$; reflexivity, symmetry and transitivity are consequences of $n^\perp$ being a linear subspace and are not physical assumptions.

**(d) Rest distance.** For $p,q$ with $q\in H(p,n)$ define $d_n(p,q):=\sqrt{\eta(q-p,q-p)}$. This is a real number $\ge0$, symmetric in $p,q$, vanishes exactly when $p=q$, and satisfies the triangle inequality on each slice, because the restriction of $\eta$ to $n^\perp$ is a positive-definite inner product.

**(e) Dependence on $n$ and scope.** The relation $\sim_n$ and the slices $H(p,n)$ depend on the chosen future unit timelike vector $n$: an event $q$ with $\eta(n,q-p)=0$ generally has $\eta(n',q-p)\ne0$ for another future unit $n'$ (an explicit witness is given on this page). Simultaneity here is defined relative to a prescribed observer vector and is not an absolute relation. For a congruence $n(\cdot)$ one may form the pointwise slices $H\bigl(p,n(p)\bigr)$; the separate integrability question concerns the tangent distribution $p\mapsto n(p)^\perp$, not the assertion that these affine hyperplanes themselves are its integral hypersurfaces. Integral hypersurfaces can be curved; no global foliation is asserted.

Let $(A,V,\eta,C^+)$ be an oriented time-oriented affine Minkowski space and let
$(o;e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$ be an inertial frame
([[def-inertial-frame-and-inertial-chart]]). Put

$$S:=\operatorname{span}(e_1,e_2,e_3)=\{w\in V:\eta(e_0,w)=0\},$$

the equality holding because a vector $w=\sum_aw^ae_a$ satisfies
$\eta(e_0,w)=-w^0$ by $\eta$-orthonormality, so $\eta(e_0,w)=0$ exactly when
$w$ is a linear combination of $e_1,e_2,e_3$. In particular $S$ is the linear
subspace of $V$ spanned by the three spatial basis vectors of the frame, and
$V=S\oplus\operatorname{span}(e_0)$.

Let $\delta$ be the restriction of $\eta$ to $S$, i.e.
$\delta(w,z):=\eta(w,z)$ for $w,z\in S$. Writing $w=\sum_{i=1}^3w^ie_i$ and
$z=\sum_{i=1}^3z^ie_i$ and using $\eta(e_i,e_j)=\delta_{ij}$ for $i,j\ge1$, one
has

$$\delta(w,z)=w^1z^1+w^2z^2+w^3z^3,\qquad \delta(w,w)=(w^1)^2+(w^2)^2+(w^3)^2 .$$

Hence $\delta$ is a symmetric bilinear form on $S$ that is positive definite:
$\delta(w,w)\ge0$, with equality exactly for $w=0$ by uniqueness of coordinates
in the basis $(e_1,e_2,e_3)$ of $S$
([[thm-unique-coordinates-with-respect-to-an-ordered-basis]]). Thus $\delta$
is an inner product on the real vector space $S$
([[def-inner-product-space]]); the induced function

$$\lvert w\rvert:=\sqrt{\delta(w,w)}=\bigl\lVert(w^1,w^2,w^3)\bigr\rVert_2$$

is the Euclidean norm of the coordinate vector of $w$
([[def-euclidean-inner-product]]), and it is a norm on $S$
([[cor-triangle-inequality-for-inner-product-norm]]). The ordered basis
$(e_1,e_2,e_3)$ of $S$ is $\delta$-orthonormal, and it is declared **positively
oriented** in $S$ by the convention that an ordered triple $(u_1,u_2,u_3)$ of
elements of $S$ is positively oriented when the ordered basis
$(e_0,u_1,u_2,u_3)$ of $V$ is positively oriented for the fixed orientation of
$V$. The pair $(S,\delta)$, together with this orientation and the frame's
basis, is the **Euclidean spatial structure of the inertial frame**
$(o;e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$.

**Vector product.** For $w=\sum_{i=1}^3w^ie_i$ and $z=\sum_{i=1}^3z^ie_i$ in
$S$, define the **vector product** $w\times z$ to be the unique element of $S$
whose coordinates are

$$(w\times z)^1=w^2z^3-w^3z^2,\qquad (w\times z)^2=w^3z^1-w^1z^3,\qquad (w\times z)^3=w^1z^2-w^2z^1 .$$

This is well defined by uniqueness of coordinates in the basis
$(e_1,e_2,e_3)$. It is bilinear in $(w,z)$, alternating
($z\times w=-(w\times z)$ and $w\times w=0$), and it satisfies, for all
$w,z,y\in S$,

$$\delta(w\times z,y)=\det\begin{pmatrix}w^1&z^1&y^1\\ w^2&z^2&y^2\\ w^3&z^3&y^3\end{pmatrix},\qquad \lvert w\times z\rvert^2=\lvert w\rvert^2\lvert z\rvert^2-\delta(w,z)^2 .$$

The first identity is the expansion of the determinant along its columns, both
sides equalling $\sum_i(w\times z)^iy^i$; the second is Lagrange's identity,
obtained by expanding $\lvert w\times z\rvert^2+\delta(w,z)^2$ and comparing
termwise with $\lvert w\rvert^2\lvert z\rvert^2$ using
$\lvert w\rvert^2=\delta(w,w)$
([[def-determinant-of-a-square-matrix]]).

**Frame dependence.** The objects $S$, $\delta$, $\lvert\cdot\rvert$ and
$\times$ belong to the spatial three-space of the **named** inertial frame:
replacing the spatial basis by another $\delta$-orthonormal positively oriented
basis of $S$ transforms coordinates by an orientation-preserving orthogonal
matrix, under which $\delta$, the norm and the displayed identities are
unchanged, while a general change of inertial frame with a different time axis
$e_0$ changes $S$ itself and hence changes the domains of $\delta$ and $\times$.
The Lorentz form, the fixed orientation of $V$, and the time orientation $C^+$
are data of the model independent of the named inertial frame
([[def-sr-affine-minkowski-model]]). The Euclidean spatial structure instead
requires the choice of a time axis $e_0$; it is not an additional
frame-independent structure on the whole of $V$.

Let $(A,V,\eta,C^+)$ be an oriented time-oriented affine Minkowski space
([[def-sr-affine-minkowski-model]]), with orientation fixed as a positive ray of
the determinant line $\Lambda^4V$
([[def-determinant-line-orientation-of-a-finite-dimensional-real-vector-space]])
and with the corresponding class of positively oriented ordered bases of $V$
([[def-orientation-of-a-finite-dimensional-real-vector-space]]); by
[[prop-orientations-and-positive-basis-classes-agree-in-positive-dimension]] the
positive ray selects exactly one such class for $\dim V=4>0$.

An **inertial frame** of the model is a tuple $(o;e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$ consisting
of an event $o\in A$ and an ordered basis $(e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$ of $V$ that is

1. **$\eta$-orthonormal**: $\eta(e_a,e_b)=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)_{ab}$ for all $a,b$ ([[lem-lorentz-form-has-orthonormal-basis]]);
2. **future**: $e_0\in C^+$, i.e. $e_0$ is future timelike; and
3. **positively oriented**: the ordered basis lies in the positive-basis class
   selected by the fixed orientation.

The event $o$ is the **origin** of the frame and $e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3$ are its
**basis vectors**.

**Inertial charts.** For an inertial frame $(o;e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$, define

$$E:\mathbb R^4\longrightarrow V,\qquad E(u):=\sum_{a=0}^3u^ae_a .$$

Then $E$ is a linear isomorphism ([[def-linear-isomorphism-and-invertible-linear-map]]):
it is linear by construction, and it is bijective because
$(e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$ is an ordered basis, every $v\in V$ having exactly one
coordinate list $u$ with $v=\sum_au^ae_a$
([[thm-unique-coordinates-with-respect-to-an-ordered-basis]]). The **inertial
chart** of the frame is the map

$$x:A\longrightarrow\mathbb R^4,\qquad x(p):=E^{-1}(p-o),$$

and its values $x^a(p)$ are the **inertial coordinates of the event $p$** in the
frame. Since $E$ and $v\mapsto p+v$ are bijections, $x$ is a bijection
$A\to\mathbb R^4$; and $x(p)=0$ exactly when $p-o=0_V$, that is, exactly when
$p=o$.

**Transition law.** Let $(o';e'_0,e'_1,e'_2,e'_3)$ be another inertial frame
with chart $x'$, and let $M=(M^b_a)$ be the change-of-basis matrix defined by
$e'_a=\sum_bM^b_ae_b$, a $4\times4$ real matrix that is invertible because both
families are ordered bases. Then $E'(u)=\sum_au^ae'_a=E(Mu)$ for all
$u\in\mathbb R^4$, for the matrix-vector product $Mu$ in the coordinates of the
first frame, because $\sum_au^a\sum_bM^b_ae_b=\sum_b(\sum_aM^b_au^a)e_b$; hence
$E'=E\circ M$ and $E'^{-1}=M^{-1}\circ E^{-1}$, so for every event $p$,

$$x'(p)=M^{-1}\bigl(x(p)-x(o')\bigr)=M^{-1}x(p)-M^{-1}x(o') .$$

In particular the transition between two inertial charts is an affine map of
$\mathbb R^4$ with invertible linear part $M^{-1}$ and constant part
$-M^{-1}x(o')$, and it is a bijection of $\mathbb R^4$ with inverse
$u\mapsto Mu+x(o')$, which is the transition in the reverse direction.

**The inertial atlas.** The **inertial atlas** of the model is the family of
all inertial frames together with their inertial charts. Its charts are
available at every event by [[lem-future-oriented-inertial-frames-exist]], which
supplies for every $o\in A$ an inertial frame with origin $o$; and any two of
its charts are related by the affine transition displayed above.

Let $(A,V,\eta,C^{+})$ be an oriented time-oriented affine Minkowski space
([[def-sr-affine-minkowski-model]]) and let $I$ be an order-convex subset of
$\mathbb{R}$ with at least two elements ([[def-interval]]); a **curve** of the
model is a map $x : I \to A$.

### Derivative and regularity of the parametrization

For $s \in I$ and $h \ne 0$ with $s+h \in I$ the **difference quotient**
$\bigl(x(s+h)-x(s)\bigr)/h$ is an element of $V$, the displacement from $x(s)$
to $x(s+h)$ divided by the real number $h$
([[def-sr-affine-minkowski-model]]). Convergence in $V$ is understood through
an inertial frame: for the frame isomorphism $E : \mathbb{R}^{4} \to V$ of an
inertial frame ([[def-inertial-frame-and-inertial-chart]]) put
$|v|_{E} := |E^{-1}v|_{2}$, the Euclidean norm transported by $E$. If $E'$ is
the isomorphism of another inertial frame, then $E'^{-1}E$ and its inverse are
linear maps $\mathbb{R}^{4} \to \mathbb{R}^{4}$, so they are bounded with
constants $K, K' \ge 0$ ([[lem-euclidean-linear-maps-have-matrices-and-are-bounded]]):
$|v|_{E'} \le K'\,|v|_{E}$ and $|v|_{E} \le K\,|v|_{E'}$ for all $v \in V$.
The two transported norms are therefore equivalent, give the same limits, and
give the same notion of differentiability. The curve is **differentiable at
$s$** when the limit of the difference quotients as $h \to 0$ (over
$h \ne 0$, $s+h \in I$; one-sided at the endpoints of $I$) exists in $V$; then
this limit, written $x'(s) \in V$, is the **tangent vector** of $x$ at $s$, and
it does not depend on the inertial frame used to describe the convergence.

If $x_A : A \to \mathbb{R}^{4}$ is the global chart of an inertial frame
([[def-inertial-frame-and-inertial-chart]], [[lem-affine-minkowski-charts-form-a-smooth-atlas]]),
then $x$ is differentiable at $s$ exactly when the $\mathbb{R}^{4}$-valued map
$x_A \circ x$ is differentiable at $s$ in the sense of
[[def-vector-valued-derivative-and-integral]], because $E^{-1}$ is linear and
carries the difference quotients of $x$ to those of $x_A \circ x$; and then

$$x'(s) = E\bigl((x_A \circ x)'(s)\bigr),$$

where $E : \mathbb{R}^{4} \to V$ is the frame isomorphism
$E(u) = \sum_{a} u^{a} e_{a}$. This value does not depend on the inertial chart
used: two inertial charts are related by an affine bijection with an invertible
linear part ([[lem-affine-minkowski-charts-form-a-smooth-atlas]]), the chain
rule transports the coordinate derivative accordingly, and all norms on the
finite-dimensional space $V$ give the same limit.

The curve is **$C^{1}$** when it is differentiable at every point of $I$ and
the derivative map $s \mapsto x'(s)$, $I \to V$, is continuous, meaning that
the $\mathbb{R}^{4}$-valued map $s \mapsto (x_A \circ x)'(s)$ is continuous
([[def-vector-valued-functions-limits-and-continuity]]); by the equivalence of
transported norms this condition is independent of the inertial frame. It is
**$C^{k}$** for $k \ge 1$ when the derivative map is $C^{k-1}$, with the same
transported reading. A curve on a compact interval $[a,b]$ contained
in $I$ is **piecewise $C^{1}$** when there is a finite partition
$a = s_0 < s_1 < \cdots < s_m = b$ such that $x$ is $C^{1}$ on every open
subinterval $(s_{i-1},s_i)$ and the finite one-sided difference-quotient
derivatives at both ends of every piece exist in $V$. These are limits of
$\bigl(x(t+h)-x(t)\bigr)/h$ over the relevant side of the piece, not assertions
that $x'(s)$ has a limit as $s$ approaches a corner; their finiteness implies
continuity of $x$ at the corners (for a one-sided quotient derivative $v$ at $t$
one has $x(t+h)-x(t) = h\,(v+o(1))$ as $h \to 0$ on that side). No continuous
extension of the open-piece derivative is required. Derivatives at the endpoints
of $I$ are the one-sided difference-quotient limits over $I$.

### Causal character

Let $x$ be differentiable at $s \in I$. Then $x$ is **regular at $s$** if
$x'(s) \ne 0$; $x$ is **timelike** (respectively **null**, **spacelike**,
**causal**) **at $s$** if the vector $x'(s)$ is timelike (respectively null,
spacelike, causal) in the sense of
[[def-causal-classification-of-lorentz-vectors]], and $x$ is
**future-directed at $s$** if $x'(s)$ is future timelike or future null in the
sense of [[def-time-orientation-and-future-causal-sets]]. The zero vector has
no causal character, so only a regular curve has a causal character at $s$.

### Worldlines

A **future timelike worldline** (equivalently, a **massive worldline**) is a
$C^{1}$ curve $x : I \to A$ with $x'(s)$ future timelike for every $s \in I$; a
**future causal curve** (respectively a **future null curve**) is a $C^{1}$
curve with $x'(s)$ future causal (respectively future null) for every
$s \in I$. A **piecewise $C^{1}$ worldline** is a piecewise $C^{1}$ curve whose
tangents at every point of each open smooth piece and whose finite one-sided
difference-quotient tangents at both endpoints of every piece are future
timelike; a **$C^{k}$ worldline** is a worldline whose parametrization is
$C^{k}$. $C^{2}$ regularity is what makes the four-acceleration of
[[def-sr-four-velocity-and-four-acceleration]] available.

The parametrization is part of the curve: the image of a future timelike
worldline is also the image of the past-directed curve $s \mapsto x(-s)$, which
is not a worldline of this model, and no worldline or clock claim is attached to
it. The definition asserts the existence of no worldline beyond those given by
an explicit formula.

Let $(V,\eta)$ be a Lorentz vector space of signature $(-,+,+,+)$
([[def-lorentz-form-and-inertia]]), with associated quadratic form
$q(v)=\eta(v,v)$. A vector $v\in V$ is

- **timelike** when $q(v)<0$;
- **null**, or **lightlike**, when $v\neq 0$ and $q(v)=0$;
- **spacelike** when $q(v)>0$;
- **causal** when it is timelike or null.

The zero vector $0\in V$ satisfies $q(0)=0$ and is consequently **none** of
timelike, null or spacelike: the null case explicitly excludes it, and the
timelike and spacelike cases exclude it by $q(0)=0$ together with the strict
inequalities. The **causal character** of a nonzero vector $v$ is the sign of
the real number $q(v)$, and the three names are attached to the three signs as
above. When no confusion arises, the pairing $\eta$ itself is written
$\langle v,w\rangle:=\eta(v,w)$.

**Each nonzero vector has exactly one causal character.** For a nonzero
$v\in V$ the real number $q(v)$ satisfies exactly one of $q(v)<0$, $q(v)=0$,
$q(v)>0$ by trichotomy of the order on $\mathbb R$, so $v$ is timelike, null or
spacelike, and no two of the three alternatives can hold at once. The causal
vectors are therefore exactly the nonzero vectors that are timelike or null,
and the zero vector is causal in no sense introduced here.

derivations.claim: With $o:=x^{-1}(0,0,0,0)$ the axis is $W=\{o+\lambda e_0:\lambda\in\mathbb R\}$ and $e_\pm=x^{-1}(\lambda_\pm,0,0,0)=o+\lambda_\pm e_0$; the tangent of $W$ is the constant vector $e_0=n$ with $\eta(n,n)=-1$, so $W$ is a straight future timelike worldline and its proper-time function satisfies $\tau'(\lambda)=c^{-1}\sqrt{1}=1/c$, hence $\tau(\lambda)=\lambda/c+const$ by [F1] and [F4].

The hypotheses of the radar midpoint lemma [F3] are satisfied with $\lambda_\pm=x^0(q)\pm|r|$: since $|r|=0$ is excluded, $\lambda_-<\lambda_+$; the event $q$ has displacement $q-o=x^0(q)n+r_1e_1+r_2e_2+r_3e_3$ by [F4], so $q=o+\tfrac{\lambda_-+\lambda_+}{2}n+u$ with $u:=r_1e_1+r_2e_2+r_3e_3\in n^\perp$ and $|u|=|r|=(\lambda_+-\lambda_-)/2$, because $e_1,e_2,e_3$ span $n^\perp$ and the norm of $u$ is the Euclidean norm of the spatial part by [F4]. By [F3] the displacements $q-e_-$ and $e_+-q$ are future null; hence the radar protocol applies with emission $e_-$, reflection $q$ and reception $e_+$ by [F2].

The radar assignments of clause (ii): by [F2] and step 2.1, $\tau_{\mathrm{rad}}(q)=\tfrac12\bigl(\tau(\lambda_-)+\tau(\lambda_+)\bigr)$ and $\rho_{\mathrm{rad}}(q)=\tfrac{c}{2}\bigl(\tau(\lambda_+)-\tau(\lambda_-)\bigr)$, and substituting the proper-time function of step 1.1 gives $\tau_{\mathrm{rad}}(q)=\tfrac{\lambda_-+\lambda_+}{2c}+const=\tfrac{x^0(q)}{c}+const$ and $\rho_{\mathrm{rad}}(q)=\tfrac{c}{2}\cdot\tfrac{\lambda_+-\lambda_-}{c}=\tfrac{\lambda_+-\lambda_-}{2}=|r|$, where the additive constant is the same for all events measured by this observer. Hence the radar time is the chart time and the radar distance is the chart's rest-frame distance, up to the fixed additive constant of the following.

Clause (iii): by [F3] and step 2.1 the midpoint of the round trip is $m=\tfrac{e_-+e_+}{2}=x^{-1}\bigl(x^0(q),0,0,0\bigr)$, the displacement $q-m=u$ lies in $n^\perp$, and the rest distance in the slice $H(m,n)$ is $d_n(m,q)=|u|=|r|$, which equals $\rho_{\mathrm{rad}}(q)$ by step 3.1; and since $\tau_{\mathrm{rad}}$ differs from $x^0/c$ by a constant depending only on the observer, two events measured by this observer have equal radar times if and only if they have equal chart time $x^0$, so radar simultaneity coincides with chart simultaneity on the stated region.

Conclusion and scope: steps 1.1 and 2.1 prove (i) — the events $e_\pm$ lie on the observer's worldline and the two displacements are future null, so the operational protocol applies; steps 3.1 and 4.1 prove (ii) and (iii); clause (iv) is the honest qualification of the result: the deduction is conditional on the adopted ideal-clock and ideal-light postulates and the SI conventions, it identifies the operational content of inertial simultaneity as the two-way radar convention, and it asserts no one-way light-speed measurement without a synchronization convention, no empirical calibration and no result for accelerated, rotating or dispersive situations.

boundaries.evidence: The theorem excludes the axis events with $r=0$ from the region where the radar identification is asserted, so the distinguished empty-spatial case is handled as a hypothesis rather than by an empty computation. This disposition is part of the statement.

Step 3.1 computes $\rho_{\mathrm{rad}}(q)=\tfrac{\lambda_+-\lambda_-}{2}=|r|$, including the value zero at the boundary of the stated region; the additive constant of the observer's proper time is retained so the radar time is not fixed at zero.
One inertial observer and one straight axis are used; the theorem makes no claim about a second observer. This disposition is part of the statement.
The degenerate configuration $r=0$ is excluded by hypothesis, and clause (iv) records that no accelerated, rotating or dispersive situation is covered. This disposition is part of the statement.

The emission and reception parameters $\lambda_\pm=x^0(q)\pm|r|$ are strict because $|r|>0$, and the additive proper-time constant is carried through the comparison of radar times. This disposition is part of the statement.

The observer, the frame and the event $q$ are given data; the ideal apparatus and the ideal-light postulate are adopted assumptions, and no choice principle is used. This disposition is part of the statement.
Steps 2.1 and 3.1 prove the forward identifications: the radar time is the chart time and the radar distance is the chart rest-frame distance.
Step 4.1 proves the reverse operational reading: equal radar times are equal chart times, and the rest distance in the midpoint slice equals the radar distance.

Let $x:I\to A$ be a $C^2$ future timelike worldline with four-velocity $U=dx/d\tau$ and four-acceleration $A=dU/d\tau$ ([[def-sr-four-velocity-and-four-acceleration]], [[def-sr-regular-causal-curve-and-worldline]]), so that $\eta(U,U)=-c^2$ and $\eta(U,A)=0$ ([[thm-sr-proper-time-and-observer-decomposition]]), write $s$ for its given parameter and $\tau$ for its proper-time function, with $\tau'(s)>0$, and let $X:I\to V$ be a $C^1$ field along $x$ ([[def-vector-field-and-section-along-a-smooth-curve]]).

**(a) Fermi–Walker derivative.** The **Fermi–Walker derivative of $X$** is

$$\frac{D_{\mathrm{FW}}X}{d\tau}:=\frac{X'}{\tau'}-\frac{1}{c^2}\bigl(\eta(A,X)U-\eta(U,X)A\bigr),$$

where $X'$ denotes differentiation with respect to $s$ and $dX/d\tau:=X'/\tau'$. Here $\tau'=c^{-1}\sqrt{-\eta(x',x')}>0$ by [[def-sr-four-velocity-and-four-acceleration]]. The derivative $X'$ is the ordinary $V$-valued derivative of $X$, which is the covariant derivative of $X$ along $x$ in the flat model ([[def-flat-covariant-derivative-on-affine-minkowski-space]], clause (d)). The field $X$ is **Fermi–Walker transported along $x$** when $D_{\mathrm{FW}}X/d\tau=0$, that is, when

$$X'=\frac{\tau'}{c^2}\bigl(\eta(A,X)U-\eta(U,X)A\bigr).$$

**(b) The four-velocity is Fermi–Walker transported.** Substituting $X=U$ and using $\eta(A,U)=0$ and $\eta(U,U)=-c^2$ gives $D_{\mathrm{FW}}U/d\tau=U'/\tau'-c^{-2}\bigl(\eta(A,U)U-\eta(U,U)A\bigr)=A-A=0$.

**(c) Comparison with parallel transport.** If $A=0$ on an interval $J\subseteq I$, then on $J$ the Fermi–Walker equation reduces to $X'=0$ and coincides with ordinary parallel transport; if $A$ is not zero, the definition includes exactly the correction that also transports the time leg $U/c$ along the worldline.

**(d) Fermi–Walker transported tetrad.** A **Fermi–Walker transported tetrad along $x$** is a tuple $(E_0,E_1,E_2,E_3)$ of $C^1$ fields along $x$ with $\eta(E_a(s),E_b(s))=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)_{ab}$ at every $s\in I$, $E_0=U/c$ future, and every $E_a$ Fermi–Walker transported along $x$. These pairings make the four vectors a basis: pairing a linear relation with each $E_b$ forces every coefficient to vanish. Existence and uniqueness from initial data are proved in the following lemma; metric preservation is proved in the subsequent theorem. The physical interpretation as a nonrotating spatial frame carried by an accelerated observer is not asserted here; only the transport rule is defined.

Let $x:I\to A$ be a $C^2$ future timelike worldline with four-velocity $U$ and four-acceleration $A$ ([[def-sr-four-velocity-and-four-acceleration]], [[def-sr-regular-causal-curve-and-worldline]]), let $\tau_0\in I$ and $X_0\in V$. Then there is exactly one $C^1$ field $X:I\to V$ along $x$ with $D_{\mathrm{FW}}X/d\tau=0$ and $X(\tau_0)=X_0$ ([[def-sr-fermi-walker-transport]]); if $x$ is $C^k$ with $k\ge2$ then $X$ is $C^{k-1}$. The map $X_0\mapsto X$, from $V$ to the $C^1$ fields along $x$ satisfying the transport equation, is linear. Consequently, for every tetrad $(E_0(\tau_0),\dots,E_3(\tau_0))$ at $x(\tau_0)$ with $E_0(\tau_0)=U(\tau_0)/c$ there is a unique tuple of Fermi–Walker transported fields with those initial values; whether that tuple remains a tetrad at every time is proved in the following item.

Let $(A,V,\eta,C^+)$ be the affine Minkowski space with tangent spaces canonically identified with $V$ ([[def-sr-affine-minkowski-model]], [[lem-tangent-space-of-affine-minkowski-space-is-v]]), and let $\Omega\subseteq A$ be a nonempty open subset. All tensor fields below are $C^k$ fields in the sense of [[def-ck-tensor-field-on-minkowski-space]], with $k=\infty$ unless a clause says otherwise.

**(a) Vector fields.** For smooth vector fields $X,Y$ on $\Omega$ define the **covariant derivative of $Y$ in the direction $X$** at $p\in\Omega$ by

$$ igl(
abla_XY igr)(p):= rac{d}{dt}\Big|_{t=0}Y igl(p+tX(p) igr),$$

the derivative of the $V$-valued composite $t\mapsto Y(p+tX(p))$, which is defined for $t$ in a neighbourhood of $0$ because $\Omega$ is open ([[def-vector-valued-derivative-and-integral]], [[def-derivative]]). In the inertial chart $x$ of any inertial frame one has $(
abla_XY)^a=X^b\,\partial_bY^a$; the value does not depend on the inertial chart: for another inertial chart $x'=\Lambda x+b$ one has $\partial'_a=(\Lambda^{-1})^b_{\ a}\,\partial_b$ and $Y'^a=\Lambda^a_{\ b}Y^b$ ([[thm-sr-tensor-and-current-transformation]], [[def-inertial-frame-and-inertial-chart]]), and $\Lambda$ is constant, so $(\Lambda^{-1})^a_{\ c}\,X'^b\,\partial'_bY'^c=X^b\,\partial_bY^a$. The field $
abla_XY$ is again a smooth vector field on $\Omega$.

**(b) Covector and general tensor fields.** For a smooth covector field $\alpha$ set $(
abla_X\alpha)(Y):=X(\alpha(Y))-\alpha(
abla_XY)$ for every smooth vector field $Y$, and for a type $(r,s)$ tensor field $T$ define $
abla_XT$ by the derivation rule on the evaluation of $T$: for $T:(V^*)^r	imes V^s	o\mathbb R$,

$$(
abla_XT)(\alpha_1,\dots,\alpha_r;Y_1,\dots,Y_s)=X igl[T(\alpha_1,\dots,\alpha_r;Y_1,\dots,Y_s) igr]-\sum_{i=1}^rT(\alpha_1,\dots,
abla_X\alpha_i,\dots,\alpha_r;Y_1,\dots,Y_s)-\sum_{j=1}^sT(\alpha_1,\dots,\alpha_r;Y_1,\dots,
abla_XY_j,\dots,Y_s),$$

where the vector and covector arguments are smooth fields on $\Omega$. In inertial coordinates every component of $
abla_XT$ is $X^b\,\partial_b$ applied to that component, with no connection coefficients.

**(c) Properties.** The operator $
abla$ is $\mathbb R$-bilinear, is $C^\infty(\Omega)$-linear in $X$, and satisfies the Leibniz rules $
abla_X(fY)=X(f)Y+f
abla_XY$ and the analogous rules for tensor fields; it is metric compatible, $
abla\eta=0$, because $\partial_a\eta_{bc}=0$ in every inertial chart; it is torsion-free, $
abla_XY-
abla_YX=[X,Y]$, by the coordinate formula for the Lie bracket ([[def-lie-bracket-of-smooth-vector-fields]], [[prop-coordinate-formula-for-the-lie-bracket]]); and it has zero curvature, $
abla_X
abla_YZ-
abla_Y
abla_XZ-
abla_{[X,Y]}Z=0$, by equality of mixed partial derivatives of the components ([[thm-young-mixed-partial-theorem]]).

**(d) Fields along a curve.** If $\gamma:I	o A$ is a $C^1$ curve and $W:I	o V$ is a $C^1$ field along it ([[def-vector-field-and-section-along-a-smooth-curve]]), the **covariant derivative of $W$ along $\gamma$** is the ordinary $V$-valued derivative $DW/ds:=W'$ ([[def-vector-valued-derivative-and-integral]]), because the canonical identification $T_pA=V$ is independent of $p$; consequently parallel transport along any curve is the identity and a field is parallel exactly when it is constant. This derivative is the one used for the acceleration of congruences, for Fermi–Walker transport and for the kinematic decomposition below; the model needs no Christoffel symbols and no parallel-transport ODE in this formulation.

**(e) First-order $C^1$ version.** For $C^1$ vector fields $X,Y$ and $C^1$ covector or tensor fields on $\Omega$ the same directional and evaluation definitions are well-defined and have continuous coefficients: in an inertial chart $(
abla_XY)^a=X^b\partial_bY^a$, and each tensor component is differentiated in the same way. The component recovery and the subtraction of all argument derivatives remain valid; $C^1$ scalar multiplication satisfies the same first-order Leibniz rules; metric compatibility remains $
abla\eta=0$; and the first-order torsion identity uses the continuous coordinate bracket $[X,Y]^a=X^b\partial_bY^a-Y^b\partial_bX^a$. No $C^1$ closure of this bracket and no second covariant derivative of arbitrary $C^1$ data are asserted. For $C^2$ vector fields the second derivatives needed for the zero-curvature identity of (c) exist, and that identity follows by equality of the continuous mixed second partials. All smooth-field properties above and the $C^1$ along-curve derivative in (d) are retained.

Let $(A,V,\eta,C^+)$ be the affine Minkowski space of
[[def-sr-affine-minkowski-model]], with its inertial smooth structure
([[lem-affine-minkowski-charts-form-a-smooth-atlas]], [[def-smooth-manifold]]).
Let $\Omega\subseteq A$ be open, let $r,s\in\mathbb N$, and let
$k\in\mathbb N\cup\{\infty\}$. Empty $\Omega$ is allowed; it has the unique
empty field of each type.

Write $T^{r,s}(V)$ for the real vector space, under pointwise operations, of
multilinear maps $(V^*)^r\times V^s\to\mathbb R$
([[def-type-r-s-tensor-on-a-finite-dimensional-vector-space]],
[[def-algebraic-dual-and-linear-functional]]). Identify $T_pA$ with $V$ by
[[lem-tangent-space-of-affine-minkowski-space-is-v]]. For an inertial frame
$(o;e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$ with chart $x$, let $(e^{*a})$ be its dual basis,
defined by $e^{*a}(e_b)=\delta^a_b$
([[def-dual-family-associated-to-a-basis]]). The components of a map
$T:\Omega\to T^{r,s}(V)$ are

$$T^{a_1\dots a_r}{}_{b_1\dots b_s}(p):=T(p)(e^{*a_1},\dots,e^{*a_r},e_{b_1},\dots,e_{b_s}).$$

A **$\mathcal C^k$ type-$(r,s)$ tensor field on $\Omega$** is such a map for
which each component, regarded as a function of $u=x(p)$ on the open set
$x(\Omega)\subseteq\mathbb R^4$, is of class $C^k$ in the sense of
[[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]; for $k=\infty$ all finite
orders are required.

**Finite-dimensional construction and intrinsic regularity.** Put
$N=4^{r+s}\ge1$, with the component array ordered lexicographically. Every
array of $N$ real numbers defines exactly one tensor: expand each input as
$\alpha_i=\sum_a\alpha_i(e_a)e^{*a}$ and
$v_j=\sum_b e^{*b}(v_j)e_b$, then sum the array entries multiplied by
$\prod_i\alpha_i(e_{a_i})\prod_j e^{*b_j}(v_j)$. This is multilinear and
recovers the array by evaluation on the indicated basis inputs; multilinearity
forces the same formula for any tensor. Thus the component map is a linear
isomorphism $T^{r,s}(V)\to\mathbb R^N$. Pulling back the Euclidean norm gives
a norm on this space ([[def-norm-and-normed-space]]), and every norm makes it
Banach by [[cor-finite-dimensional-normed-spaces-are-banach]]. Any two norms
are equivalent by transporting them to $\mathbb R^N$ and applying
[[thm-all-norms-on-rn-are-equivalent]].

A change of inertial frame expresses each new basis and dual-basis vector as
a constant finite linear combination of the old ones; multilinearity therefore
makes the new component array an invertible constant linear transformation of
the old array. The coordinate precomposition is an invertible affine map by
[[lem-affine-minkowski-charts-form-a-smooth-atlas]]. Finite linear combinations
and affine precomposition preserve $C^k$: each first derivative follows from
[[thm-chain-rule-for-total-derivatives]], and successive derivatives repeat
that rule with constant affine coefficients. Applying the inverse transformations
proves the converse. Hence the definition is independent of frame. Continuous
partials give total derivatives by
[[thm-continuous-partial-derivatives-imply-total-differentiability]], and
induction on order gives the equivalent finite-dimensional Banach-space
$C^k$ definition of [[def-c-k-map-between-banach-spaces]] for $T\circ x^{-1}$.
The norm equivalence inequalities preserve the derivative remainder limits and
continuity of each iterated derivative, so this formulation is also independent
of norm. No definition of a Banach-space map with manifold domain is presumed.

A type-$(0,0)$ field is a **scalar field**, a $C^k$ real-valued function.
A type-$(1,0)$ field is a **vector field**, with the vector $v$ identified with
$\alpha\mapsto\alpha(v)$: conversely a linear functional $Q$ on $V^*$ has
$v=\sum_aQ(e^{*a})e_a$ and $Q(\alpha)=\alpha(v)$. A type-$(0,1)$ field is a
**covector field**, taking values in $V^*$.

Let $n$ be an observer congruence on a nonempty open subset $\Omega\subseteq A$ ([[def-sr-chart-tetrad-and-congruence-distinction]]), let $\nabla$ be the flat covariant derivative of the affine model ([[def-flat-covariant-derivative-on-affine-minkowski-space]]), and write $n_b:=\eta_{bc}n^c$ for the associated covector field ([[def-ck-tensor-field-on-minkowski-space]]).

**(a) Rest metric and projection.** Define $h(v,w):=\eta(v,w)+\eta(n,v)\eta(n,w)$ for vectors at the same point, so that $h=\eta+n^\flat\otimes n^\flat$ in components. Then $h(v,w)=\eta(h(v),h(w))$ for the orthogonal projection $h(v):=v+\eta(n,v)n$ of [[thm-sr-proper-time-and-observer-decomposition]] clause (c). At every point $h$ is symmetric with radical spanned by $n(p)$, and its restriction to $n(p)^\perp$ is positive definite ([[def-lorentz-orthogonality-and-orthogonal-complement]]).

**(b) Acceleration.** The **acceleration** of the congruence is $a:=\nabla_nn$. Then $\eta(n,a)=0$ pointwise, because $2\eta(n,\nabla_nn)=n\bigl(\eta(n,n)\bigr)=0$; consequently $a(p)$ is spacelike or zero by the causal classification ([[def-causal-classification-of-lorentz-vectors]]). In the model's physical interpretation the four-acceleration of the congruence observers is $c^2a$ and its magnitude is $c^2\sqrt{\eta(a,a)}$; the numerical units belong to the model's SI conventions and are not part of the affine geometry ([[def-sr-four-velocity-and-four-acceleration]]).

**(c) Kinematic decomposition.** Set $\theta_{ab}:=h_a{}^ch_b{}^d\nabla_{(c}n_{d)}$ and $\omega_{ab}:=h_a{}^ch_b{}^d\nabla_{[c}n_{d]}$, where $\nabla_{(c}n_{d)}=\tfrac12(\nabla_cn_d+\nabla_dn_c)$ and $\nabla_{[c}n_{d]}=\tfrac12(\nabla_cn_d-\nabla_dn_c)$. Then

$$\nabla_an_b=-n_aa_b+\theta_{ab}+\omega_{ab},$$

with $\theta$ symmetric, $\omega$ antisymmetric, both horizontal ($\theta_{ab}n^b=\omega_{ab}n^b=n^a\theta_{ab}=n^a\omega_{ab}=0$), and this decomposition is unique with these properties. The tensor $\theta$ is the **expansion (and shear) tensor**, $h^{ab}\theta_{ab}$ is the **expansion scalar** (write it as $\vartheta:=h^{ab}\theta_{ab}$ to distinguish it from the tensor), the **shear tensor** is $\sigma_{ab}:=\theta_{ab}-(\vartheta/3)h_{ab}$, and $\omega$ is the **vorticity 2-tensor**. Here $h^{ab}:=\eta^{ac}\eta^{bd}h_{cd}$ and all indices are moved with $\eta$.

**(d) Born rigidity.** For a smooth covariant two-tensor $T$, the Lie derivative used here is $(\mathcal L_nT)(X,Y):=n(T(X,Y))-T([n,X],Y)-T(X,[n,Y])$; brackets have the meaning given in the flat-derivative supplier. The congruence is **Born rigid** (it describes a rigid motion) when $\mathcal L_nh=0$. Since $(\mathcal L_nh)_{ab}=2\theta_{ab}$, Born rigidity is equivalent to $\theta_{ab}=0$ for every $a,b$, equivalently to the projected symmetrized derivative of $n^\flat$ vanishing.

**(e) Scope.** These are kinematic definitions for a prescribed smooth field $n$ on the affine model; no dynamical equation, matter model, global synchronization or completeness is assumed, and $a$, $\theta$, $\omega$ and $h$ are local objects on $\Omega$.

Let $\Omega$ be a nonempty open subset of $A$ ([[def-sr-affine-minkowski-model]]).

**(i) Flow box.** If $X$ is a smooth vector field on $\Omega$ ([[def-ck-tensor-field-on-minkowski-space]]) and $X(p)\ne0$ at a point $p\in\Omega$, then there is an open neighbourhood $U$ of $p$ in $\Omega$ and a chart $(u^0,u^1,u^2,u^3):U\to\mathbb R^4$ in which $X=\partial/\partial u^0$; the integral curves of $X$ in $U$ are therefore the $u^0$-coordinate lines up to reparametrization. In particular every observer congruence $n$ on $\Omega$ ([[def-sr-chart-tetrad-and-congruence-distinction]]) admits a local $n$-adapted chart, and in such a chart $n=\partial/\partial u^0$.

**(ii) Frobenius criterion.** For a smooth nowhere-zero one-form $\alpha$ on $\Omega$ ([[def-closed-and-exact-differential-forms]]) let $D:=\ker\alpha$ be the hyperplane distribution $D_p=\{v\in V:\alpha_p(v)=0\}$. Then $D$ is integrable on $\Omega$ (through every point there passes a local hypersurface whose tangent space at each of its points is the corresponding $D_p$) if and only if $\alpha\wedge d\alpha=0$ on $\Omega$ ([[def-wedge-product-of-differential-forms]]).

**(iii) Rest distributions of observer congruences.** Let $n$ be an observer congruence on $\Omega$ ([[def-sr-chart-tetrad-and-congruence-distinction]]), let $\alpha:=n^\flat$, and let $\theta,\omega$ be its expansion and vorticity ([[def-sr-observer-congruence-and-kinematics]]). Then:

(a) $d\alpha=2\nabla_{[a}n_{b]}$, that is, $d\alpha(X,Y)=(\nabla_Xn^\flat)(Y)-(\nabla_Yn^\flat)(X)$ for smooth vector fields $X,Y$;

(b) for every $p$ and all $X,Y$ with $\alpha(X)=\alpha(Y)=0$ one has $d\alpha(X,Y)=2\omega(X,Y)$; consequently $(\alpha\wedge d\alpha)(p)=0$ if and only if $\omega(p)=0$, and on an open set $U\subseteq\Omega$ the following are equivalent: $\alpha\wedge d\alpha=0$ on $U$, $\omega=0$ on $U$, and the rest distribution $\ker\alpha$ is integrable on $U$;

(c) when the rest distribution is integrable on $U$, its integral hypersurfaces are orthogonal to $n$ at every point and the restriction of $\eta$ to each of them is positive definite, so they are rest slices of the congruence.

**(iv) Scope.** All statements are local on $\Omega$; no global foliation, global synchronization, completeness or product structure is asserted, and no claim is made about variable-rank or non-smooth distributions.

For all real $x,y$,
$$\sinh(x+y)=\sinh x\cosh y+\cosh x\sinh y,\qquad\cosh(x+y)=\cosh x\cosh y+\sinh x\sinh y,$$
$$\cosh^2x-\sinh^2x=1,\qquad(\sinh x)'=\cosh x,\qquad(\cosh x)'=\sinh x.$$
Moreover $\sinh:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$ is odd, strictly increasing, and onto;
$\cosh:\mathbb R\to[1,\infty)$ is even and positive, and its restriction
to $[0,\infty)$ is strictly increasing and onto $[1,\infty)$; and
$\tanh:\mathbb R\to(-1,1)$ is strictly increasing and onto. On their declared domains,
$$(\tanh x)'=\operatorname{sech}^2x,\quad(\coth x)'=-\operatorname{csch}^2x,\quad(\operatorname{sech}x)'=-\operatorname{sech}x\tanh x,\quad(\operatorname{csch}x)'=-\operatorname{csch}x\coth x.$$

For $x\in\mathbb R$, define
$$\sinh x:=\frac{\exp x-\exp(-x)}2,\qquad\cosh x:=\frac{\exp x+\exp(-x)}2,$$
$$\tanh x:=\frac{\sinh x}{\cosh x},\qquad\operatorname{sech}x:=\frac1{\cosh x}.$$
For $x\ne0$, define
$$\coth x:=\frac{\cosh x}{\sinh x},\qquad\operatorname{csch}x:=\frac1{\sinh x}.$$

The positivity of $\exp$ makes $\cosh x>0$ for every $x$. If $x\ne0$, then
$x\ne-x$, so strict increase of $\exp$ makes $\exp x\ne\exp(-x)$; hence
$\sinh x\ne0$. Thus all four quotients above are defined on exactly their
stated domains ([[cor-exponential-reciprocal-and-positivity]],
[[thm-exponential-is-strictly-increasing]]).

Let $\alpha\in\Omega^k(M)$ and $\beta\in\Omega^\ell(M)$. Their **wedge product**
is the differential form defined pointwise by

$$ (\alpha\wedge\beta)_p:=\alpha_p\wedge\beta_p\in\operatorname{Alt}^{k+\ell}(T_pM). $$

The next proposition verifies that this pointwise field is smooth.

For $\omega\in\Omega^k(M)$, define the candidate $d\omega$ on smooth vector fields by $$d\omega(X_0,\ldots,X_k)=\sum_i(-1)^iX_i\omega(X_0,\widehat X_i,\ldots,X_k)+\sum_{i<j}(-1)^{i+j}\omega([X_i,X_j],X_0,\widehat X_i,\widehat X_j,\ldots,X_k).$$ The next lemma proves that this candidate is a form.

For the complex [[def-de-rham-cochain-complex]], put $Z^k(M)=\ker(d:\Omega^k(M)\to\Omega^{k+1}(M))$ and $B^k(M)=\operatorname{im}(d:\Omega^{k-1}(M)\to\Omega^k(M))$. A form is **closed** if it belongs to $Z^k$ and **exact** if it belongs to $B^k$.

If $\omega=d\eta$, then $d\omega=d^2\eta=0$ by [[thm-the-exterior-derivative-squares-to-zero]], so $B^k\subseteq Z^k$. In particular $B^0=0$, since $\Omega^{-1}=0$. The zero form is both closed and exact in every degree.

Let $X$ and $Y$ be smooth vector fields on $M$. Their **Lie bracket** is the
operator on smooth functions defined by

$$ [X,Y]f:=X(Yf)-Y(Xf). $$

The next results show that this commutator is again induced by a smooth vector
field on $M$.

Let $(A,V,\eta,C^+)$ be the affine Minkowski space with tangent spaces canonically identified with $V$ ([[def-sr-affine-minkowski-model]], [[lem-tangent-space-of-affine-minkowski-space-is-v]]), and let $\Omega\subseteq A$ be a nonempty open subset. All tensor fields below are $C^k$ fields in the sense of [[def-ck-tensor-field-on-minkowski-space]], with $k=\infty$ unless a clause says otherwise.

**(a) Vector fields.** For smooth vector fields $X,Y$ on $\Omega$ define the **covariant derivative of $Y$ in the direction $X$** at $p\in\Omega$ by

$$ igl(
abla_XY igr)(p):= rac{d}{dt}\Big|_{t=0}Y igl(p+tX(p) igr),$$

the derivative of the $V$-valued composite $t\mapsto Y(p+tX(p))$, which is defined for $t$ in a neighbourhood of $0$ because $\Omega$ is open ([[def-vector-valued-derivative-and-integral]], [[def-derivative]]). In the inertial chart $x$ of any inertial frame one has $(
