Work in the oriented time-oriented affine Minkowski space $(A,V,\eta,C^+)$ ([[def-sr-affine-minkowski-model]]) with its inertial atlas ([[lem-affine-minkowski-charts-form-a-smooth-atlas]]) and the canonical identification of tangent spaces with $V$ ([[lem-tangent-space-of-affine-minkowski-space-is-v]]). The objects defined below are, in general, different objects, and the distinctions between them are part of the definition.

**(a) Chart and inertial chart.** A **chart** of the model is a diffeomorphism $u:U\to u(U)$ from a nonempty open subset $U\subseteq A$ onto an open subset of $\mathbb R^4$ ([[def-diffeomorphism-and-local-diffeomorphism-of-manifolds]], [[def-smooth-manifold]]), written with components $(u^0,u^1,u^2,u^3)$. An **inertial chart** is the global chart $x(p)=E^{-1}(p-o)$ of an inertial frame $(o;e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$ ([[def-inertial-frame-and-inertial-chart]]). A general chart need not be inertial: if $x$ is an inertial chart and $N:x(U)\to\mathbb R^4$ is a diffeomorphism onto its image which is not the restriction of an affine map, then $u:=N\circ x$ is a chart that is not inertial, because if $u$ were the inertial chart of a frame then $x\circ u^{-1}=N^{-1}$ would be affine by [[lem-inertial-chart-transitions-are-affine-lorentz]] and hence $N=(N^{-1})^{-1}$ would be affine as the inverse of an affine bijection, a contradiction; the map $N(y)=(y^0,y^1+(y^0)^2,y^2,y^3)$ on $\mathbb R^4$ is an explicit example.

**(b) Tetrad at an event and tetrad field.** A **tetrad at $p\in A$** is an ordered basis $(e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$ of $V$ with $\eta(e_a,e_b)=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)_{ab}$ and $e_0$ future, $e_0\in C^+$ ([[def-causal-classification-of-lorentz-vectors]], [[def-time-orientation-and-future-causal-sets]]): this is the basis of an inertial frame without an origin and without the orientation condition. A **tetrad field** on a nonempty open subset $\Omega\subseteq A$ is a tuple $(E_0,E_1,E_2,E_3)$ of smooth vector fields on $\Omega$ ([[def-ck-tensor-field-on-minkowski-space]], type $(1,0)$) whose values at every $p\in\Omega$ form a tetrad at $p$. A tetrad field is **observer-adapted** to a prescribed congruence $n$ when $E_0=n$. Along a prescribed $C^1$ future timelike worldline $x:I\to A$, observer adaptation means $E_0(x(s))=x'(s)/\sqrt{-\eta(x'(s),x'(s))}$ whenever $x(s)\in\Omega$; this is its normalized future unit tangent ([[def-sr-regular-causal-curve-and-worldline]]).

**(c) Observer congruence.** An **observer congruence** on a nonempty open subset $\Omega\subseteq A$ is a smooth vector field $n:\Omega\to V$ with $\eta(n,n)=-1$ and $n(p)\in C^+$ for every $p\in\Omega$. Its **observers** are its maximal integral curves ([[def-integral-curve-of-a-vector-field]], [[thm-unique-maximal-integral-curve-through-each-point]]). Each observer is a future timelike worldline ([[def-sr-regular-causal-curve-and-worldline]]): its tangent at a parameter value $s$ is $n(x(s))$, which is future timelike, and it is regular because $\eta(n,n)=-1$ makes $n$ nowhere zero. **Completeness** of the integral curves, a global product structure of $\Omega$, and global synchronization are not asserted by this definition.

**(d) Adapted chart.** For a congruence $n$ on $\Omega$, an **$n$-adapted chart** is a chart $(u^0,u^1,u^2,u^3):U\to\mathbb R^4$ with $U$ a nonempty open subset of $\Omega$ whose spatial coordinates $u^1,u^2,u^3$ are constant along every integral curve of $n$ contained in $U$. No global adapted chart is asserted, and $u^0$ is not required to be affine.

**(e) Distinctions.** A chart need not be inertial, as in (a); a chart need not be $n$-adapted for any congruence. A tetrad field is not in general the coordinate frame of a chart: if $(E_0,E_1,E_2,E_3)$ is the coordinate frame of a chart $(v^0,v^1,v^2,v^3)$, that is, $E_a=\partial/\partial v^a$, then $[E_a,E_b]=0$ for all $a,b$ ([[def-lie-bracket-of-smooth-vector-fields]], [[prop-coordinate-formula-for-the-lie-bracket]]), so a tetrad field whose members do not commute pairwise is not the coordinate frame of a chart; no converse is claimed here. A congruence need not be the flow of a coordinate, and its pointwise rest spaces need not assemble into hypersurfaces; that integrability question is decided later on this page. In an inertial chart $x$ of $(o;e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$, the coordinate vector fields $\partial/\partial x^a=e_a$ form a constant tetrad field, with values equal to the frame's ordered basis under $T_pA=V$. Its time vector field $n=\partial/\partial x^0=e_0$ alone defines the congruence of stationary observers, whose integral curves are $s\mapsto x^{-1}(s+s_0,r^1,r^2,r^3)$ for fixed $s_0,r^1,r^2,r^3$. The chart, the ordered tetrad and the single vector field $n$ remain distinct objects.

Let $(V,\eta)$ be a Lorentz vector space of signature $(-,+,+,+)$
([[def-lorentz-form-and-inertia]]), with associated quadratic form
$q(v)=\eta(v,v)$. A vector $v\in V$ is

- **timelike** when $q(v)<0$;
- **null**, or **lightlike**, when $v\neq 0$ and $q(v)=0$;
- **spacelike** when $q(v)>0$;
- **causal** when it is timelike or null.

The zero vector $0\in V$ satisfies $q(0)=0$ and is consequently **none** of
timelike, null or spacelike: the null case explicitly excludes it, and the
timelike and spacelike cases exclude it by $q(0)=0$ together with the strict
inequalities. The **causal character** of a nonzero vector $v$ is the sign of
the real number $q(v)$, and the three names are attached to the three signs as
above. When no confusion arises, the pairing $\eta$ itself is written
$\langle v,w\rangle:=\eta(v,w)$.

**Each nonzero vector has exactly one causal character.** For a nonzero
$v\in V$ the real number $q(v)$ satisfies exactly one of $q(v)<0$, $q(v)=0$,
$q(v)>0$ by trichotomy of the order on $\mathbb R$, so $v$ is timelike, null or
spacelike, and no two of the three alternatives can hold at once. The causal
vectors are therefore exactly the nonzero vectors that are timelike or null,
and the zero vector is causal in no sense introduced here.

Let $(V,\eta)$ be a Lorentz vector space of signature $(-,+,+,+)$ and let
$(e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$ be an $\eta$-orthonormal ordered basis. Write
$v=v^0e_0+v^1e_1+v^2e_2+v^3e_3$ for the coordinates of $v$
([[thm-unique-coordinates-with-respect-to-an-ordered-basis]]) and

$$\lvert v_{\mathrm{vec}}\rvert:=\sqrt{(v^1)^2+(v^2)^2+(v^3)^2}.$$

Then $\eta(v,v)=-(v^0)^2+\lvert v_{\mathrm{vec}}\rvert^2$, and the timelike set
$T:=\{v\in V:\eta(v,v)<0\}$ satisfies

$$T=T_+\cup T_-,\qquad T_+:=\{v:v^0>\lvert v_{\mathrm{vec}}\rvert\},\qquad T_-:=\{v:v^0<-\lvert v_{\mathrm{vec}}\rvert\}.$$

The sets $T_+$ and $T_-$ are nonempty, disjoint, open in $V$ (for the metric
topology of the distance $d(u,w):=\lVert c(u)-c(w)\rVert_2$ induced by the
coordinates $c(v):=(v^0,v^1,v^2,v^3)$), convex and path-connected, and they are
exactly the two connected components of $T$. In every $\eta$-orthonormal
ordered basis the two displayed coordinate sets coincide with the two
components of $T$ in some order, and they may be interchanged relative to a
previously fixed naming of the components. Moreover

$$\operatorname{cl}(T_+)=\{v:v^0\ge\lvert v_{\mathrm{vec}}\rvert\},\qquad \operatorname{cl}(T_-)=\{v:v^0\le-\lvert v_{\mathrm{vec}}\rvert\},\qquad \operatorname{cl}(T_+)\cap\operatorname{cl}(T_-)=\{0\}.$$

Let $(V,\eta)$ be a Lorentz vector space of signature $(-,+,+,+)$
([[def-lorentz-form-and-inertia]]), with causal terminology as in
[[def-causal-classification-of-lorentz-vectors]], and let

$$T:=\{v\in V:\eta(v,v)<0\}$$

be its **timelike set**. Components and closures refer to the topology obtained
by using any ordered basis to identify $V$ with Euclidean $\mathbb R^4$;
[[lem-timelike-cone-has-two-convex-components]], step 5.1, proves that the
resulting open sets are independent of the basis. By that lemma the
set $T$ has exactly two connected components, and each of them is nonempty,
open, convex and path-connected. A **time orientation** of $(V,\eta)$ is a
choice of one of these two components. Fixing such a choice, write $C^+$ for the
chosen component and

$$C^-:=T\setminus C^+$$

for the other component; thus $T=C^+\sqcup C^-$ is a disjoint union and
$C^+$, $C^-$ are exactly the two components supplied by the lemma. Relative to
this choice a vector $v\in V$ is

- **future timelike** when $v\in C^+$;
- **past timelike** when $v\in C^-$;
- **future null** when $v\neq 0$, $\eta(v,v)=0$ and $v\in\operatorname{cl}(C^+)$;
- **past null** when $v\neq 0$, $\eta(v,v)=0$ and $v\in\operatorname{cl}(C^-)$;
- **future causal** when it is future timelike or future null;
- **past causal** when it is past timelike or past null.

The sets $\operatorname{cl}(C^+)$ and $\operatorname{cl}(C^-)$ are the
**future closed cone** and the **past closed cone** of the time-oriented space
$(V,\eta,C^+)$. By [[lem-timelike-cone-has-two-convex-components]] each of them
is a convex cone, their intersection is $\{0\}$, and a vector is causal exactly
when it is future causal or past causal, in which case exactly one of these two
alternatives holds: no nonzero vector is both future causal and past causal.
The timelike vectors are exactly the points of $T=C^+\cup C^-$, and
$0\notin T$ because $\eta(0,0)=0$; since a null vector is nonzero with
$\eta(v,v)=0$, no vector is both timelike and null, so the classes above are
mutually exclusive where the definitions say they are: no vector is both future
and past causal, and no timelike vector is null.

Let $A, B \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ with
$g[A] \subseteq B$ and let $f : B \to \mathbb{R}$, so that the composite
$f \circ g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ is defined. Let $c \in A$ be a limit point of
$A$ ([[def-limit-point-r]]) at which $g$ is differentiable
([[def-derivative]]), put $b := g(c)$, and suppose $b$ is a limit point of $B$
at which $f$ is differentiable. Then $f \circ g$ is differentiable at $c$ and

$$(f \circ g)'(c) \;=\; f'\bigl(g(c)\bigr)\,g'(c) .$$

**Both limit-point hypotheses are needed, and neither is automatic.** That $c$
is a limit point of $A$ is what makes $g'(c)$ and $(f \circ g)'(c)$ defined
symbols; that $b = g(c)$ is a limit point of $B$ is what makes $f'(b)$ one.
Nothing forces the second: $g$ may be differentiable at $c$ and send $c$ to an
isolated point of $B$, and there $f'(b)$ is not defined and the formula asserts
nothing.

**No case analysis appears anywhere.** The naive difference-quotient proof
writes $\frac{f(g(x)) - f(g(c))}{g(x) - g(c)} \cdot \frac{g(x) - g(c)}{x - c}$
and then has to say what happens where $g(x) = g(c)$, which may occur at points
arbitrarily close to $c$. Carathéodory's factorisation never divides by the
inner increment, so the difficulty does not arise.

Throughout, $\mathbb{R}$ is the complete ordered field
([[def-complete-ordered-field]]), neighbourhoods are those of
[[def-neighbourhood-r]] and limit points those of [[def-limit-point-r]].

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $f : A \to \mathbb{R}$ and let $c \in A$ be a
**limit point of $A$**. The **difference quotient of $f$ at $c$** is the function

$$q_{f,c} : A \setminus \{c\} \to \mathbb{R}, \qquad q_{f,c}(x) := \frac{f(x) - f(c)}{x - c} .$$

The division is legitimate at every point of the domain, since $x \ne c$ gives
$x - c \ne 0$.

**The point $c$ is a limit point of $A \setminus \{c\}$, not merely of $A$.**
For every real $\varepsilon > 0$ the punctured neighbourhood
$N^{*}_{\varepsilon}(c)$ omits $c$, so

$$N^{*}_{\varepsilon}(c) \cap A \;=\; N^{*}_{\varepsilon}(c) \cap (A \setminus \{c\}) ,$$

and the left-hand side is nonempty because $c$ is a limit point of $A$. So
$q_{f,c}$ is a function on a set having $c$ as a limit point, and
$\lim_{x \to c} q_{f,c}(x)$ is a notion that [[def-function-limit]] defines.

$f$ is **differentiable at $c$** when that limit exists, and then the
**derivative of $f$ at $c$** is

$$f'(c) \;:=\; \lim_{x \to c} q_{f,c}(x) \;=\; \lim_{x \to c} \frac{f(x) - f(c)}{x - c} .$$

**Two obligations are carried by that notation, and both are discharged here.**

1. **Uniqueness.** Writing $f'(c)$ treats the right-hand side as a name for a
   single real number. That is legitimate: $c$ is a limit point of the domain
   $A \setminus \{c\}$ of $q_{f,c}$, so at most one real can satisfy the
   $\varepsilon$-$\delta$ condition, by [[lem-function-limit-unique]] applied to
   $q_{f,c}$. Two reals both meeting the condition are therefore equal, and the
   symbol denotes.
2. **Meaningfulness.** The hypothesis that $c$ is a limit point of $A$ is not
   decoration. At an **isolated** point of $A$ the punctured condition
   $0 < |x - c| < \delta$ is met by no point of the domain at all, so the
   $\varepsilon$-$\delta$ formula is satisfied vacuously by *every* real at
   once; this is why [[def-function-limit]] leaves the limit undefined there,
   and it is why this library defines $f'(c)$ only at a limit point of $A$. At
   an isolated point of its domain a function is neither differentiable nor
   non-differentiable here: the question is not posed.

**The limit sees only $A \setminus \{c\}$, so how the difference quotient is
extended to $c$ is irrelevant.** Let $Q : A \to \mathbb{R}$ agree with
$q_{f,c}$ at every point of $A \setminus \{c\}$, and let $L \in \mathbb{R}$.
Then $\lim_{x \to c} Q(x) = L$ if and only if $\lim_{x \to c} q_{f,c}(x) = L$.
Both conditions read: for every real $\varepsilon > 0$ there is a real
$\delta > 0$ such that every point $x$ of the relevant domain with
$0 < |x - c| < \delta$ satisfies $|{\cdot} - L| < \varepsilon$
([[def-function-limit]]). The clause $0 < |x - c|$ removes $x = c$ from both
quantifiers, so in both cases the points quantified over are exactly the
$x \in A \setminus \{c\}$ with $0 < |x - c| < \delta$, at which $Q$ and
$q_{f,c}$ take the same value. The two conditions are the same condition.

**Differentiability on a set.** For $S \subseteq A$, $f$ is **differentiable on
$S$** when it is differentiable at every $c \in S$; implicit in that phrase is
that every point of $S$ is a limit point of $A$. $f$ is **differentiable** when
it is differentiable on the whole of $A$.

**Restriction of the domain.** Let $B \subseteq A$, let $c \in B$ and suppose
$c$ is a limit point of $B$. If $f$ is differentiable at $c$, then so is the
restriction $f|_B : B \to \mathbb{R}$, and

$$(f|_B)'(c) \;=\; f'(c) .$$

Indeed $B \setminus \{c\} \subseteq A \setminus \{c\}$; the displayed identity
of punctured neighbourhoods above, applied to $B$, shows that $c$ is a limit
point of $B \setminus \{c\}$; the difference quotient $q_{f|_B, c}$ is the
restriction of $q_{f,c}$ to $B \setminus \{c\}$, since $f|_B(c) = f(c)$; and
claim 2 of [[lem-limit-is-local]] carries the limit to that restriction.

**Every point of a nondegenerate interval is a limit point of it.** Let
$J \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ be order-convex ([[def-interval]]) with at least two
elements and let $p \in J$. Choose $q \in J$ with $q \ne p$, and let a real
$\varepsilon > 0$ be given. If $p < q$, put $y := p + \tfrac{1}{2}\min\{\varepsilon,\ q - p\}$;
then $p < y$, and $y - p \le \tfrac{1}{2}(q-p) < q - p$, so $p < y < q$ and
order-convexity gives $y \in J$, while $0 < |y - p| < \varepsilon$. If $q < p$,
the point $y := p - \tfrac{1}{2}\min\{\varepsilon,\ p - q\}$ serves in the same
way. So $N^{*}_{\varepsilon}(p) \cap J \ne \varnothing$ for every real
$\varepsilon > 0$, that is, $p$ is a limit point of $J$
([[def-limit-point-r]]).

Consequently, for $f$ defined on a nondegenerate interval $I$, the symbol
$f'(c)$ is meaningful at **every** $c \in I$, endpoints included. At an endpoint
the difference quotient is taken over the points of $I$ lying on the one side
that is available, so what other texts call a one-sided derivative is, here,
simply the derivative of $f$ on $I$.

For $x\in\mathbb R$, define
$$\sin x:=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{(-1)^nx^{2n+1}}{(2n+1)!},\qquad\cos x:=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{(-1)^nx^{2n}}{(2n)!}.$$

These are real power series in the sense of [[def-real-power-series-and-radius-of-convergence]]. Their convergence for every real argument is discharged by [[lem-sine-and-cosine-series-converge-everywhere]].

The functions $\sin$ and $\cos$ are differentiable on $\mathbb R$, with
$$(\sin x)'=\cos x,\qquad(\cos x)'=-\sin x.$$
Also $\sin0=0$ and $\cos0=1$.

For every real $x$,
$$\sin(-x)=-\sin x,\qquad\cos(-x)=\cos x,\qquad\sin^2x+\cos^2x=1.$$
Consequently $|\sin x|\le1$ and $|\cos x|\le1$.

For every real $x$,
$$\sin x=0\Longleftrightarrow x=m\pi\text{ for some }m\in\mathbb Z,\qquad \cos x=0\Longleftrightarrow x=(m+1/2)\pi\text{ for some }m\in\mathbb Z.$$
Both sine and cosine have period $2\pi$, and no smaller positive number is a common period.

The map $t\mapsto(\cos t,\sin t)$ is a bijection from $[0,2\pi)$ onto $S^1=\{(x,y)\in\mathbb R^2:x^2+y^2=1\}$. The conventions and prerequisite facts used below are recorded in [[cor-trigonometric-parity-and-pythagorean-identity]], [[thm-sine-cosine-signs-monotonicity-and-ranges]], [[thm-sine-cosine-zero-sets-and-fundamental-period]], [[def-pi-via-first-positive-cosine-zero]].

For $x>0$, define $\log x$ to be the unique real $y$ such that $\exp(y)=x$. This is well-defined because [[cor-exponential-is-a-bijection-onto-positive-reals]] states that $\exp:\mathbb R\to(0,\infty)$ is a bijection.

Thus $\log:(0,\infty)\to\mathbb R$ is the inverse function of $\exp$. In particular, $\log(\exp y)=y$ for every $y\in\mathbb R$ and $\exp(\log x)=x$ for every $x>0$.

In ZF, let $n\ge1$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open, let $f:U\to\mathbb R^n$ be smooth, and let $a\in U$. If $Df(a)$ is invertible, then there are open neighbourhoods $a\in V\subseteq U$ and $f(a)\in W$ such that $f|_V:V\to W$ is a diffeomorphism. Writing $g=(f|_V)^{-1}$,
$$Dg(y)=Df(g(y))^{-1}\qquad(y\in W).$$
No choice axiom is used.

Let $X$ be a smooth vector field on $M$, and let $p\in M$ satisfy $X_p\neq 0$.
Then there are local coordinates $(u^1,\dots,u^n)$ near $p$ in which

$$ X=\frac{\partial}{\partial u^1}. $$

derivations.claim: Preservation (a): write $s$ for the given parameter and $\tau'(s)>0$ for its proper-time derivative. By [F1], $X'=\tau'c^{-2}(\eta(A,X)U-\eta(U,X)A)$ and likewise for $Y$. Bilinearity gives $\frac{d}{ds}\eta(X,Y)=\eta(X',Y)+\eta(X,Y')=\tau'c^{-2}[\eta(A,X)\eta(U,Y)-\eta(U,X)\eta(A,Y)+\eta(A,Y)\eta(U,X)-\eta(U,Y)\eta(A,X)]=0$. The two pairs cancel, so the scalar pairing is constant on the interval by [[cor-zero-derivative-implies-constant]]; the fields are $C^1$, including continuity at any included endpoints. Norms and orthogonality are therefore preserved. For the unique transported fields with prescribed tetrad initial values, all pairings remain $\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)_{ab}$, and the time leg is $U/c$ because [F1] makes $U/c$ transported with the same initial value. Hence the family remains an observer-adapted tetrad.

Rindler coordinates (b), part 1: the map $\Phi(\theta,\rho,y,z)=(\rho\sinh\theta,\rho\cosh\theta,y,z)$ is smooth on $\mathbb R\times(0,\infty)\times\mathbb R^2$ by [F4] and [F8], and its image is contained in $W$ because $\cosh\theta>|\sinh\theta|$ for every $\theta$; conversely, for $(x^0,x)$ with $x>|x^0|$ the numbers $\rho:=\sqrt{x^2-(x^0)^2}>0$ and $\theta:=\tfrac12\log\bigl((x+x^0)/(x-x^0)\bigr)\in\mathbb R$ are well defined, and the identities $\rho\sinh\theta=x^0$, $\rho\cosh\theta=x$ follow from $e^{\pm\theta}=\sqrt{(x\pm x^0)/(x\mp x^0)}$ and $\cosh^2-\sinh^2=1$; hence $\Phi$ is a bijection of its domain onto $W$. Its $(\theta,\rho)$ derivative block has determinant $\rho(\cosh^2\theta-\sinh^2\theta)=\rho>0$ and the transverse block is the identity; the inverse-function theorem in [F10] therefore makes its inverse smooth locally at every point of $W$, hence smooth on $W$. Differentiating the four component functions gives $dx^0=\sinh\theta\,d\rho+\rho\cosh\theta\,d\theta$ and $dx=\cosh\theta\,d\rho+\rho\sinh\theta\,d\theta$, so the pullback metric is $-(\sinh\theta\,d\rho+\rho\cosh\theta\,d\theta)^2+(\cosh\theta\,d\rho+\rho\sinh\theta\,d\theta)^2+dy^2+dz^2=d\rho^2-\rho^2d\theta^2+dy^2+dz^2$, the cross terms cancelling and the $\sinh^2-\cosh^2=-1$ identity producing the term $-\rho^2d\theta^2$.

Computing the symmetric derivative of the components $\eta_{ab}K^b=(-1,-\tfrac{\Omega}{c}x^2,\tfrac{\Omega}{c}x^1,0)$ gives $\partial_a(\eta K)_b+\partial_b(\eta K)_a=0$: the only nonzero first partials are $\partial_1(\eta K)_2=\Omega/c$ and $\partial_2(\eta K)_1=-\Omega/c$, which cancel in the symmetrization, so $K$ is a Killing field.

e0$. boundaries.evidence: The theorem is a conjunction of explicit constructions: the Rindler map and the rotating and Bell-type fields are displayed on nonempty open sets, and no empty quantifier occurs. This disposition is part of the statement.

Zero cases are included: $\Omega=0$ makes the rotating congruence inertial and irrotational, and the Rindler acceleration is nonzero but its theta-slice metric is constant; step 2.2 treats $\Omega=0$ explicitly.
Clause (b) computes the single Rindler congruence and clause (c) restricts to the single ring cylinder; the ring offset is the one-turn integral. This disposition is part of the statement.

The degenerate vorticity cases are separated: the rotating field has nowhere-zero vorticity for $\Omega\ne0$, while the one-dimensional ring rest distribution is locally integrable with nonzero global holonomy (steps 2.2, 3.1, 4.1).

The ring integral is taken from $\varphi=0$ to $2\pi$, including both endpoints of one positive circuit; the strict inequality $|\Omega|R<c$ keeps the cylinder timelike. This disposition is part of the statement.

Every construction is displayed; the Fermi-Walker tetrad is produced by the linear existence-uniqueness theory, and the scope note records that no choice principle is used. This disposition is part of the statement.
Step 1.1 proves the forward preservation direction for Fermi-Walker transported fields, and step 2.2 proves integrability $\Rightarrow$ $omega=0$ via the Frobenius form.
Step 2.1 proves the reverse reading for the Rindler slices (rest distribution integrable with $\omega=0$), and step 4.1 proves that no single-valued synchronization function exists on the ring.

An **oriented time-oriented affine Minkowski space** is a quadruple
$(A,V,\eta,C^+)$ with the following data. In this notation $V$ includes its
specified orientation; forgetting that orientation gives only the underlying
real vector space, not the full datum $V$ of the model.

1. A nonempty affine space $A$ over a $4$-dimensional real vector space $V$,
   with action $(p,v)\mapsto p+v$ and displacement $q-p\in V$
   ([[def-affine-space-and-displacement]]). In particular $V$ is a real vector
   space of dimension $4$.
2. A Lorentz form $\eta$ on $V$, i.e. a nondegenerate symmetric bilinear form of
   inertia $(3,1,0)$ ([[def-lorentz-form-and-inertia]]). Its associated quadratic
   form is $q(v)=\eta(v,v)$.
3. An **orientation** of $V$: a positive ray of the determinant line
   $\Lambda^4V$, fixed once and for all
   ([[def-determinant-line-orientation-of-a-finite-dimensional-real-vector-space]]).
4. A **time orientation** $C^+$ of $(V,\eta)$: one of the two connected
   components of the timelike set $T=\{v\in V:\eta(v,v)<0\}$, the other being
   $C^-:=T\setminus C^+$ ([[def-time-orientation-and-future-causal-sets]]).

The following terminology is attached to such a quadruple.

- The elements $p$ of $A$ are the **events**; for events $p,q$ the vector
  $q-p\in V$ is the **displacement from $p$ to $q$**.
- The **interval** of $p,q\in A$ is the real number
  $I(p,q):=\eta(q-p,q-p)=q(q-p)$.
- Events $p,q$ are **timelike**, **null**, **spacelike** or **causally
  related** when the displacement $q-p$ is timelike, null, spacelike or causal
  in the sense of [[def-causal-classification-of-lorentz-vectors]]; they are
  **future-related** when $q-p$ is future causal and **past-related** when
  $q-p$ is past causal in the sense of
  [[def-time-orientation-and-future-causal-sets]].

**No point of $A$ is distinguished.** For every $v\in V$ the translation
$\tau_v:A\to A$, $\tau_v(p):=p+v$, is a bijection, since it is inverse to
$\tau_{-v}$: $\tau_{-v}(\tau_v(p))=(p+v)+(-v)=p+(v-v)=p$ and symmetrically, by
the affine action axioms ([[def-affine-space-and-displacement]]). Displacements
are translation invariant, $\tau_v(q)-\tau_v(p)=q-p$, so every $\tau_v$ preserves
the interval, the causal classification of every ordered pair, and the sets
$C^+$, $C^-$ (which are subsets of $V$, independent of the point of $A$); it
changes only the labelling of points. The mathematical structure of the model is
exactly the quadruple $(A,V,\eta,C^+)$; no derived physical quantity (proper
time, four-velocity, momentum, energy, charge or any field) is part of this
definition, and all later structure of the framework (frames, charts, tensor
fields, worldlines) is built on this model.

**Well-definedness.** The affine-space definition supplies the action and the
unique displacements; the Lorentz-form definition supplies $\eta$ and its
inertia; the determinant-line definition supplies orientations; and the two
components of $T$ between which the time-orientation definition chooses exist by
the components lemma recorded in the well-definedness clause of
[[def-time-orientation-and-future-causal-sets]], which is also what makes the
names future and past causal in item 4 well defined.

Let $(A,V,\eta,C^+)$ be the affine Minkowski space of
[[def-sr-affine-minkowski-model]], with its inertial smooth structure
([[lem-affine-minkowski-charts-form-a-smooth-atlas]], [[def-smooth-manifold]]).
Let $\Omega\subseteq A$ be open, let $r,s\in\mathbb N$, and let
$k\in\mathbb N\cup\{\infty\}$. Empty $\Omega$ is allowed; it has the unique
empty field of each type.

Write $T^{r,s}(V)$ for the real vector space, under pointwise operations, of
multilinear maps $(V^*)^r\times V^s\to\mathbb R$
([[def-type-r-s-tensor-on-a-finite-dimensional-vector-space]],
[[def-algebraic-dual-and-linear-functional]]). Identify $T_pA$ with $V$ by
[[lem-tangent-space-of-affine-minkowski-space-is-v]]. For an inertial frame
$(o;e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$ with chart $x$, let $(e^{*a})$ be its dual basis,
defined by $e^{*a}(e_b)=\delta^a_b$
([[def-dual-family-associated-to-a-basis]]). The components of a map
$T:\Omega\to T^{r,s}(V)$ are

$$T^{a_1\dots a_r}{}_{b_1\dots b_s}(p):=T(p)(e^{*a_1},\dots,e^{*a_r},e_{b_1},\dots,e_{b_s}).$$

A **$\mathcal C^k$ type-$(r,s)$ tensor field on $\Omega$** is such a map for
which each component, regarded as a function of $u=x(p)$ on the open set
$x(\Omega)\subseteq\mathbb R^4$, is of class $C^k$ in the sense of
[[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]; for $k=\infty$ all finite
orders are required.

**Finite-dimensional construction and intrinsic regularity.** Put
$N=4^{r+s}\ge1$, with the component array ordered lexicographically. Every
array of $N$ real numbers defines exactly one tensor: expand each input as
$\alpha_i=\sum_a\alpha_i(e_a)e^{*a}$ and
$v_j=\sum_b e^{*b}(v_j)e_b$, then sum the array entries multiplied by
$\prod_i\alpha_i(e_{a_i})\prod_j e^{*b_j}(v_j)$. This is multilinear and
recovers the array by evaluation on the indicated basis inputs; multilinearity
forces the same formula for any tensor. Thus the component map is a linear
isomorphism $T^{r,s}(V)\to\mathbb R^N$. Pulling back the Euclidean norm gives
a norm on this space ([[def-norm-and-normed-space]]), and every norm makes it
Banach by [[cor-finite-dimensional-normed-spaces-are-banach]]. Any two norms
are equivalent by transporting them to $\mathbb R^N$ and applying
[[thm-all-norms-on-rn-are-equivalent]].

A change of inertial frame expresses each new basis and dual-basis vector as
a constant finite linear combination of the old ones; multilinearity therefore
makes the new component array an invertible constant linear transformation of
the old array. The coordinate precomposition is an invertible affine map by
[[lem-affine-minkowski-charts-form-a-smooth-atlas]]. Finite linear combinations
and affine precomposition preserve $C^k$: each first derivative follows from
[[thm-chain-rule-for-total-derivatives]], and successive derivatives repeat
that rule with constant affine coefficients. Applying the inverse transformations
proves the converse. Hence the definition is independent of frame. Continuous
partials give total derivatives by
[[thm-continuous-partial-derivatives-imply-total-differentiability]], and
induction on order gives the equivalent finite-dimensional Banach-space
$C^k$ definition of [[def-c-k-map-between-banach-spaces]] for $T\circ x^{-1}$.
The norm equivalence inequalities preserve the derivative remainder limits and
continuity of each iterated derivative, so this formulation is also independent
of norm. No definition of a Banach-space map with manifold domain is presumed.

A type-$(0,0)$ field is a **scalar field**, a $C^k$ real-valued function.
A type-$(1,0)$ field is a **vector field**, with the vector $v$ identified with
$\alpha\mapsto\alpha(v)$: conversely a linear functional $Q$ on $V^*$ has
$v=\sum_aQ(e^{*a})e_a$ and $Q(\alpha)=\alpha(v)$. A type-$(0,1)$ field is a
**covector field**, taking values in $V^*$.

Let $n$ be an observer congruence on a nonempty open subset $\Omega\subseteq A$ ([[def-sr-chart-tetrad-and-congruence-distinction]]), let $\nabla$ be the flat covariant derivative of the affine model ([[def-flat-covariant-derivative-on-affine-minkowski-space]]), and write $n_b:=\eta_{bc}n^c$ for the associated covector field ([[def-ck-tensor-field-on-minkowski-space]]).

**(a) Rest metric and projection.** Define $h(v,w):=\eta(v,w)+\eta(n,v)\eta(n,w)$ for vectors at the same point, so that $h=\eta+n^\flat\otimes n^\flat$ in components. Then $h(v,w)=\eta(h(v),h(w))$ for the orthogonal projection $h(v):=v+\eta(n,v)n$ of [[thm-sr-proper-time-and-observer-decomposition]] clause (c). At every point $h$ is symmetric with radical spanned by $n(p)$, and its restriction to $n(p)^\perp$ is positive definite ([[def-lorentz-orthogonality-and-orthogonal-complement]]).

**(b) Acceleration.** The **acceleration** of the congruence is $a:=\nabla_nn$. Then $\eta(n,a)=0$ pointwise, because $2\eta(n,\nabla_nn)=n\bigl(\eta(n,n)\bigr)=0$; consequently $a(p)$ is spacelike or zero by the causal classification ([[def-causal-classification-of-lorentz-vectors]]). In the model's physical interpretation the four-acceleration of the congruence observers is $c^2a$ and its magnitude is $c^2\sqrt{\eta(a,a)}$; the numerical units belong to the model's SI conventions and are not part of the affine geometry ([[def-sr-four-velocity-and-four-acceleration]]).

**(c) Kinematic decomposition.** Set $\theta_{ab}:=h_a{}^ch_b{}^d\nabla_{(c}n_{d)}$ and $\omega_{ab}:=h_a{}^ch_b{}^d\nabla_{[c}n_{d]}$, where $\nabla_{(c}n_{d)}=\tfrac12(\nabla_cn_d+\nabla_dn_c)$ and $\nabla_{[c}n_{d]}=\tfrac12(\nabla_cn_d-\nabla_dn_c)$. Then

$$\nabla_an_b=-n_aa_b+\theta_{ab}+\omega_{ab},$$

with $\theta$ symmetric, $\omega$ antisymmetric, both horizontal ($\theta_{ab}n^b=\omega_{ab}n^b=n^a\theta_{ab}=n^a\omega_{ab}=0$), and this decomposition is unique with these properties. The tensor $\theta$ is the **expansion (and shear) tensor**, $h^{ab}\theta_{ab}$ is the **expansion scalar** (write it as $\vartheta:=h^{ab}\theta_{ab}$ to distinguish it from the tensor), the **shear tensor** is $\sigma_{ab}:=\theta_{ab}-(\vartheta/3)h_{ab}$, and $\omega$ is the **vorticity 2-tensor**. Here $h^{ab}:=\eta^{ac}\eta^{bd}h_{cd}$ and all indices are moved with $\eta$.

**(d) Born rigidity.** For a smooth covariant two-tensor $T$, the Lie derivative used here is $(\mathcal L_nT)(X,Y):=n(T(X,Y))-T([n,X],Y)-T(X,[n,Y])$; brackets have the meaning given in the flat-derivative supplier. The congruence is **Born rigid** (it describes a rigid motion) when $\mathcal L_nh=0$. Since $(\mathcal L_nh)_{ab}=2\theta_{ab}$, Born rigidity is equivalent to $\theta_{ab}=0$ for every $a,b$, equivalently to the projected symmetrized derivative of $n^\flat$ vanishing.

**(e) Scope.** These are kinematic definitions for a prescribed smooth field $n$ on the affine model; no dynamical equation, matter model, global synchronization or completeness is assumed, and $a$, $\theta$, $\omega$ and $h$ are local objects on $\Omega$.

Let $c > 0$ and let $(A,V,\eta,C^{+})$ be an oriented time-oriented affine
Minkowski space ([[def-sr-affine-minkowski-model]]).

**(a) Norm of the four-velocity.** Let $x : I \to A$ be a $C^{1}$ future
timelike worldline with four-velocity $U$
([[def-sr-four-velocity-and-four-acceleration]]). Then
$\eta(U(s),U(s)) = -c^{2}$ for every $s \in I$; equivalently the dimensionless
four-velocity $u = U/c$ satisfies $\eta(u,u) = -1$, and $U(s)$ is future
timelike. Thus the dimensionless four-velocity lies on the future unit
hyperboloid $\{v \in C^{+}:\eta(v,v)=-1\}$.

**(b) Orthogonality of the four-acceleration.** If $x$ is $C^{2}$ at $s$, then
$\eta(U(s),A(s)) = 0$: the four-acceleration has no component along the
four-velocity; if in addition $A(s) \ne 0$, then $A(s)$ is spacelike.

**(c) Rest space and projection.** Let $n \in V$ be future unit timelike,
$\eta(n,n) = -1$, and put $n^{\perp} := \{\,v \in V : \eta(n,v) = 0\,\}$
([[def-lorentz-orthogonality-and-orthogonal-complement]]). Then $n^{\perp}$ is a
3-dimensional linear subspace of $V$, the restriction of $\eta$ to $n^{\perp}$
is positive definite, and the map $h : V \to V$, $h(v) := v + \eta(n,v)\,n$, is
linear, idempotent with $h \circ h = h$, has image $n^{\perp}$ and kernel
$\operatorname{span}(n)$, satisfies $h(n) = 0$ and $\eta(n,h(v)) = 0$ for all
$v \in V$, and every $v \in V$ has the unique decomposition
$v = -\eta(n,v)\,n + h(v)$. Moreover $|w| := \sqrt{\eta(w,w)}$ defines a norm
on $n^{\perp}$.

**(d) Relative velocity and Lorentz factor.** Let $n$ and $u$ be future unit
timelike vectors, put $\gamma := -\eta(n,u)$ and $w := c\,h(u)/\gamma$. Then
$\gamma \ge 1$, $w$ lies in $n^{\perp}$,
$u = \gamma\,(n + w/c)$, $|w|^{2} = c^{2}(1-\gamma^{-2}) < c^{2}$,
$\gamma = (1-|w|^{2}/c^{2})^{-1/2}$, and $\gamma = 1$ if and only if $u = n$.
The vector $w$ is the velocity of a worldline with four-velocity $cu$ relative
to the observer $n$, and $\gamma$ is its Lorentz factor.

**(e) Coordinate form.** Let $(o;e_0,\dots,e_3)$ be an inertial frame and let
$y$ be a $C^{1}$ future timelike worldline whose inertial coordinates are
$t \mapsto (ct,r(t))$, with coordinate velocity $w(t) := r'(t)$ in
$\mathbb{R}^{3}$ and, when $y$ is $C^{2}$, coordinate acceleration
$a(t) := w'(t)$. Then $|w(t)| < c$, the four-velocity is
$U = \gamma_w\,(c,w)$ with $\gamma_w := (1-|w|^{2}/c^{2})^{-1/2}$, and the
four-acceleration is $A = \gamma_w\,\frac{d}{dt}\bigl(\gamma_w(c,w)\bigr)$, so
that

$$A^{0} = \gamma_w^{4}\,\frac{w \cdot a}{c}, \qquad A_{\mathrm{vec}} = \gamma_w^{2}\,a + \gamma_w^{4}\,\frac{(w \cdot a)\,w}{c^{2}} ;$$

consequently
$\eta(A,A) = \gamma_w^{4}|a|^{2} + \gamma_w^{6}(w \cdot a)^{2}/c^{2} \ge 0$,
with $\eta(A,A) = 0$ if and only if $a = 0$, and $\eta(U,A) = 0$. For the
observer $n = e_0$ of the chart, clauses (c) and (d) specialize to
$\gamma = \gamma_w$ and $w_{\mathrm{rel}} = (0,w)$ in the frame coordinates, identified with $w$ via the spatial basis.

**(f) Scope.** The statement is a theorem about the affine Minkowski model with
a fixed positive constant $c$; it asserts no clock reading and identifies no
physical four-velocity. No choice principle is used.

Let $(V,\eta)$ be a Lorentz vector space of signature $(-,+,+,+)$
([[def-lorentz-form-and-inertia]]). Two vectors $u,v\in V$ are
**$\eta$-orthogonal**, written $u\perp v$, when $\eta(u,v)=0$. For a subset
$S\subseteq V$ the **orthogonal complement** of $S$ is

$$S^{\perp}:=\{v\in V:\eta(v,s)=0\text{ for every }s\in S\},$$

and for a vector $u$ one writes $u^{\perp}:=\{u\}^{\perp}$.

**Elementary properties.** For every subset $S\subseteq V$:

- $S^{\perp}$ is a linear subspace of $V$: if $v,w\in S^{\perp}$ and
  $\lambda\in\mathbb R$, then for every $s\in S$ bilinearity gives
  $\eta(v+\lambda w,s)=\eta(v,s)+\lambda\eta(w,s)=0$, so $v+\lambda w\in S^{\perp}$.
  In particular the zero vector lies in $S^{\perp}$ and $S^{\perp}$ is never
  empty.
- $S\subseteq (S^{\perp})^{\perp}$: if $s\in S$, then $\eta(v,s)=0$ for every
  $v\in S^{\perp}$ by the definition of $S^{\perp}$, and symmetry of $\eta$
  gives $\eta(s,v)=0$ for every $v\in S^{\perp}$, that is,
  $s\in(S^{\perp})^{\perp}$.
- $S^{\perp}=(\operatorname{span}S)^{\perp}$: the inclusion
  $S\subseteq\operatorname{span}S$ gives
  $(\operatorname{span}S)^{\perp}\subseteq S^{\perp}$; conversely, if
  $v\in S^{\perp}$ and $u=\sum_i\lambda_i s_i$ is a finite linear combination
  with $s_i\in S$, then linearity in the second argument gives
  $\eta(v,u)=\sum_i\lambda_i\eta(v,s_i)=0$, so $v\in(\operatorname{span}S)^{\perp}$.

In particular, for every $u\in V$ one has $u\in u^{\perp}$ exactly when
$\eta(u,u)=0$, that is, exactly when $u$ is null or $u=0$
([[def-causal-classification-of-lorentz-vectors]]).

**A nonzero vector can be orthogonal to itself.** Take a basis
$e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3$ of $V$ in which the matrix of $\eta$ is diagonal with
diagonal entries $-1,1,1,1$; such a basis exists by clause 2 of the definition
of a Lorentz form. Then $v:=e_0+e_1$ is nonzero while
$\eta(v,v)=\eta(e_0,e_0)+2\eta(e_0,e_1)+\eta(e_1,e_1)=-1+0+1=0$, so
$v\in v^{\perp}$ with $v\neq 0$. This is exactly what fails for a
positive-definite inner product and is why orthogonal complements in a Lorentz
vector space need not be positive definite.

Let $X$ be a smooth vector field on $M$, and let $p\in M$ satisfy $X_p\neq 0$.
Then there are local coordinates $(u^1,\dots,u^n)$ near $p$ in which

$$ X=\frac{\partial}{\partial u^1}. $$

Let $\Omega$ be a nonempty open subset of $A$ ([[def-sr-affine-minkowski-model]]).

**(i) Flow box.** If $X$ is a smooth vector field on $\Omega$ ([[def-ck-tensor-field-on-minkowski-space]]) and $X(p)\ne0$ at a point $p\in\Omega$, then there is an open neighbourhood $U$ of $p$ in $\Omega$ and a chart $(u^0,u^1,u^2,u^3):U\to\mathbb R^4$ in which $X=\partial/\partial u^0$; the integral curves of $X$ in $U$ are therefore the $u^0$-coordinate lines up to reparametrization. In particular every observer congruence $n$ on $\Omega$ ([[def-sr-chart-tetrad-and-congruence-distinction]]) admits a local $n$-adapted chart, and in such a chart $n=\partial/\partial u^0$.

**(ii) Frobenius criterion.** For a smooth nowhere-zero one-form $\alpha$ on $\Omega$ ([[def-closed-and-exact-differential-forms]]) let $D:=\ker\alpha$ be the hyperplane distribution $D_p=\{v\in V:\alpha_p(v)=0\}$. Then $D$ is integrable on $\Omega$ (through every point there passes a local hypersurface whose tangent space at each of its points is the corresponding $D_p$) if and only if $\alpha\wedge d\alpha=0$ on $\Omega$ ([[def-wedge-product-of-differential-forms]]).

**(iii) Rest distributions of observer congruences.** Let $n$ be an observer congruence on $\Omega$ ([[def-sr-chart-tetrad-and-congruence-distinction]]), let $\alpha:=n^\flat$, and let $\theta,\omega$ be its expansion and vorticity ([[def-sr-observer-congruence-and-kinematics]]). Then:

(a) $d\alpha=2\nabla_{[a}n_{b]}$, that is, $d\alpha(X,Y)=(\nabla_Xn^\flat)(Y)-(\nabla_Yn^\flat)(X)$ for smooth vector fields $X,Y$;

(b) for every $p$ and all $X,Y$ with $\alpha(X)=\alpha(Y)=0$ one has $d\alpha(X,Y)=2\omega(X,Y)$; consequently $(\alpha\wedge d\alpha)(p)=0$ if and only if $\omega(p)=0$, and on an open set $U\subseteq\Omega$ the following are equivalent: $\alpha\wedge d\alpha=0$ on $U$, $\omega=0$ on $U$, and the rest distribution $\ker\alpha$ is integrable on $U$;

(c) when the rest distribution is integrable on $U$, its integral hypersurfaces are orthogonal to $n$ at every point and the restriction of $\eta$ to each of them is positive definite, so they are rest slices of the congruence.

**(iv) Scope.** All statements are local on $\Omega$; no global foliation, global synchronization, completeness or product structure is asserted, and no claim is made about variable-rank or non-smooth distributions.

Let $X$ be a smooth vector field on $M$. A smooth curve
$\gamma:I\to M$, defined on an interval $I\subseteq\mathbb R$, is an
**integral curve** of $X$ if

$$ \gamma'(t)=X_{\gamma(t)} $$

for every $t\in I$.

If $\gamma(0)=p$, then $\gamma$ is an integral curve of $X$ **through** $p$.

Let $e=(e_1,\ldots,e_r)$ be a local frame of $E$ on an open set $U$, in the sense of [[def-local-frame-and-global-frame-of-a-vector-bundle]]. Restrict a given connection to $U$ by [[lem-a-bundle-connection-is-local-and-restricts-to-open-sets]]. Its **connection one-form in the frame $e$** is the matrix $\omega=(\omega^i{}_j)$ of scalar one-forms on $U$ characterized by
$$\nabla_X e_j=\sum_i\omega^i{}_j(X)e_i.$$
For each $j$, the smooth Hom section $\nabla e_j$ has unique fibre coordinates in $e$; these coordinates are linear in the direction and smooth, hence are scalar one-forms. Smoothness may be tested in any coordinate chart and frame, using [[prop-smoothness-of-a-section-is-equivalent-to-smooth-local-components]].

Our convention treats $e$ as a row and the coefficients $u$ of $s=eu$ as a column. A frame change is $e'=eA$ with a smooth invertible matrix $A$, so $u=Au'$ for the same section. Products of matrices and one-forms use ordinary matrix multiplication with scalar functions as coefficients. In a coordinate chart, $\omega^i{}_j=\sum_k\Gamma^i{}_{kj}\,dx^k$; this notation does not assert tensorial transformation for $\Gamma$.

For rank zero the frame and connection matrix are empty; for rank one $\omega$ is a scalar one-form. On a zero-dimensional base every one-form is zero. The frame is supplied locally, so this definition involves no global selection or existence theorem.

Let $e=(e_1,\ldots,e_r)$ be a local frame, let $\omega=(\omega^i{}_j)$ be
its connection matrix, and let $\Omega=(\Omega^i{}_j)$ be the matrix of the
curvature two-form, defined by
$R^\nabla(X,Y)e_j=\Omega^i{}_j(X,Y)e_i$. Then

$$\Omega=d\omega+\omega\wedge\omega,$$

where multiplication order is fixed by

$$(\omega\wedge\omega)^i{}_j=\sum_k\omega^i{}_k\wedge\omega^k{}_j.$$

Every supplied smooth Riemannian metric on a smooth manifold, including a manifold with boundary, has exactly one Levi–Civita connection. The construction adds no choice assumption.

For a supplied Riemannian metric $g$, a **Levi–Civita connection** is an affine connection on $TM$ that is both metric compatible and torsion free, in the senses of [[def-affine-connection-on-a-smooth-manifold]], [[def-metric-compatible-connection-on-a-riemannian-vector-bundle]] and [[def-torsion-tensor-of-an-affine-connection]]. Thus for all local fields
$$Xg(Y,Z)=g(
abla_XY,Z)+g(Y,
abla_XZ),\qquad 
abla_XY-
abla_YX=[X,Y].$$
Existence and uniqueness are proved below from the supplied metric by the Koszul formula. This definition does not choose an arbitrary connection first and does not assume the general connection-existence theorem. In dimension zero the unique tangent-bundle connection satisfies both identities; in dimension one torsion freeness alone imposes no restriction, so metric compatibility remains essential.

Let $(M,g)$ be a Riemannian manifold, let $\nabla$ be its unique
Levi–Civita connection, and let $R$ be the curvature tensor with the sign fixed
above. The **Riemann curvature four-tensor** is the covariant tensor

$$\operatorname{Rm}(X,Y,Z,W):=g(R(X,Y)Z,W).$$

Thus the first two arguments are the two differentiating slots, the third is
the field acted on, and the fourth lowers the output index. In coordinates,
if $R(\partial_i,\partial_j)\partial_k=R^m{}_{kij}\partial_m$, then
$R_{ijkl}=g_{lm}R^m{}_{kij}$ under this argument order. This convention makes
$\operatorname{Rm}(u,v,v,u)$ positive on a positively curved round sphere.

The definition uses no chosen frame. On an empty or zero-dimensional manifold
it gives the unique zero four-tensor; in dimension one the same formula applies
and later symmetries force it to vanish. It is valid up to the boundary when a
Riemannian manifold with boundary is supplied.

For $\omega\in\Omega^k(M)$, define the candidate $d\omega$ on smooth vector fields by $$d\omega(X_0,\ldots,X_k)=\sum_i(-1)^iX_i\omega(X_0,\widehat X_i,\ldots,X_k)+\sum_{i<j}(-1)^{i+j}\omega([X_i,X_j],X_0,\widehat X_i,\widehat X_j,\ldots,X_k).$$ The next lemma proves that this candidate is a form.

Let $\alpha\in\Omega^k(M)$ and $\beta\in\Omega^\ell(M)$. Their **wedge product**
is the differential form defined pointwise by

$$ (\alpha\wedge\beta)_p:=\alpha_p\wedge\beta_p\in\operatorname{Alt}^{k+\ell}(T_pM). $$

The next proposition verifies that this pointwise field is smooth.
For every differential form $\omega$, $d(d\omega)=0$.
For every vector field $X$ and differential form $\omega$, $$\mathcal L_X\omega=d(\iota_X\omega)+\iota_X(d\omega).$$
Every closed smooth $k$-form on a star-shaped open domain is exact for $k\ge1$. For centre $0$, one primitive is $\eta_x(v_1,\ldots,v_{k-1})=\int_0^1t^{k-1}\omega_{tx}(x,v_1,\ldots,v_{k-1})\,dt$.

Let $(A,V,\eta,C^+)$ be an oriented time-oriented affine Minkowski space ([[def-sr-affine-minkowski-model]]), let $U\subseteq A$ be a nonempty open subset which, with the topology of [[lem-affine-minkowski-charts-form-a-smooth-atlas]], is path-connected and simply connected ([[def-simply-connected]]), and let $\alpha$ be a $C^1$ one-form on $U$ with $d\alpha=0$ ([[def-closed-and-exact-differential-forms]]); here closedness of a $C^1$ one-form means that in an inertial chart ([[def-inertial-frame-and-inertial-chart]]) one has $\alpha=\sum_{i=0}^3 a_i\,dx^i$ with $\partial_i a_j=\partial_j a_i$, the exterior derivative being understood by this coefficient formula ([[def-exterior-derivative-by-the-invariant-vector-field-formula]], [[thm-local-coordinate-formula-for-the-exterior-derivative]]). Then:

(a) there is a $C^2$ function $F:U\to\mathbb R$ with $dF=\alpha$;

(b) for any two piecewise-$C^1$ paths $\gamma_0,\gamma_1$ in $U$ ([[def-piecewise-c1-path-connected-conservative-and-path-independent]]) with the same endpoints, the integrals of $\alpha$ along them are equal, and consequently the integral of $\alpha$ along every piecewise-$C^1$ loop in $U$ vanishes.

If $\alpha$ is smooth, $F$ may be taken smooth.

**Conventions (what the objects mean here).** Fix one inertial chart $x:A\to\mathbb R^4$ and put $\Omega:=x(U)\subseteq\mathbb R^4$; by [[lem-affine-minkowski-charts-form-a-smooth-atlas]] the chart $x$ is a diffeomorphism of $A$ onto $\mathbb R^4$ carrying the model's topology, and every other inertial chart $x'$ satisfies $x'=M^{-1}(x-b)$ for an invertible matrix $M$ and a vector $b$. The $C^1$ one-form $\alpha$ is represented in the chart as $\alpha=\sum_{i=0}^3 a_i\,dx^i$ with coefficient functions $a_i:\Omega\to\mathbb R$ of class $C^1$; write $A:=(a_0,a_1,a_2,a_3):\Omega\to\mathbb R^4$ for the coefficient field, so that $A$ is $C^1$ and closedness reads $\partial_i a_j=\partial_j a_i$ on $\Omega$. For a piecewise-$C^1$ path $\gamma$ in $U$ the integral is $\int_\gamma\alpha:=\int_{x\circ\gamma}A\cdot d\mathbf r$, the vector-field line integral of [[def-scalar-and-vector-line-integrals-along-piecewise-c1-paths]]. For a $C^1$ function $F:U\to\mathbb R$ with $\tilde F:=F\circ x^{-1}$, the differential $dF$ is the one-form whose chart coefficients are the partial derivatives $\partial_i\tilde F$, and $dF=\alpha$ means $\partial_i\tilde F=a_i$ on $\Omega$ for all $i$. Under the transition $x'=M^{-1}(x-b)$ the chain rule gives $a'_j=\sum_i M^i_j a_i$, $\partial_j\tilde F'=\sum_i M^i_j\,\partial_i\tilde F$ and $(x'\circ\gamma)'=M^{-1}(x\circ\gamma)'$, so the integral $\int_\gamma\alpha$ and the identity $dF=\alpha$ do not depend on which inertial chart is used; likewise, $F$ being $C^2$, respectively smooth, is chart-independent. It therefore suffices to prove the following statement about the open set $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^4$ and the $C^1$ closed field $A$: every closed piecewise-$C^1$ path in $\Omega$ has zero $A$-integral, the $A$-integral is path-independent on $\Omega$, and there is a $C^2$ function $\tilde F$ on $\Omega$ with $\nabla\tilde F=A$ which can be taken smooth when $A$ is smooth.

For the complex [[def-de-rham-cochain-complex]], put $Z^k(M)=\ker(d:\Omega^k(M)\to\Omega^{k+1}(M))$ and $B^k(M)=\operatorname{im}(d:\Omega^{k-1}(M)\to\Omega^k(M))$. A form is **closed** if it belongs to $Z^k$ and **exact** if it belongs to $B^k$.

If $\omega=d\eta$, then $d\omega=d^2\eta=0$ by [[thm-the-exterior-derivative-squares-to-zero]], so $B^k\subseteq Z^k$. In particular $B^0=0$, since $\Omega^{-1}=0$. The zero form is both closed and exact in every degree.

Let $(v_0,\ldots,v_{r-1})$ be a finite linearly independent list in a real or complex inner product space. There is an orthonormal list $(e_0,\ldots,e_{r-1})$ such that, for every $k\le r$,

$$\operatorname{span}(e_0,\ldots,e_{k-1})=\operatorname{span}(v_0,\ldots,v_{k-1}).$$

It is obtained recursively from

$$u_k=v_k-\sum_{j<k}\langle v_k,e_j\rangle e_j,\qquad e_k=\frac{u_k}{\lVert u_k\rVert}.$$

For $r=0$, both lists are empty.

In ZF, let $n\ge1$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open, let $f:U\to\mathbb R^n$ be smooth, and let $a\in U$. If $Df(a)$ is invertible, then there are open neighbourhoods $a\in V\subseteq U$ and $f(a)\in W$ such that $f|_V:V\to W$ is a diffeomorphism. Writing $g=(f|_V)^{-1}$,
$$Dg(y)=Df(g(y))^{-1}\qquad(y\in W).$$
No choice axiom is used.

If $X$ has local flow $\Phi_t$ and $T$ is a smooth tensor field of type $(r,s)$, its Lie derivative is $$\mathcal L_XT=\left.\frac d{dt}\right|_{t=0}\Phi_t^*T,$$ on every local flow domain where this derivative is defined. Here the pullback by the local diffeomorphism $\Phi_t$ acts by $d\Phi_{-t}$ on each contravariant slot and by $d\Phi_t$ on each covariant slot.

Let $X$ be a smooth vector field on $M$.  For $\omega\in\Omega^k(M)$,
$\mathcal L_X\omega$ is the Lie derivative of $\omega$ regarded as an
alternating covariant tensor.

Let $X$ be a smooth vector field with maximal flow $\Phi$, and let $Y$ be another
smooth vector field on $M$. The **Lie derivative of $Y$ along $X$** is the vector
field defined by

$$ (\mathcal L_XY)_p:=\left.\frac{d}{dt}\right|_{t=0} (\Phi_{-t})_*Y_{\Phi_t(p)}. $$

The inverse-time pushforward is the sign convention that later yields
$\mathcal L_XY=[X,Y]$.

Let $X$ and $Y$ be smooth vector fields on $M$. Their **Lie bracket** is the
operator on smooth functions defined by

$$ [X,Y]f:=X(Yf)-Y(Xf). $$

The next results show that this commutator is again induced by a smooth vector
field on $M$.

Let $X$ be a smooth vector field on $M$. A smooth curve
$\gamma:I\to M$, defined on an interval $I\subseteq\mathbb R$, is an
**integral curve** of $X$ if

$$ \gamma'(t)=X_{\gamma(t)} $$

for every $t\in I$.

If $\gamma(0)=p$, then $\gamma$ is an integral curve of $X$ **through** $p$.

For every point $p\in M$ and every smooth vector field $X$ on $M$, there is a
unique maximal integral curve $\gamma_p:I_p\to M$ of $X$ with $\gamma_p(0)=p$.

Let $f:U\to V\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be totally differentiable at $a\in U$ and let $g:V\to\mathbb R^p$ be totally differentiable at $f(a)$. Then $g\circ f$ is totally differentiable at $a$ and

$$D(g\circ f)(a)=Dg(f(a))\circ Df(a).$$

Throughout, $\mathbb{R}$ is the complete ordered field
([[def-complete-ordered-field]]), neighbourhoods are those of
[[def-neighbourhood-r]] and limit points those of [[def-limit-point-r]].

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $f : A \to \mathbb{R}$ and let $c \in A$ be a
**limit point of $A$**. The **difference quotient of $f$ at $c$** is the function

$$q_{f,c} : A \setminus \{c\} \to \mathbb{R}, \qquad q_{f,c}(x) := \frac{f(x) - f(c)}{x - c} .$$

The division is legitimate at every point of the domain, since $x \ne c$ gives
$x - c \ne 0$.

**The point $c$ is a limit point of $A \setminus \{c\}$, not merely of $A$.**
For every real $\varepsilon > 0$ the punctured neighbourhood
$N^{*}_{\varepsilon}(c)$ omits $c$, so

$$N^{*}_{\varepsilon}(c) \cap A \;=\; N^{*}_{\varepsilon}(c) \cap (A \setminus \{c\}) ,$$

and the left-hand side is nonempty because $c$ is a limit point of $A$. So
$q_{f,c}$ is a function on a set having $c$ as a limit point, and
$\lim_{x \to c} q_{f,c}(x)$ is a notion that [[def-function-limit]] defines.

$f$ is **differentiable at $c$** when that limit exists, and then the
**derivative of $f$ at $c$** is

$$f'(c) \;:=\; \lim_{x \to c} q_{f,c}(x) \;=\; \lim_{x \to c} \frac{f(x) - f(c)}{x - c} .$$

**Two obligations are carried by that notation, and both are discharged here.**

1. **Uniqueness.** Writing $f'(c)$ treats the right-hand side as a name for a
   single real number. That is legitimate: $c$ is a limit point of the domain
   $A \setminus \{c\}$ of $q_{f,c}$, so at most one real can satisfy the
   $\varepsilon$-$\delta$ condition, by [[lem-function-limit-unique]] applied to
   $q_{f,c}$. Two reals both meeting the condition are therefore equal, and the
   symbol denotes.
2. **Meaningfulness.** The hypothesis that $c$ is a limit point of $A$ is not
   decoration. At an **isolated** point of $A$ the punctured condition
   $0 < |x - c| < \delta$ is met by no point of the domain at all, so the
   $\varepsilon$-$\delta$ formula is satisfied vacuously by *every* real at
   once; this is why [[def-function-limit]] leaves the limit undefined there,
   and it is why this library defines $f'(c)$ only at a limit point of $A$. At
   an isolated point of its domain a function is neither differentiable nor
   non-differentiable here: the question is not posed.

**The limit sees only $A \setminus \{c\}$, so how the difference quotient is
extended to $c$ is irrelevant.** Let $Q : A \to \mathbb{R}$ agree with
$q_{f,c}$ at every point of $A \setminus \{c\}$, and let $L \in \mathbb{R}$.
Then $\lim_{x \to c} Q(x) = L$ if and only if $\lim_{x \to c} q_{f,c}(x) = L$.
Both conditions read: for every real $\varepsilon > 0$ there is a real
$\delta > 0$ such that every point $x$ of the relevant domain with
$0 < |x - c| < \delta$ satisfies $|{\cdot} - L| < \varepsilon$
([[def-function-limit]]). The clause $0 < |x - c|$ removes $x = c$ from both
quantifiers, so in both cases the points quantified over are exactly the
$x \in A \setminus \{c\}$ with $0 < |x - c| < \delta$, at which $Q$ and
$q_{f,c}$ take the same value. The two conditions are the same condition.

**Differentiability on a set.** For $S \subseteq A$, $f$ is **differentiable on
$S$** when it is differentiable at every $c \in S$; implicit in that phrase is
that every point of $S$ is a limit point of $A$. $f$ is **differentiable** when
it is differentiable on the whole of $A$.

**Restriction of the domain.** Let $B \subseteq A$, let $c \in B$ and suppose
$c$ is a limit point of $B$. If $f$ is differentiable at $c$, then so is the
restriction $f|_B : B \to \mathbb{R}$, and

$$(f|_B)'(c) \;=\; f'(c) .$$

Indeed $B \setminus \{c\} \subseteq A \setminus \{c\}$; the displayed identity
of punctured neighbourhoods above, applied to $B$, shows that $c$ is a limit
point of $B \setminus \{c\}$; the difference quotient $q_{f|_B, c}$ is the
restriction of $q_{f,c}$ to $B \setminus \{c\}$, since $f|_B(c) = f(c)$; and
claim 2 of [[lem-limit-is-local]] carries the limit to that restriction.

**Every point of a nondegenerate interval is a limit point of it.** Let
$J \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ be order-convex ([[def-interval]]) with at least two
elements and let $p \in J$. Choose $q \in J$ with $q \ne p$, and let a real
$\varepsilon > 0$ be given. If $p < q$, put $y := p + \tfrac{1}{2}\min\{\varepsilon,\ q - p\}$;
then $p < y$, and $y - p \le \tfrac{1}{2}(q-p) < q - p$, so $p < y < q$ and
order-convexity gives $y \in J$, while $0 < |y - p| < \varepsilon$. If $q < p$,
the point $y := p - \tfrac{1}{2}\min\{\varepsilon,\ p - q\}$ serves in the same
way. So $N^{*}_{\varepsilon}(p) \cap J \ne \varnothing$ for every real
$\varepsilon > 0$, that is, $p$ is a limit point of $J$
([[def-limit-point-r]]).

Consequently, for $f$ defined on a nondegenerate interval $I$, the symbol
$f'(c)$ is meaningful at **every** $c \in I$, endpoints included. At an endpoint
the difference quotient is taken over the points of $I$ lying on the one side
that is available, so what other texts call a one-sided derivative is, here,
simply the derivative of $f$ on $I$.

Let $(A,V,\eta,C^{+})$ be an oriented time-oriented affine Minkowski space
([[def-sr-affine-minkowski-model]]) and let $I$ be an order-convex subset of
$\mathbb{R}$ with at least two elements ([[def-interval]]); a **curve** of the
model is a map $x : I \to A$.

### Derivative and regularity of the parametrization

For $s \in I$ and $h \ne 0$ with $s+h \in I$ the **difference quotient**
$\bigl(x(s+h)-x(s)\bigr)/h$ is an element of $V$, the displacement from $x(s)$
to $x(s+h)$ divided by the real number $h$
([[def-sr-affine-minkowski-model]]). Convergence in $V$ is understood through
an inertial frame: for the frame isomorphism $E : \mathbb{R}^{4} \to V$ of an
inertial frame ([[def-inertial-frame-and-inertial-chart]]) put
$|v|_{E} := |E^{-1}v|_{2}$, the Euclidean norm transported by $E$. If $E'$ is
the isomorphism of another inertial frame, then $E'^{-1}E$ and its inverse are
linear maps $\mathbb{R}^{4} \to \mathbb{R}^{4}$, so they are bounded with
constants $K, K' \ge 0$ ([[lem-euclidean-linear-maps-have-matrices-and-are-bounded]]):
$|v|_{E'} \le K'\,|v|_{E}$ and $|v|_{E} \le K\,|v|_{E'}$ for all $v \in V$.
The two transported norms are therefore equivalent, give the same limits, and
give the same notion of differentiability. The curve is **differentiable at
$s$** when the limit of the difference quotients as $h \to 0$ (over
$h \ne 0$, $s+h \in I$; one-sided at the endpoints of $I$) exists in $V$; then
this limit, written $x'(s) \in V$, is the **tangent vector** of $x$ at $s$, and
it does not depend on the inertial frame used to describe the convergence.

If $x_A : A \to \mathbb{R}^{4}$ is the global chart of an inertial frame
([[def-inertial-frame-and-inertial-chart]], [[lem-affine-minkowski-charts-form-a-smooth-atlas]]),
then $x$ is differentiable at $s$ exactly when the $\mathbb{R}^{4}$-valued map
$x_A \circ x$ is differentiable at $s$ in the sense of
[[def-vector-valued-derivative-and-integral]], because $E^{-1}$ is linear and
carries the difference quotients of $x$ to those of $x_A \circ x$; and then

$$x'(s) = E\bigl((x_A \circ x)'(s)\bigr),$$

where $E : \mathbb{R}^{4} \to V$ is the frame isomorphism
$E(u) = \sum_{a} u^{a} e_{a}$. This value does not depend on the inertial chart
used: two inertial charts are related by an affine bijection with an invertible
linear part ([[lem-affine-minkowski-charts-form-a-smooth-atlas]]), the chain
rule transports the coordinate derivative accordingly, and all norms on the
finite-dimensional space $V$ give the same limit.

The curve is **$C^{1}$** when it is differentiable at every point of $I$ and
the derivative map $s \mapsto x'(s)$, $I \to V$, is continuous, meaning that
the $\mathbb{R}^{4}$-valued map $s \mapsto (x_A \circ x)'(s)$ is continuous
([[def-vector-valued-functions-limits-and-continuity]]); by the equivalence of
transported norms this condition is independent of the inertial frame. It is
**$C^{k}$** for $k \ge 1$ when the derivative map is $C^{k-1}$, with the same
transported reading. A curve on a compact interval $[a,b]$ contained
in $I$ is **piecewise $C^{1}$** when there is a finite partition
$a = s_0 < s_1 < \cdots < s_m = b$ such that $x$ is $C^{1}$ on every open
subinterval $(s_{i-1},s_i)$ and the finite one-sided difference-quotient
derivatives at both ends of every piece exist in $V$. These are limits of
$\bigl(x(t+h)-x(t)\bigr)/h$ over the relevant side of the piece, not assertions
that $x'(s)$ has a limit as $s$ approaches a corner; their finiteness implies
continuity of $x$ at the corners (for a one-sided quotient derivative $v$ at $t$
one has $x(t+h)-x(t) = h\,(v+o(1))$ as $h \to 0$ on that side). No continuous
extension of the open-piece derivative is required. Derivatives at the endpoints
of $I$ are the one-sided difference-quotient limits over $I$.

### Causal character

Let $x$ be differentiable at $s \in I$. Then $x$ is **regular at $s$** if
$x'(s) \ne 0$; $x$ is **timelike** (respectively **null**, **spacelike**,
**causal**) **at $s$** if the vector $x'(s)$ is timelike (respectively null,
spacelike, causal) in the sense of
[[def-causal-classification-of-lorentz-vectors]], and $x$ is
**future-directed at $s$** if $x'(s)$ is future timelike or future null in the
sense of [[def-time-orientation-and-future-causal-sets]]. The zero vector has
no causal character, so only a regular curve has a causal character at $s$.

### Worldlines

A **future timelike worldline** (equivalently, a **massive worldline**) is a
$C^{1}$ curve $x : I \to A$ with $x'(s)$ future timelike for every $s \in I$; a
**future causal curve** (respectively a **future null curve**) is a $C^{1}$
curve with $x'(s)$ future causal (respectively future null) for every
$s \in I$. A **piecewise $C^{1}$ worldline** is a piecewise $C^{1}$ curve whose
tangents at every point of each open smooth piece and whose finite one-sided
difference-quotient tangents at both endpoints of every piece are future
timelike; a **$C^{k}$ worldline** is a worldline whose parametrization is
$C^{k}$. $C^{2}$ regularity is what makes the four-acceleration of
[[def-sr-four-velocity-and-four-acceleration]] available.

The parametrization is part of the curve: the image of a future timelike
worldline is also the image of the past-directed curve $s \mapsto x(-s)$, which
is not a worldline of this model, and no worldline or clock claim is attached to
it. The definition asserts the existence of no worldline beyond those given by
an explicit formula.

Let $(V,\eta)$ be a Lorentz vector space of signature $(-,+,+,+)$
([[def-lorentz-form-and-inertia]]), with associated quadratic form
$q(v)=\eta(v,v)$. A vector $v\in V$ is

- **timelike** when $q(v)<0$;
- **null**, or **lightlike**, when $v\neq 0$ and $q(v)=0$;
- **spacelike** when $q(v)>0$;
- **causal** when it is timelike or null.

The zero vector $0\in V$ satisfies $q(0)=0$ and is consequently **none** of
timelike, null or spacelike: the null case explicitly excludes it, and the
timelike and spacelike cases exclude it by $q(0)=0$ together with the strict
inequalities. The **causal character** of a nonzero vector $v$ is the sign of
the real number $q(v)$, and the three names are attached to the three signs as
above. When no confusion arises, the pairing $\eta$ itself is written
$\langle v,w\rangle:=\eta(v,w)$.

**Each nonzero vector has exactly one causal character.** For a nonzero
$v\in V$ the real number $q(v)$ satisfies exactly one of $q(v)<0$, $q(v)=0$,
$q(v)>0$ by trichotomy of the order on $\mathbb R$, so $v$ is timelike, null or
spacelike, and no two of the three alternatives can hold at once. The causal
vectors are therefore exactly the nonzero vectors that are timelike or null,
and the zero vector is causal in no sense introduced here.

Let $(V,\eta)$ be a Lorentz vector space of signature $(-,+,+,+)$
([[def-lorentz-form-and-inertia]]), with causal terminology as in
[[def-causal-classification-of-lorentz-vectors]], and let

$$T:=\{v\in V:\eta(v,v)<0\}$$

be its **timelike set**. Components and closures refer to the topology obtained
by using any ordered basis to identify $V$ with Euclidean $\mathbb R^4$;
[[lem-timelike-cone-has-two-convex-components]], step 5.1, proves that the
resulting open sets are independent of the basis. By that lemma the
set $T$ has exactly two connected components, and each of them is nonempty,
open, convex and path-connected. A **time orientation** of $(V,\eta)$ is a
choice of one of these two components. Fixing such a choice, write $C^+$ for the
chosen component and

$$C^-:=T\setminus C^+$$

for the other component; thus $T=C^+\sqcup C^-$ is a disjoint union and
$C^+$, $C^-$ are exactly the two components supplied by the lemma. Relative to
this choice a vector $v\in V$ is

- **future timelike** when $v\in C^+$;
- **past timelike** when $v\in C^-$;
- **future null** when $v\neq 0$, $\eta(v,v)=0$ and $v\in\operatorname{cl}(C^+)$;
- **past null** when $v\neq 0$, $\eta(v,v)=0$ and $v\in\operatorname{cl}(C^-)$;
- **future causal** when it is future timelike or future null;
- **past causal** when it is past timelike or past null.

The sets $\operatorname{cl}(C^+)$ and $\operatorname{cl}(C^-)$ are the
**future closed cone** and the **past closed cone** of the time-oriented space
$(V,\eta,C^+)$. By [[lem-timelike-cone-has-two-convex-components]] each of them
is a convex cone, their intersection is $\{0\}$, and a vector is causal exactly
when it is future causal or past causal, in which case exactly one of these two
alternatives holds: no nonzero vector is both future causal and past causal.
The timelike vectors are exactly the points of $T=C^+\cup C^-$, and
$0\notin T$ because $\eta(0,0)=0$; since a null vector is nonzero with
$\eta(v,v)=0$, no vector is both timelike and null, so the classes above are
mutually exclusive where the definitions say they are: no vector is both future
and past causal, and no timelike vector is null.

Let $f:U\to V\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be totally differentiable at $a\in U$ and let $g:V\to\mathbb R^p$ be totally differentiable at $f(a)$. Then $g\circ f$ is totally differentiable at $a$ and

$$D(g\circ f)(a)=Dg(f(a))\circ Df(a).$$

Let $\Omega$ be a nonempty open subset of $A$ ([[def-sr-affine-minkowski-model]]).

**(i) Flow box.** If $X$ is a smooth vector field on $\Omega$ ([[def-ck-tensor-field-on-minkowski-space]]) and $X(p)\ne0$ at a point $p\in\Omega$, then there is an open neighbourhood $U$ of $p$ in $\Omega$ and a chart $(u^0,u^1,u^2,u^3):U\to\mathbb R^4$ in which $X=\partial/\partial u^0$; the integral curves of $X$ in $U$ are therefore the $u^0$-coordinate lines up to reparametrization. In particular every observer congruence $n$ on $\Omega$ ([[def-sr-chart-tetrad-and-congruence-distinction]]) admits a local $n$-adapted chart, and in such a chart $n=\partial/\partial u^0$.

**(ii) Frobenius criterion.** For a smooth nowhere-zero one-form $\alpha$ on $\Omega$ ([[def-closed-and-exact-differential-forms]]) let $D:=\ker\alpha$ be the hyperplane distribution $D_p=\{v\in V:\alpha_p(v)=0\}$. Then $D$ is integrable on $\Omega$ (through every point there passes a local hypersurface whose tangent space at each of its points is the corresponding $D_p$) if and only if $\alpha\wedge d\alpha=0$ on $\Omega$ ([[def-wedge-product-of-differential-forms]]).

**(iii) Rest distributions of observer congruences.** Let $n$ be an observer congruence on $\Omega$ ([[def-sr-chart-tetrad-and-congruence-distinction]]), let $\alpha:=n^\flat$, and let $\theta,\omega$ be its expansion and vorticity ([[def-sr-observer-congruence-and-kinematics]]). Then:

(a) $d\alpha=2\nabla_{[a}n_{b]}$, that is, $d\alpha(X,Y)=(\nabla_Xn^\flat)(Y)-(\nabla_Yn^\flat)(X)$ for smooth vector fields $X,Y$;

(b) for every $p$ and all $X,Y$ with $\alpha(X)=\alpha(Y)=0$ one has $d\alpha(X,Y)=2\omega(X,Y)$; consequently $(\alpha\wedge d\alpha)(p)=0$ if and only if $\omega(p)=0$, and on an open set $U\subseteq\Omega$ the following are equivalent: $\alpha\wedge d\alpha=0$ on $U$, $\omega=0$ on $U$, and the rest distribution $\ker\alpha$ is integrable on $U$;

(c) when the rest distribution is integrable on $U$, its integral hypersurfaces are orthogonal to $n$ at every point and the restriction of $\eta$ to each of them is positive definite, so they are rest slices of the congruence.

**(iv) Scope.** All statements are local on $\Omega$; no global foliation, global synchronization, completeness or product structure is asserted, and no claim is made about variable-rank or non-smooth distributions.

Let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ be open and let $f:U\to\mathbb R^n$. Suppose every partial derivative $\partial_jf$ exists on a neighbourhood of $a\in U$ and is continuous at $a$. Then $f$ is totally differentiable at $a$, and $Df(a)$ is the linear map with matrix $Jf(a)$.

Let $m\ge1$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ be open, and let $f:U\to\mathbb R$. A **multi-index** is $\alpha=(\alpha_0,\ldots,\alpha_{m-1})\in\mathbb N^m$. Put

$$|\alpha|:=\sum_{i<m}\alpha_i,\qquad \alpha!:=\prod_{i<m}\alpha_i!,\qquad h^\alpha:=\prod_{i<m}h_i^{\alpha_i}\quad(h\in\mathbb R^m).$$

Here $|\alpha|$ and $\alpha!$ use the natural-number sum and product of [[def-nat-finite-sum-and-product]], and $n!$ is the factorial of [[def-factorial-and-falling-factorial]]. By contrast, $h^\alpha$ is the finite product in $\mathbb R$ of [[def-finite-sum]], with the natural exponents interpreted by [[def-integer-power]]. For the zero multi-index $0$, set $D^0f:=f$. For nonzero $\alpha$, write

$$D^\alpha f:=\partial_0^{\alpha_0}\cdots\partial_{m-1}^{\alpha_{m-1}}f$$

for this displayed, canonical order whenever it exists. Coordinate partial derivatives have the meaning fixed in [[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]].

For $k\in\mathbb N$, $f$ is of class $C^k$ on $U$ when, for every word $(i_1,\ldots,i_r)$ of coordinate indices with $0\le r\le k$, the iterated derivative $\partial_{i_r}\cdots\partial_{i_1}f$ exists and is continuous on $U$; the word of length $0$ denotes $f$. Thus this definition does **not** presuppose that differently ordered derivatives are equal. Equality of their values is a later theorem under these regularity hypotheses.

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $c \in A$ be a limit point of $A$
([[def-limit-point-r]]), let $f, g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at $c$
([[def-derivative]]) and let $\alpha \in \mathbb{R}$. Then:

1. $f + g$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(f+g)'(c) = f'(c) + g'(c)$;
2. $\alpha f$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(\alpha f)'(c) = \alpha f'(c)$;
3. $fg$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(fg)'(c) = f'(c)g(c) + f(c)g'(c)$;
4. if $g(c) \ne 0$ then, writing $A_0 := \{\, x \in A : g(x) \ne 0 \,\}$, the
   point $c$ lies in $A_0$ and is a limit point of $A_0$, the quotient
   $(f/g)|_{A_0} : A_0 \to \mathbb{R}$, $x \mapsto f(x)/g(x)$, is differentiable
   at $c$ as a function on $A_0$, and
   $$\bigl((f/g)|_{A_0}\bigr)'(c) \;=\; \frac{f'(c)\,g(c) - f(c)\,g'(c)}{g(c)^{2}} .$$

Each claim asserts two things: that the derivative on the left exists, and that
it has the stated value. Both are proved.

**Why claim 4 is stated on $A_0$.** The function $f/g$ is not defined where $g$
vanishes, and $g$ may vanish at points of $A$ far from $c$; restricting to $A_0$
is forced. That the restriction still has $c$ as a limit point, so that a
derivative there means anything at all, is not free either, and it is the last
claim of [[lem-sign-preservation-near-a-limit]] applied to $g$. The hypothesis
is $g(c) \ne 0$, not "$g$ vanishes nowhere".

**Everything is proved through
[[thm-caratheodory-characterisation]].** No difference quotient is estimated and
no limit theorem beyond continuity is used, so no choice principle is spent.
The four identities are four algebraic rearrangements of an increment, each
followed by a reading of [[thm-algebra-of-continuous-functions]].

The real exponential function is $C^\infty$, and for every $m\in\mathbb N$,
$$\exp^{(m)}=\exp.$$
In particular $(\exp)'=\exp$.

$$\exp:\mathbb R\longrightarrow(0,\infty)$$
is a bijection.

Let $f$ be defined on a disk $U$ about $(a,b)$, with $f_x$ and $f_y$ existing on $U$. If $f_x$ and $f_y$ are totally differentiable at $(a,b)$, then both mixed partials exist there and $f_{xy}(a,b)=f_{yx}(a,b)$.

Put $f:=1/\varphi>0$, so $K=fn$. By [F10], $0=\mathcal L_K\eta=\mathcal L_{fn}\eta=f\mathcal L_n\eta+df\otimes n^\flat+n^\flat\otimes df$, and by step 10.1, $\mathcal L_n\eta=2\theta-(n^\flat\otimes a^\flat+a^\flat\otimes n^\flat)$ where $\theta,a$ are the expansion and acceleration of $n$. Evaluating on two smooth horizontal fields $Y,Z$ kills the terms containing $n^\flat$ and gives $0=2f\,\theta(Y,Z)$; since $f>0$, $\theta=0$ and $n$ is Born rigid.

Conclusion: step 1.1 proves clause (i); steps 1.2, 1.3 and 2.1 construct the adapted coframe and frame; steps 3.2, 4.2 and 4.3 compute the connection forms and the differential of $\theta^0$; steps 5.2 and 6.1 extract the flatness equations and the curvature identity for the slice; step 7.1 proves that the vorticity is basic; steps 5.1 and 8.1 prove the mixed identity and that the acceleration is basic; step 9.1 proves $da^\flat=0$; and step 10.1 produces the positive Killing rescaling both on the coordinate box (Poincare primitive in its coordinate image) and on connected simply connected $U$ (primitive of the closed one-form), completing clause (ii); steps 1.4 and 2.2 prove the rotational/irrotational dichotomy of the vorticity and step 11.1 the Born rigidity of normalized Killing fields; steps 2.3, 3.1 and 4.1 prove clause (iii) in both directions; and clause (iv) records the local scope, the absence of any global orbit quotient or completeness assertion, and the fact that the argument uses no choice principle (the only inverse-function input is the choice-free Euclidean theorem of [F9], and all other suppliers are choice-free).

boundaries.evidence: The theorem is local on a nonempty open $\Omega$ with a smooth nowhere-zero field $n$; the flow boxes and the simply-connected region are nonempty by hypothesis. This disposition is part of the statement.
Zero-vorticity cases are separated: the irrotational branch (clause (iii)) is treated by the tubular construction, and step 3.1 proves the dichotomy $\omega\equiv0$ or $\omega$ nowhere zero.
Clause (ii) is the rotational case with $\omega$ nowhere zero; the positive rescaling $f=e^F$ is a single function on the flow box or simply-connected $U$. This disposition is part of the statement.

The degenerate rank cases of the constant Killing form are analysed in step 3.1: rank $0$, $2$ or $4$, excluding the possibility of a rank-4 form annihilating a three-plane and reducing the rank-2 case to the affine normal $u_\perp$.
The arguments are local on flow boxes and open simply-connected sets; no interval endpoint occurs, and the scope clause (iv) records the local limitation. This disposition is part of the statement.

The only inverse-function input is the choice-free Euclidean theorem, and the primitive of the closed one-form is supplied by the grid-argument lemma; the scope clause records that no choice principle is used. This disposition is part of the statement.
Clause (ii) proves the forward direction: a rotational rigid motion has basic vorticity and acceleration, $da^\flat=0$, and $K=e^Fn$ is a timelike Killing field (steps 6.1-9.1).
Step 10.1 proves the converse: every future timelike Killing field, normalized to unit length, is Born rigid, and step 3.1 gives the rotational/irrotational dichotomy of its vorticity.
